chimaira.archaeology: She had no sanctuary — monsters seldom do — but her landscape survives: the natural-gas flames of Yanartaş near ancient Phaselis in Lycia have burned without fuel for millennia, and ancient writers from Ctesias to Pliny (Natural History 2.111) knew the undying fire of Mount Chimaera as a landmark for sailors. In art she is among the earliest Greek monsters, attacked by Bellerophôn and Pegasos on Corinthian and Attic vases from the seventh century BC onward, and the Etruscans cast her masterpiece — the bronze Chimaira of Arezzo (c. 400 BC), a lion with the goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail, dedicated to the god Tinia as its inscribed leg (tinścvil) records. Pausanias (2.4.1) still points out the spring Peirene at Corinth, where Bellerophôn was said to have seized the winged horse for the hunt.

phonemes.desc: [kl], a voiceless velar stop released straight into a clear lateral — a sharp, liquid onset.
The digraph ει, by the classical period a close long [eː], held steady and bright.
Long omega [ɔ́ː] bearing the acute accent: the voice rises on the final syllable and holds it long.

pronunciation.approximation: 'kleh-OH' — two syllables; keep the first short and bright, then rise and linger on the long final ō. Not the modern 'KLY-oh'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: κλέος (kleos), 'glory, fame, that which is heard of someone' — the noun behind the name; compare κλείω, 'to proclaim, celebrate'.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *ḱlew-, 'to hear' — the same root as Sanskrit śrávas ('fame') and, through Germanic, English loud.

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Clio, adopted directly into Latin poetry without alteration.

pronunciation.note: Kleiṓ is Tier 1: the Greek original Κλειώ carries both acute stress and the long vowel ω. The restoration preserves both features — the macron marking the long ō and the acute marking the accented syllable — which the ASCII form 'Kleio' loses.

domains.title: The Proclaimer of Glory
domains.subtitle: Muse of History · Memory, Fame, and the Written Record
domains.lead: Kleiṓ is the Muse of history — in Greek terms, of ἱστορία, 'inquiry, research'. First-named of the nine daughters of Zeus and Mnēmosýnē, her name is her office: from κλέος, 'glory', she is she who proclaims fame, the power that keeps great deeds from being erased by time. In art she sits with an open scroll or a chest of books — the archive made divine.

cards.name: The Written Record
cards.desc: Her unrolled scroll — the volumen of the Roman portraits — is history itself: deeds fixed against forgetting.

cards.name: The Voice of Fame
cards.desc: To proclaim, κλείειν, is to make heard; later allegory gives her the trumpet that blows renown down the generations.

cards.name: The Archive
cards.desc: The book-chest at her feet: the memory of the world, stored, ordered, and retrievable.

symbols.name: Open scroll (volumen)
symbols.meaning: Her constant attribute in Roman Muse-sarcophagi and later art: the unrolled record of human deeds.

symbols.name: Chest of books (capsa)
symbols.meaning: The archive she guards — history as something collected, ordered, and kept.

symbols.name: Writing tablets and stylus
symbols.meaning: The instruments of the recorder; ἱστορία begins as inquiry set down in notes.

symbols.name: Laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: The crown of poet and victor alike — kleos is the immortality that song confers.

symbols.name: Trumpet of Fame
symbols.meaning: A post-classical addition to her iconography: renown proclaimed across the ages.

symbols.name: The spring Hippokrene
symbols.meaning: The 'horse's spring' on Helicon, struck open by Pēgasos' hoof, sacred to Kleiṓ and her sisters (Pausanias 9.31).

mythology.lead: Kleiṓ rarely acts in myths of her own; she is the authority behind them. Her province is not adventure but memory — the fame by which every other story survives.

myths.title: Daughter of Memory
myths.text: In the Theogony (53–62) Hesiod tells how Zeus lay with Mnēmosýnē, Memory, for nine nights, and how she bore nine daughters in Pieria 'of one mind, whose hearts are set upon song'. At 76–79 he names them, and Kleiṓ stands first: 'Κλειώ τ᾽ Εὐτέρπη τε…'. Their purpose is stated plainly (Theogony 55): they were born to be 'forgetfulness of evils and rest from cares' — memory, paradoxically, as the cure of sorrow.

myths.title: The First History
myths.text: Kleiṓ's office becomes literature in the proem of Herodotus (1.1): he publishes his ἱστορίη — literally 'inquiry, research' — 'so that the deeds of men may not be erased by time, nor the great and wondrous works of Greeks and barbarians become aklea, without glory'. The word ἀκλεᾶ is her own name negated: history exists so that κλέος survives. Cicero would later call Herodotus the father of history (De Legibus 1.5), but the Greeks had already given history a Muse.

myths.title: The Mother of Hyacinthus
myths.text: Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.3.3) records that Pierus of Macedon begot Hyacinthus by Kleiṓ. The beautiful youth was loved by Apollo and killed by a ricocheting discus; from his blood sprang the flower marked with the cry of lamentation. The fuller telling is Ovid's (Metamorphoses 10.162–219). A late scholastic tradition adds that Kleiṓ had mocked Aphrodítē's passion for Adōnis and was repaid with this bitter love of her own — a rare, unhappy glimpse of the Muse drawn into a story rather than telling one.

myths.title: The Invocation of the Nine
myths.text: The Orphic Hymn to the Muses (76) calls on Kleiṓ together with her eight sisters as daughters of Zeus and Mnēmosýnē, queens of the Pierian spring, and begs them to come to the initiates bringing fame and wisdom. Here the sisterhood is one power: song, memory, and the glory that outlasts death.

kleio.syncretism: Rome received the Muses wholesale and gave them no new names: Kleiṓ became Clio, invoked by Latin poets and pictured on sarcophagi with her scroll. The native Camenae — Italic spring-nymphs equated with the Muses since Livius Andronicus rendered the Odyssey's 'Musa' as 'Camena' — absorbed the cult but never the individual names. In the Renaissance, Clio was lifted out of the sisterhood altogether and made the personification of History itself, book and trumpet in hand, in iconographic manuals such as Cesare Ripa's Iconologia.
kleio.culturalLegacy: She is the one Muse whose name became a discipline's nickname: historians still speak of 'Clio' when they mean their craft personified. The quantitative school of history that rose in the 1960s called itself cliometrics — her name wedded to measurement. The asteroid 84 Klio, discovered in 1865, carries her into the sky, and the Clio Awards borrow her proclamation for advertising. The word 'history' itself descends from her Greek province, ἱστορία, 'inquiry'.
kleio.extendedMeditation: That the Greeks made history a Muse is the fact worth pausing on: the recording of the past was not clerical work but an inspired art, daughter of Memory herself. Her parentage states a whole philosophy — Zeus begets on Mnēmosýnē the power that turns what is remembered into what is proclaimed. For κλέος was what heroes died to win, and Kleiṓ is the arbiter of it: she decides what is still heard when the generations have turned to dust. There is ambivalence in that gift, for memory selects as much as it preserves, and every archive is also an act of omission. Herodotus, her first great servant, understood this: his ἱστορίη is research in the service of fame, so that the deeds of Greeks and barbarians alike should not go aklea — ungloried, unheard.
kleio.archaeology: Kleiṓ never had a sanctuary of her own; her cult is the collective cult of the Muses. Pausanias (9.29–31) walked the Valley of the Muses below Mount Helicon and describes the sacred grove, the statues of the nine, and the springs Aganippe and Hippokrene near the festival ground where the Thespians held the Mouseia. Beyond Greece, the great Mouseion of Alexandria — literally a 'shrine of the Muses' — made the sisterhood the patronesses of scholarship itself, while Roman sarcophagi identify Kleiṓ within the Muse-choir by her unrolled scroll.

phonemes.desc: Kappa with a short iota under the acute — the pitch springs high, then the rolled rho snaps it shut, like a falcon turning on the wind.
A second kappa released into the long open eta [ɛː] — the name ends wide and held, never the English 'see'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KEER-keh' — high pitch on the first syllable, a trilled rho, and a long open final vowel; English 'SUR-see' has wandered far from the falcon's name.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: κίρκος (kírkos), 'hawk, falcon' — also 'ring, circle'; the word her name is usually traced to

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: no secure Indo-European etymology; Beekes treats Κίρκη as Pre-Greek, a divine name of the Aegean substrate

pronunciation.note: Kírkē is the boundary case of the Greek list. The Greek Κίρκη carries both features the mechanical tier rule watches for — the acute pitch of the first syllable and the long final eta — and the restoration Kírkē preserves both against the Latinized 'Circe,' which shed them. This entry follows the catalog's Tier-2 assignment; a strict reading of the rule would promote her to the first rank, and her double signature is recorded here so the classification never hardens into doctrine.

domains.title: The Dread Goddess of Aiaia
domains.subtitle: Sorcery, Transformation, and Isolation
domains.lead: Kírkē is the daughter of Hēlios and the Oceanid Perse, sister of Aiētēs and Pasiphaē, aunt of Médeia — the Sun's own child keeping house alone on Aiaia, an island at the edge of the charted world. Homer calls her a dread goddess endowed with speech (δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα) and polýpharmakos, mistress of many drugs. She is the first great enchantress of Western literature, and her wand does not kill men: it unmakes them, penning the human mind inside the bodies of beasts.

cards.name: Pharmaka
cards.desc: Her art runs through drugs: barley, cheese, and pale honey stirred into Pramneian wine, the pharmaka hidden in the food (Odyssey 10.234–235).

cards.name: Metamorphosis
cards.desc: She is the Greeks' first great thought-experiment on form: the body unmade, the mind left watching from inside the beast.

cards.name: Aiaia
cards.desc: Her island at the world's edge: Homer moors it where the dawn rises; Rome moved it west to the cape that still bears her name.

symbols.name: The wand (rhábdos)
symbols.meaning: With a single stroke she pens the crew in the sties — the original witch's wand of European literature (Odyssey 10.238)

symbols.name: The cup
symbols.meaning: Barley, cheese, and pale honey in Pramneian wine, with the pharmaka stirred into the food (Odyssey 10.234–235)

symbols.name: Swine
symbols.meaning: Her transformed company: beast in head, voice, bristle, and shape — 'but the mind remained as before' (Odyssey 10.239–243)

symbols.name: Wolves and lions
symbols.meaning: Mountain beasts charmed by her evil drugs that fawn like dogs at her door (Odyssey 10.212–219)

symbols.name: The loom
symbols.meaning: The sailors first hear her singing at a great immortal web — goddesses' work, delicate and glorious (Odyssey 10.221–223)

symbols.name: Moly
symbols.meaning: The black-rooted, milk-white-flowered herb Hermes gives against her drugs — hard for mortals to dig (Odyssey 10.302–306)

symbols.name: The falcon
symbols.meaning: Kírkos, the hawk: the word her name is usually traced to — the predator hidden inside the enchantress

mythology.lead: Kírkē's myths turn on the unstable border between human and animal — and on Homer's strangest reversal: the goddess who defeats every man she meets becomes, the hour she is beaten, the hero's most useful ally.

myths.title: The Men Made Swine
myths.text: In Odyssey 10 (208–243), Eurylochus leads twenty-two scouts to Kírkē's hall, past mountain wolves and lions that fawn like dogs — creatures she herself had charmed with evil drugs. She mixes the men a potion of barley, cheese, and pale honey in Pramneian wine, hides pharmaka in the food, strikes them with her wand, and pens them in the sties. They take the heads, the voice, the bristles, and the shape of swine — 'but their mind remained as firm as before' (10.240). Homer does not say she made them beasts; he says the men went on thinking inside the beast, the most quietly horrifying line in the poem. Odysseus comes for them armed with the moly Hermes gives him (10.275–306) — the black-rooted, milk-flowered herb that is hard for mortals to dig, but the gods can do all things.

myths.title: A Year of Feasting, Then the Road to the Dead
myths.text: Her drugs fail against the moly, and Kírkē — recognizing an old prophecy fulfilled — changes sides: she swears the great oath to plot no further harm and takes him to her bed (Odyssey 10.343–346). She restores the crew younger, taller, and fairer than before (10.388–396), and they sit a whole year feasting on abundant flesh and sweet wine (10.467–477). When Odysseus asks to leave, she does not hinder him; she gives him the voyage no living man has sailed — down to the house of Hades and dread Persephone, to consult the soul of the blind seer Teiresias (10.487–540). She names the rock where Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus fall into Acheron and prescribes the blood of a black ram and a ewe to summon the dead. The enchantress becomes the guide: the katabasis of the Odyssey is her itinerary.

myths.title: Telegonus, the Son Born from Afar
myths.text: Hesiod already knows children of the union: Kírkē, 'in love with steadfast Odysseus,' bears Agrius, Latinus, and Telegonus, 'who ruled over all the much-famed Tyrrhenians' (Theogony 1011–1016 — lines some editors bracket as post-Hesiodic, but our oldest witness to her Italian afterlife). The lost Telegony of Eugammon of Cyrene, preserved in Proclus's summary, completes the tragedy: grown Telegonus sails to find his father and, raiding a coast he does not know, kills Odysseus in ignorance with a spear tipped with a sting-ray's barb — the gentle death 'from the sea' that Teiresias foretold (Odyssey 11.134). He carries the body and Penelope home to Aiaia; Telegonus marries Penelope, Telemachus marries Kírkē herself, and the goddess makes them all immortal and sends them to the Isles of the Blest.

myths.title: The Poisoning of Scylla
myths.text: Ovid gives her the witch's cruelest afterlife. The sea-god Glaucus comes to Kírkē for a charm to win the nymph Scylla; Kírkē offers herself instead, is refused, and answers like the daughter of the Sun she is — she grinds her herbs, crosses to the pool, and poisons the water where Scylla bathes (Metamorphoses 14.1–74). Scylla rises to the waist in a ring of barking dogs and becomes the monster of the strait that will one day face Charybdis — the very Scylla whom Kírkē herself teaches Odysseus to pass (Odyssey 12.116–126). In the same book she turns the Latian king Picus into a woodpecker for loving Canens (14.320–434). Rome's Circe does not retire; she curdles the seas and forests of Italy.

circe.syncretism: Rome did not need to invent a Latin Kírkē; it simply moved her in. Hesiod had already posted her sons to the Tyrrhenian coast, and Virgil's Aeneas skirts 'the shores of Circe's land,' where the daughter of the Sun sings ceaselessly in her groves while the groans of her transformed men roll out across the water (Aeneid 7.10–24). The promontory of Circeii claimed her temple (Strabo 5.3.6), and Horace calls Tusculum 'the hills of Telegonus the parricide' (Odes 3.29.8) — her son naturalized as a founder of Latin towns. From there she passes into the European imagination as the archetype of the enchantress: the witch with a pedigree, a loom, and a cup.
circe.culturalLegacy: English keeps her as an adjective: Circean — bewitching, dangerously seductive, charming in the way that unmakes a man. Cape Circeo still bears her name on the Tyrrhenian coast, and if the old derivation of her name from kírkos ('ring; hawk') holds, she shares a root with Latin circus — and so with English circle and circus. The nineteenth century painted her endlessly — Waterhouse's Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses (1891) and Circe Invidiosa (1892) are the icons — and every island sorceress with a wand and a potion since is her descendant. Restoring Kírkē restores the falcon in the enchantress's name.
circe.extendedMeditation:
The Greeks never decided whether Kírkē was danger or salvation, and Homer refuses to help. He calls her a dread goddess, then lets her feed the hero for a year, arm him against the Sirens and Scylla, and draw him the only map of the underworld Greek epic possesses. She is the poem's most accomplished divinity after Athēnâ — and the only one whose power is chemical. Pharmaka, not thunderbolts: the Greeks suspected that transformation, like poisons and potions, was women's work, and Kírkē is that suspicion deified and stranded on an island where no husband can check her.

Her deepest moment is a piece of grammar: the swine keep their noos, their mind, 'firm as before' (Odyssey 10.240) — what is a person, Homer asks, if the body can be unmade around it? Even her geography is a riddle: he moors Aiaia 'where are the dancing-floors of Dawn and the risings of the sun' (Odyssey 12.3–4), the far east, while Rome dragged her west to the Tyrrhenian cape. The honest answer is that Aiaia lies wherever the charted world ends — and Kírkē is what waits there: the intelligence of the wild, articulate, patient, and not to be trifled with.
circe.archaeology: No excavated sanctuary of Kírkē herself survives; her cult was Roman and coastal. Strabo (5.3.6) reports that the promontory of Circeii — modern Monte Circeo in Lazio — was believed to have once been an island, as Homer's Aiaia was, and that a temple of Circe was pointed out there; the marshy plain behind the cape still shows how the 'island' silted into the mainland. Archaic art took her up earlier than almost any other Homeric episode: Boeotian black-figure vases of the sixth century BCE paint Odysseus drawing his sword on her amid men already bristling into beasts, and an archaic painter is named 'the Circe Painter' for the scene.

phonemes.desc: from Old Japanese opo-, 'great, large' — the coalesced long vowel the macron preserves
'land, province, realm' — written 国 in the chronicles, phonetic 久邇 in older spellings
主, 'lord, master, owner' — a standing title in divine names (cf. Kotoshironushi)

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-koo-nee-NOO-shee' — five even morae; the long Ō is a doubled plain O, never an English diphthong; 'shi' is the soft Japanese shibilant.

kin.label: Old Japanese
kin.form: opo-kuni-nusi, 'great-land-master' — the 8th-century pre-coalescence form attested in the Kojiki

kin.label: Alternate name
kin.form: Ōnamuchi-no-kami (大己貴命), 'Great-Name-Possessor' — his second primary name in the Kojiki cycle

kin.label: Folk reading
kin.form: Daikoku-sama — the vernacular reading of 大国 that later fused him with the Buddhist Daikokuten

pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the restoration Ōkuninushi preserves the long vowel (macron Ō) that the ASCII Okuninushi erases — the very feature that marks Ō- 'great' as distinct from a plain o-. One preserved feature, mechanically verifiable: a single-tier Tier-1 name.

domains.title: The Lord of the Reed-Plain
domains.subtitle: Nation-Building & Marriage
domains.lead: Ōkuninushi — the Great Land-Master — is the earthly sovereign of Japanese myth: the heir of Susanoo who subdued wild Izumo, built it into a nation with the dwarf-god Sukunabikona, and codified medicine, agriculture and the rites of marriage. His was the visible world — Ashihara no Nakatsukuni, the Central Land of Reed-Plains — until he ceded it to the heavenly line of Amaterasu in the act of statecraft the chronicles call kuni-yuzuri, the transfer of the land.

cards.name: Land-Building
cards.desc: With the dwarf god Sukunabikona he “made the land”, binding the borders of the Reed-Plain in the Kojiki’s land-building cycle.

cards.name: Marriage & Alliance
cards.desc: He survives Susanoo’s underworld trials to win Suseri-hime and takes the Yakami bride, sealing rule through union (Kojiki).

cards.name: Medicine & Spellcraft
cards.desc: Remembered as a healer: with Sukunabikona he teaches the medicines and incantations that cure both men and beasts.

symbols.name: White hare of Inaba
symbols.meaning: His first patient and his prophet: the flayed hare of Cape Keta whose healing proved Ōkuninushi's medicine and foretold his marriage to Yakami-hime; emblem of the province of Inaba.

symbols.name: The great shimenawa
symbols.meaning: The colossal sacred rope hung across the halls of Izumo-taisha — among the largest in Japan — marking the boundary of his enshrined presence.

symbols.name: Susanoo's sword, bow and lute
symbols.meaning: The regalia of lordship he carried out of Ne-no-Kuni with Susanoo's blessing — the storm-god's own charter for his rule over the land.

symbols.name: The tiny boat of Sukunabikona
symbols.meaning: The skiff of Metaplexis pod-husks (ama-no-kagami-no-fune) and the moth-skin cloak of the dwarf-god, emblem of the small partner in nation-building.

symbols.name: Herbs and the mortar
symbols.meaning: The pharmacology he and Sukunabikona devised for gods and men — beginning with the remedy of fresh water and katami (cattail) pollen prescribed for the hare.

symbols.name: The high pillars of Izumo
symbols.meaning: The towering hall promised at the kuni-yuzuri, to be raised with pillars 'high as the heaven of the gods' — his eternal seat after the surrender of the land.

mythology.lead: Ōkuninushi's cycle, preserved in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), is the longest and most novelistic narrative in Japanese myth — a story of escape, ordeal, sovereignty and renunciation at the meeting-point of earth and heaven.

myths.title: The White Hare of Inaba
myths.text: In the Kojiki (Book I), a hare from the isle of Oki tricks the wani sea-beasts into forming a bridge, is flayed for the deception, and meets the eighty cruel brothers of Ōnamuji, who mockingly prescribe a bath in salt sea-water — agony for its wounds. The youngest brother, Ōnamuji (later Ōkuninushi), advises instead a rinse in fresh river water and a roll in the pollen of katami, the cattail rush; the hare is healed. Grateful, the hare prophesies that Ōnamuji — not his eighty brothers — will win the hand of the princess Yakami-hime of Inaba. It is the first medical prescription in Japanese myth, and the deed that marks the future land-master out from his rivals.

myths.title: The Trials of Ne-no-Kuni
myths.text: Fleeing his brothers' repeated attempts to kill him, Ōnamuji descends to Ne-no-Kuni, the root-land of Susanoo, as the Kojiki (Book I) relates. There he loves Susanoo's daughter Suseribime, and the storm-god tests him: a night in a hall of snakes, a night in a hall of centipedes and wasps — each survived through Suseribime's protective scarves — and a burning meadow where a mouse leads him to safety underground and retrieves the arrow Susanoo had fired. When Ōnamuji at last washes the great god's hair and steals away with Suseribime, Susanoo's sword, bow and heavenly lute, the pursuing god yields and proclaims him Ōkuninushi-no-kami, Great Land-Master, bidding him drive out his brothers and rule the land.

myths.title: The Dwarf from Across the Sea
myths.text: While Ōkuninushi labours to order the land, the Kojiki (Book I) tells, a tiny god arrives across the waves in a skiff of kagami pod-husks, wearing the skin of a moth: Sukunabikona, son of the great producer Kamimusubi (the Nihon Shoki variants name Takamimusubi). The two make and consolidate the land together, and devise the arts of medicine and protective magic for gods, men and beasts. When the work is done, Sukunabikona departs for Tokoyo no kuni, the far land beyond the sea, leaving Ōkuninushi to guard the realm they built.

myths.title: Kuni-yuzuri — the Transfer of the Land
myths.text: When Amaterasu resolves that her line shall rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains, the Kojiki (Book I; cf. the Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods scrolls) records that the warrior-god Takemikazuchi is sent to Izumo, where he thrusts his sword into the shore and demands Ōkuninushi's answer. The land-master defers to his sons: Kotoshironushi consents at once, while Ajisuki-takahikone resists and is subdued in a divine wrestling-bout. Ōkuninushi then cedes the land — on terms: a grand palace is to be built for him with pillars raised high and crossbeams thick, and his worship is to be perpetuated by the heavenly line itself. That promised palace is Izumo no Ōyashiro, the Grand Shrine of Izumo, and the treaty-in-myth is remembered as kuni-yuzuri.

okuninushi.syncretism: Japan's gods met no Roman pantheon; Ōkuninushi's later travels ran through Buddhism instead. Through the folk reading Daikoku-sama of the characters 大国, he was identified with Daikokuten, the Japanese form of Mahākāla, becoming the smiling god of wealth and the household hearth — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. At Izumo the older identity survived intact: there he remains the great matchmaker of en-musubi, the binding of marriage fates, and in the month the rest of Japan calls Kannazuki, 'the godless month', Izumo calls it Kami-ari-zuki — 'the month the gods are here', when the eight million kami convene at his shrine.
okuninushi.culturalLegacy: Ōkuninushi still anchors the Izumo region of Shimane, where Izumo-taisha draws millions of pilgrims and couples across Japan pray to him as the nation's matchmaker. The white hare of Inaba endures as the emblem of Tottori prefecture, and his son Kotoshironushi presides over the great pilgrimage shrine of Kotohira in Shikoku. The word kuni-yuzuri itself remains the standard term for the peaceful cession of sovereignty — the god's abdication absorbed into the political vocabulary of Japan.
okuninushi.extendedMeditation: The Ōkuninushi cycle is a treaty written as myth. The 8th-century mythographers of the Yamato court preserved, almost lovingly, a rival sovereignty — an earth-line descended from Susanoo that owned the visible world — and then sanctified its surrender to the sun-line of Amaterasu. What Ōkuninushi received in exchange is telling: not power but cult, the towering shrine and the empire's perpetual worship. He is therefore the god of everything the heavenly line does not do — healing, farming, matchmaking, the pragmatic order of the reed-plain. Many scholars read the cycle as encoding real negotiations between Yamato and the old Izumo region; whether charter or memory, it makes Ōkuninushi the most humane of sovereigns: a ruler who learned kingship through ordeals beneath the earth, and who gave up his kingdom so that his land — and his god — could endure.
okuninushi.archaeology: Izumo-taisha (Taisha-machi, Izumo, Shimane) is among the oldest and grandest shrines of Japan; the present main hall dates to 1744, but excavations in 2000 uncovered massive clustered pillar bases confirming medieval records of a towering earlier hall — the 'high pillars' the kuni-yuzuri myth demands. The region's cultic antiquity is independently attested by the 1984 Kojindani discovery, a ritual cache of 358 bronze swords, the largest single find of its kind in Japan.

phonemes.desc: aspirated pʰ — a 'p' released with breath, not an English 'f' — plus the diphthong oi as in οἶκος; the acute accent means the voice rises across this syllable
voiced b followed by long eta (η), an open 'eh' held twice the length of a short vowel — never the English 'ee' the modern name has drifted to

pronunciation.approximation: 'FOY-beh' — the first syllable rhymes with 'boy' and carries the rising pitch; the second is a long, open 'eh', not 'bee'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: φοῖβος (phoîbos), 'bright, shining, pure' — the masculine form, Apollo's standing epithet, which Aeschylus derives outright from her name (Eumenides 7–8)

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *bʰeh₂- 'to shine, appear' (compare φαίνω, 'to bring to light', φάος, 'light') — proposed but contested; Beekes and Chantraine both treat the derivation cautiously

pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the Greek Φοίβη carries both an accent (the acute on the diphthong οί) and a long vowel (η), so the restoration Phoíbē preserves stress and quantity together — two facts of the name that plain ASCII 'Phoebe' silently erases.

domains.title: The Third Voice of Delphi
domains.subtitle: Titaness of Prophecy, Keeper of the Oracle before Apollo
domains.lead: Phoíbē is the Titaness of prophecy, the 'shining one' whose name is simply the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright'. Before Apollo ever spoke at Delphi, the Pythia's own prayer names her the oracle's third keeper — after Gaia and Themis — who passed the seat to her grandson as a birthday gift. She is light as foresight: the radiance that sees before it shines.

cards.name: The Oracular Seat
cards.desc: Aeschylus gives Delphi’s succession as Earth, then Themis, then Phoíbē — who yields the seat to Apollo as a birthday gift (Eumenides 1–8).

cards.name: Prophetic Light
cards.desc: Her name is the feminine of Phoîbos, “the bright one” — the shining, prophetic power she hands down to her grandson.

cards.name: The Golden Line
cards.desc: Daughter of Ouranos and Gaia, wife of Koios, mother of Lētō — grandmother of Apollo and Ártemis (Theogony 404–410).

symbols.name: Golden Crown
symbols.meaning: Hesiod's sole epithet for her in the Titan catalogue — Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον, 'Phoebe of the golden crown' (Theogony 136): the royalty of the eldest generation, and light worn on the brow.

symbols.name: Delphic Tripod
symbols.meaning: The Pythia's three-legged seat at Delphi, which Aeschylus' succession makes hers third, after Gaia and Themis (Eumenides 1–8) — the one concrete object to which her mythic tenure attaches.

symbols.name: Omphalos
symbols.meaning: The navel-stone marking Delphi as the center of the world; part of the sanctuary landscape of the oracle she held and handed on. She has no independent iconography — her attributes are Delphi's.

symbols.name: Laurel
symbols.meaning: The prophetic tree of Delphi, inherited by Apollo together with the seat she gave him; with her it marks the continuity of the shrine rather than a personal emblem.

symbols.name: Prophetic Radiance
symbols.meaning: Her name itself — the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright, shining' — is her symbol: light understood as foresight, the gleam that sees ahead.

symbols.name: The Moon
symbols.meaning: A late association: Roman poets use Phoebē as a name of the moon paired with Phoebus the sun, and through her granddaughter Artemis she drifts lunar. Ancient, but poetic rather than cultic.

mythology.lead: Phoíbē stands quietly at the hinge of Greek myth: a Titan of the eldest generation whose role is to inherit and to hand on — the oracle to Apollo, the bloodline to Leto. Her myths are genealogies that glow: everything she touches passes light forward.

myths.title: Golden-Crowned among the Titans
myths.text: In the Theogony (132–136), Hesiod catalogues the twelve Titans born to Ouranos and Gaia — Ocean, Koios, Krios, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rheia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Tethys, and Kronos — and among them 'Phoíbē of the golden crown' (Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον). She is one of the few in the list to carry an epithet at all, and hers is an epithet of light. Hesiod records no deed of hers; the eldest Titans are not actors but origins, the generation from which the Olympian world descends.

myths.title: The Much-Desired Couch of Koios
myths.text: Later in the Theogony (404–410), Phoíbē 'ascended the much-desired couch of Koios' (Φοίβη δ' αὖ Κοίου πολυήρατον ἷξε λέχος εἰσαναβᾶσα) and conceived Leto — 'dark-robed, gentle, the mildest of all who dwell on Olympus'. The line continues without pause: Leto bears 'Apollo and arrow-pouring Artemis' to Zeus (Theogony 918–920), so Phoíbē stands at the head of the Delphic family, grandmother to the two Olympians of light. Hesiod gives the marriage no quarrel and no story beyond the bed and the child; for a Titaness of the first generation, the genealogy is the myth.

myths.title: The Third Voice of Delphi
myths.text: The opening lines of Aeschylus' Eumenides (1–8) preserve her greatest role. The Pythia, praying at Delphi, names Gaia 'first of prophets' and Themis second upon her mother's seat; third — 'with her consent, and by no violence' — sat 'another Titan, a child of Earth, Phoíbē'. Phoíbē then gave the throne to Apollo 'as a birthday gift' (γενέθλιον δόσιν), 'and he bears his name Phoíbos as a namesake from hers' (τὸ Φοίβης δ' ὄνομ' ἔχει παρώνυμον). It is the only peaceful succession in the violent history of the Greek gods: the oracle changes hands as a family inheritance, and the new god's famous epithet is, the tragedian insists, simply his grandmother's name.

myths.title: Two Daughters of Prophecy
myths.text: Apollodorus (Library 1.4.1) gives her motherhood its full shape: from Koios and Phoíbē spring two daughters, Asteria and Leto. Asteria, 'the starry one', bears Hekátē to Perses (Theogony 409–412), the torch-bearing goddess of crossroads whom Zeus honors above all; Leto bears Apollo and Artemis. Through one daughter flows the lineage of night sky and moonlight, through the other the lineage of sunlit prophecy: both of Delphi's lights, in effect, are Phoíbē's grandchildren.

phoebe.syncretism: Phoíbē never received a Roman cult of her own; Rome met her inside Apollo, whose Greek epithet Phoebus became a standard poetic name — and whose name Aeschylus had already declared to be hers (Eumenides 7–8). In Latin poetry the feminine Phoebē then hardens into a name of the moon itself, paired with Phoebus the sun, so the Titaness survives in Rome as a word rather than a worship. Through her granddaughter Artemis–Diana, later poets quietly fold her into the lunar goddess, but the equation remains poetic, never cultic, and no ancient author confuses the two genealogies.
phoebe.culturalLegacy: The name lives on in English as Phoebe — entering the Christian tradition through Phoíbē of Cenchreae, the deaconess Paul commends to the Roman church (Romans 16:1) — and it has been one of the most durable classical given names in the language ever since. Astronomy keeps the Titaness herself: Phoebe, the dark retrograde outer moon of Saturn discovered by W. H. Pickering in 1899, is named for her, a fitting moon for the Titaness of light. And whenever literature writes 'Phoebus Apollo', it repeats — whether it knows it or not — her name, which Aeschylus says Apollo took from his grandmother. The small American flycatcher called the phoebe, by contrast, is named for its call: a false friend, not a descendant.
phoebe.extendedMeditation: Phoíbē is nearly invisible in Greek worship, and that invisibility is the point: her significance is structural rather than devotional. She is the lawful transmission of prophecy. In a myth-world built on violent succession — Ouranos castrated by Kronos, Kronos overthrown by Zeus — Aeschylus makes hers the sole peaceful one: the oracle passes 'with consent and by no violence', as a gift, and even leaves its name behind as a family inheritance. The Greeks seem to have felt that foresight, unlike kingship, could not be seized; it had to be bequeathed. Her shining is therefore not the blaze of the sun but the quiet lamp of knowledge kept burning across generations — from Earth, through law in Themis, through her, into Apollo's daylight.
phoebe.archaeology: Phoíbē has no temple, sanctuary, or cult image of her own anywhere in the Greek world — she belongs to genealogy and to Delphi's remembered past rather than to ritual. Her setting is the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, where French excavations since 1892 have uncovered the Archaic and Classical temples above the adyton in which the Pythia sat, the very seat whose pre-Apolline tenants the Pythia lists in Aeschylus' prologue; Pausanias (10.5.5–7) records the parallel Delphic tradition of an older oracle of Earth and Themis, passed on until Apollo held it. The omphalos copies and tripod dedications in the Delphi museum are the material shadow of the throne she is said to have kept third.

phonemes.desc: the stressed opening syllable: short e bearing the acute accent — in the living accent system, a raised musical pitch rather than a heavy stress
trilled or tapped rhōtic r, short i, final voiceless s

pronunciation.approximation: 'EH-riss' — two quick syllables with the high note forward; nothing like the English slurring of 'heiress' or 'Eris' rhymed with 'ferrous'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἔρις (eris), 'strife, quarrel, rivalry' — the goddess is the common noun made flesh, like Kháos or Némēsis

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: uncertain; older scholarship tied it to ὀρίνω (orínō), 'to stir, rouse', but Beekes judges the formation non-Indo-European — a Pre-Greek inheritance, fitting for a daughter of Night

pronunciation.note: Tier 2, accent-preserving. Ἔρις carries the acute accent on a short initial vowel but no long vowel (η/ω) and no circumflex; the restoration Éris preserves exactly one feature the ASCII 'Eris' loses — the stress — and so the temple stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: The Uninvited
domains.subtitle: Goddess of Strife and Discord — the quarrel that topples kingdoms and the rivalry that builds them
domains.lead: Éris is strife personified — the quarrel, the feud, the rivalry that Greeks both cursed and quietly praised. Born of Nyx, Night herself, she is the one goddess who was never asked to the feast and who therefore changed the world. Yet Hesiod insists there are two Erises: the hateful one who sows war, and the praiseworthy one who stirs even the idle to work. She is the most honest deity in the pantheon — the Greeks' name for a force they could not escape and could not entirely disown.

cards.name: The Golden Apple
cards.desc: Uninvited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, she rolls the golden apple “for the fairest” — the first cause of the Trojan War (Cypria).

cards.name: The Two Erises
cards.desc: Hesiod separates the hateful Strife from her elder sister, the good Eris who stirs idle men to work (Works and Days 11–26).

cards.name: The War-Stirrer
cards.desc: In the Iliad she walks the battle small at first, her head striking the sky as she delights in the din (Iliad 4.440–443).

symbols.name: The Golden Apple
symbols.meaning: The apple of the Hesperides that Éris rolled among the wedding guests of Peleus and Thetis; the Cypria tradition (preserved in Proclus' summary) makes it the seed of the Trojan War — a single piece of fruit as the first cause of the greatest war in Greek memory.

symbols.name: The Inscription 'Kallistēi'
symbols.meaning: 'For the fairest' (τῇ καλλίστῃ) — the words cut into the apple itself. The inscription, not the fruit, is the weapon: a superlative with three claimants is a quarrel engineered in miniature.

symbols.name: Viper-Tressed Hair
symbols.meaning: Virgil gives the Roman Discordia serpent-entwined locks bound with blood-drenched fillets (Aeneid 6.280, 'Discordia demens, vipereum crinem vittis innexa cruentis'), kin to the Furies — strife wearing the visual grammar of vengeance.

symbols.name: The Swelling Stature
symbols.meaning: In Iliad 4 (440–445) Éris is 'small at first, but then she fixes her head in heaven while her feet walk the earth' — her growing body is her emblem: discord is always born tiny.

symbols.name: Place beside Árēs
symbols.meaning: Homer calls her 'sister and companion of man-slaying Ares' (Iliad 4.441), and on the shield of Achilles she strides through battle beside Tumult and Doom, clutching the wounded and the dead (Iliad 18.535–540). Her attribute is her company.

mythology.lead: Éris has no temples and almost no cult — her mythology is her meaning. Every surviving story is an anatomy of strife itself: where it comes from, whom it feeds, and how it grows.

myths.title: Born of Night, Mother of Calamities
myths.text: In the Theogony (224–232) Hesiod makes Éris a child of Nyx, Night, who bears her without father among the other dark abstractions — Death, Sleep, Blame, Woe. Éris then breeds her own terrible brood, the Kakodaimones: Toil (Ponos), Forgetfulness, Famine, Pains, Combats, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lies, Disputes, Lawlessness, Ruin (Atē), and Oath, who 'troubles most of all men on earth when anyone deliberately swears falsely'. The genealogy is a single claim stated plainly: from one quarrel, every misery descends.

myths.title: Hesiod's Correction
myths.text: The Works and Days (11–26) opens by amending the poet's own Theogony: 'there was not one kind of Strife after all — on earth there are two.' The first, the elder, men blame, for she 'fosters evil war and slaughter'. The second, whom Zeus set in the roots of the earth, is much better for mortals: she rouses even the shiftless to work, for 'potter rivals potter, carpenter carpenter; beggar envies beggar, and poet poet'. Here Éris is split in two — envy as destroyer and emulation as the engine of all human striving — one of the earliest pieces of moral reflection in Greek literature.

myths.title: The Golden Apple of the Hesperides
myths.text: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, all the gods were feasted — except Éris, whose very nature barred her from the invitation list. The Cypria, as summarized in Proclus' Chrestomathy, tells that she came anyway and threw among the guests a golden apple 'to be a prize of beauty', inscribed kallistēi — 'for the fairest'. Hera, Athēnâ, and Aphrodítē each claimed it; the dispute was sent for judgment to Paris on Mount Ida, and from that judgment, Proclus says flatly, came the Trojan War. Hyginus (Fabulae 92) retells the same scene. It is the founding myth of discord: exclusion breeds the quarrel that topples a kingdom.

myths.title: Small at First, Then Filling the Sky
myths.text: Homer's most haunting personification of war comes in Iliad 4 (440–445), as the two armies close: among them walks Éris, 'the sister and companion of man-slaying Ares — she rears only a small crest at first, but then she fixes her head in the heavens while her feet walk the earth', hurling bitterness into the midst of both hosts. She reappears on the shield of Achilles (Iliad 18.535–540), bloody-robed among the wounded and the dead. The image is precise: discord begins as a murmur and ends with its head in the clouds — and once she stands, no god can pull her down.

eris.syncretism: Rome adopted her as Discordia, and the Roman poets made her darker still. Ennius opened his account of the outbreak of the Second Punic War with her: 'Discordia taetra belli ferratos postis portasque refregit' — 'when foul Discord burst the iron-bound posts and gates of war' (Annales, fr. 225 Skutsch), an image Virgil deliberately echoes at the underworld's entrance in Aeneid 6.280, where Discordia demens stands with viper-entwined, blood-bound hair. She never acquired the civic cult that other translations did — Rome, like Greece, preferred to name strife rather than worship it. Her modern afterlife is stranger and more literal than most: the Discordian movement of the 1960s made her its patroness, and in 2006 the dwarf planet whose discovery provoked the reclassification of Pluto was formally named Eris — a fitting tribute, the IAU noted, to the goddess of strife and discord.
eris.culturalLegacy: Her Roman name survives everywhere in English: discord, discordant, discordance, and the idiom 'apple of discord' for the object of a quarrel — a phrase that walked straight out of the Cypria into the modern tongues of Europe. Discordianism's Principia Discordia canonized her as the counter-goddess of an orderly world, and the dwarf planet Eris carries her name in every astronomy textbook, so the 'tenth planet' that demoted Pluto keeps her quarrel alive in the heavens. Among the Olympian circle she remains what she always was: the goddess nobody worships and everybody obeys.
eris.extendedMeditation: Éris exposes something unusual about Greek religious thought: its willingness to personify what it disapproved of. She has essentially no cult — no sanctuary, no festival, no priesthood — yet the poets cannot write a war without her. Hesiod's two Erises show the tradition arguing with itself: strife is the curse of mankind and, simultaneously, the condition of every human excellence, for without rivalry the potter never improves his pot. The apple myth extends the insight into politics: the quarrel was not caused by wickedness but by a superlative, by the mere existence of 'fairest' among three goddesses. To the Greeks, Éris was less a villain than a diagnosis — the recognition that conflict is not an interruption of the cosmic order but one of its permanent residents, daughter of the Night that precedes all things.
eris.archaeology: Éris is the rare Olympian-circled figure with no attested temple, sanctuary, or cult anywhere in the Greek world — her existence is literary, and that absence is itself the archaeological fact. Her iconographic life is confined almost entirely to Judgment of Paris scenes: Pausanias (5.18–19), describing the Archaic chest of Cypselus at Olympia, records the wedding of Peleus and the judgment episode in which Éris and her golden apple were among the oldest identifiable figures of Greek myth in art. Roman Discordia survives mainly as the poets' personification; no temple of Discordia is recorded in the city of Rome.

phonemes.desc: Theta was an aspirated t [tʰ] in classical Attic — a t with a puff of breath, never the English 'th' fricative; the acute marks the stress on this first syllable.
The digraph ει, a long closing diphthong shading toward [eː] — the sound the ASCII form 'Thalia' flattens into a bare 'ia'.
Final short alpha, light and open, a breath rather than a beat.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TAH-lay-ah' — begin with a breathy t as in 'top', lean on the first syllable, and let the 'ei' glide long; the English 'th' of Thalia has no place in the Greek.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: θάλλω (thállō), 'to bloom, sprout, abound'; θαλλός, the young green shoot; θαλίαι, 'festivities, banquets' — one root for green growth and good cheer

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: likely from *dʰh₂l- 'to sprout, bloom' (Beekes); the wider cognate family remains debated

pronunciation.note: Tháleia is Tier 1 because the Greek Θάλεια carries both stress (the acute on the initial alpha) and length (the long diphthong ει). The restoration preserves both: the acute on the á marks the accent, and the digraph -ei- keeps the long diphthong that plain ASCII Thalia erases.

domains.title: The Blooming Muse
domains.subtitle: Comedy, Idyll, Good Cheer
domains.lead: Tháleia is the Muse of comedy and idyllic poetry, one of the nine daughters Zeus fathered on Mnémosynē. Her name is the Greek word for flourishing — from θάλλω, 'to bloom' — and in the plural, θαλίαι, it means nothing less than festivities: the good cheer of the feast. The Greeks gave laughter a Muse, and they named her Blooming.

cards.name: The Comic Mask
cards.desc: Her standing attribute in ancient art — the laughing face of the theater, held lightly in one hand.

cards.name: The Shepherd's Staff
cards.desc: The crook of bucolic song, the green world of shepherds and idylls she was said to guard.

cards.name: The Green Shoot
cards.desc: The θαλλός her name proclaims: fresh growth, festivity, the year turning toward abundance.

symbols.name: Comic mask
symbols.meaning: Her defining attribute in ancient iconography — laughter given a face

symbols.name: Shepherd's staff (pedum)
symbols.meaning: The bucolic world of idyllic poetry: flocks, shade, and song

symbols.name: Ivy wreath
symbols.meaning: The plant of Dionysos, god of the theater where comedy was performed

symbols.name: Comic slipper (soccus)
symbols.meaning: The low shoe of comic actors, set against tragedy's high cothurnus

symbols.name: Frame drum
symbols.meaning: The tambourine of the Corybantes, the ecstatic dancers said to be her sons

mythology.lead: Tháleia rarely acts alone: her myths are the myths of the Muses as a body. What the sources give us is her birth, her name, and one startling marriage — to Apollo, father of her dancing sons.

myths.title: Nine Nights, Nine Daughters
myths.text: Hesiod tells how Mnémosynē, Memory herself, lay with Zeus for nine nights and bore the nine Muses 'to be a forgetting of evils and a rest from cares' (Theogony 53–62). When he names them, Tháleia stands third: 'Kleiṓ and Eutérpē and Tháleia and Melpoménē' (Theogony 76–79). From the beginning, then, laughter and festivity are numbered among the daughters of Memory — comedy is not beneath remembrance but one of its gifts.

myths.title: The Silencing of Thamyris
myths.text: In Iliad 2 (594–600), the Catalogue of Ships pauses at Dōrion, where the Thracian singer Thamyris was stopped on his way from Oichalia. He had boasted he would outsing the Muses themselves; in their anger they maimed him, 'took away his divine song, and made him forget his lyre-playing.' The Muses act here as one undivided power — Tháleia among them — and their punishment is the precise opposite of their gift: not forgetting of cares, but forgetting of song.

myths.title: Mother of the Corybantes
myths.text: Apollodorus records that 'from Thaleia and Apollo were born the Corybantes' (Bibliotheca 1.3.4) — the ecstatic, armed dancers who clash their shields around the mountain mother. The notice is late and quietly astonishing: the Muse of comedy wed to the god of measure and the lyre, and their children are wild percussion and dance. Perhaps the genealogy knows something true — that laughter, music, and ecstatic motion are nearer kin than the genres pretend.

myths.title: A Grace of the Same Name
myths.text: The name flowers twice in Hesiod. A few hundred lines after the Muses, he names the Chárites born to Zeus and the Oceanid Eurýnomē: 'Aglaía and Euphrosýnē and lovely Thaleía' (Theogony 907–911). Pausanias (9.35) confirms that the cities of Greece disagreed about the Graces' names and number, and that Thaleia's place among them was old. The duplication is no scribal error: blooming belongs both to song and to grace, and Greek theology let one word keep both houses.

thaleia.syncretism: Rome adopted the nine Musae almost without translation, and Thalia kept her Greek name; it was in late antique and Renaissance iconography that she was fixed once and for all as comedy's patron, mask in hand, one of the paired faces of the theater. Her namesake the Charis lived a parallel afterlife as one of the three Graces of Western art — Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia, the dancers of Botticelli's Primavera. Through her collective she passes into the very words 'music' and 'museum,' both children of the Greek Mousa.
thaleia.culturalLegacy: No common English noun descends from Tháleia's name alone — her legacy travels under other flags. She presides in spirit over Theocritus's Idylls, the bucolic poems that gave English the word 'idyll' for every scene of pastoral peace. Theaters bear her name — Hamburg's Thalia Theater most famously — and the paired masks of comedy and tragedy that still sign for the stage are, by long convention, hers and Melpoménē's. As a given name, Thalia has never gone out of use; the Muse of laughter is one of the few Greek deities people still name their daughters after.
thaleia.extendedMeditation:
Honesty requires a caveat: Hesiod assigns no spheres to the Muses. The tidy division — Tháleia for comedy, Melpoménē for tragedy, Kalliṓpē for epic — is a Hellenistic and Roman codification, unknown to the archaic sources, which treat the nine as one undivided choir. Yet the later assignment is not arbitrary decoration. That comedy receives a Muse at all is the telling fact: the Greeks did not rank laughter beneath song but placed both in the care of Memory's daughters, performed together at the festivals of Dionysos.

Her name carries the argument further. Θάλλω is what the green world does in spring — and in the plural, θαλίαι is what the feast does in winter. One root holds vegetation and celebration together, as if the Greeks suspected that festivity is simply abundance made audible. A Muse named Blooming says that comedy is not escape from the serious world but its renewal: the year, and the city, flowering again.
thaleia.archaeology: The great cult center of the Muses stood in the Valley of the Muses below Mount Helicon, near Thespiai, with its grove, its statues, and the Mouseia festival games; Pausanias (9.29–30) describes the sanctuary and the nearby spring Hippocrene at length. Tháleia herself survives visually on Roman-era Muses sarcophagi and mosaics, where she sits with the comic mask and shepherd's staff that became her invariable attributes. Comic masks further appear throughout theater-related dedications and Pompeian wall painting, the material trace of the genre she was believed to rule.

phonemes.desc: stressed first syllable; classical zeta was a true 'zd' cluster, as in English 'wisdom', not a modern 'z'
phi was an aspirated p (p + breath), not an f; upsilon was a rounded French-like 'u' [y]
short final -os; the r lightly trilled

pronunciation.approximation: 'ZDEH-phee-ros' — stress the first syllable; begin with the 'zd' of 'wisdom', and let the phi puff air like an English 'up-hill', not an 'f'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ζόφος (zophos), 'gloom, darkness; the dark quarter of the sky — the west' — the word's likely kin, naming the wind from the quarter it blows from

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: uncertain; Beekes flags the formation as possibly Pre-Greek rather than securely Indo-European

pronunciation.note: Tier-2 — Accent-Preserving. The restoration Zéphyros preserves the acute stress of Ζέφυρος on the first syllable, a feature plain ASCII loses; it carries no long-vowel mark, so a single preserved feature places the name in Tier 2.

domains.title: The Breath of Spring
domains.subtitle: The West Wind, Gentlest of the Anemoi
domains.lead: Zéphyros is the west wind of the Greeks — the mildest of the four Anemoi, the breeze that loosens winter and calls up the flowers. Where Bóreas rages and Nótos drowns ships in rain, Zéphyros is the wind the poets loved: the steady, fruit-bearing breath that fans the orchards of the blessed and carries spring north into the human world.

cards.name: Herald of Spring
cards.desc: Gentlest of the Anemoi, his west wind loosens winter’s grip and brings the swallow season home.

cards.name: Father of Swift Horses
cards.desc: With the harpy Podarge he sires Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal, wind-swift horses of Achilles (Iliad 16.148–151).

cards.name: Bridegroom of Flora
cards.desc: Roman poets wed him to Flora; Ovid lets her recall she was the nymph Chloris until Zéphyros took her as his bride (Fasti 5.195–212).

symbols.name: Garland of Flowers
symbols.meaning: On the Tower of the Winds in Athens, Zéphyros is carved as a youth whose folded cloak spills blossoms — his spring-bearing nature made visible in stone.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: Like all the Anemoi, he is winged in Greek and Roman art; the winds fly, and their wings mark them as powers of the air rather than ordinary gods.

symbols.name: Swift Horses
symbols.meaning: By Pódargē the harpy he fathered Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal horses of Achilles — the wind's own speed given equine form.

symbols.name: The Swallow
symbols.meaning: The swallow's return was proverbially bound to the west wind's season; both were the first messengers that winter had broken.

symbols.name: Billowing Sail
symbols.meaning: A kind wind for sailors: steady, mild, and western — the breeze that fills canvas without violence and carries ships home.

symbols.name: Youthful Bloom
symbols.meaning: In art he appears as a beautiful, unbearded youth, a wind conceived not as a destroyer but as a lover — fitting the bridegroom of Chlōris.

mythology.lead: Zéphyros is a minor god with an outsized poetic life: born of Dawn, lover of flowers, father of the fastest horses ever to run. His myths are few but luminous — each one binds the west wind to speed, desire, and the returning spring.

myths.title: Son of Dawn and the Starry Sky
myths.text: In Theogony 378–380, Hesiod records that Eōs (Dawn) bore to Astraios, the starry dusk, the mighty winds: Zéphyros, Bóreas, and Nótos — 'a goddess lying in love with a god'. The genealogy is exact: the clearing west wind is the child of first light and the star-field, born at the seam where night opens into day.

myths.title: Father of Achilles's Horses
myths.text: In Iliad 16 (149–151), Patroklos harnesses Achilles's immortal pair, Xánthos and Bálios, 'whom Pódargē, the harpy swift of foot, bore to Zéphyros the west wind as she grazed in a meadow beside the stream of Ōkeanos'. A wind coupling with a storm-snatcher in a meadow: Homer makes the horses' supernatural speed a literal inheritance. It is Xánthos, this same wind-begotten colt, who later speaks with a human voice to foretell Achilles's death (Iliad 19, 404–417).

myths.title: The Abduction of Chlōris
myths.text: In Ovid's Fasti 5 (195–214), the goddess Flora tells her own story: 'I who am now called Flora was once Chlōris… Zéphyros saw me, desired me, and carried me off' — then made her his lawful wife and gave her dominion over every flower, so that in her garden 'it is always spring'. Hyginus (Fabulae) preserves the fruit of the union: their son Karpós, 'Fruit' itself, the harvest that follows blossom.

myths.title: The Breeze of the Blessed Orchards
myths.text: In Odyssey 7 (112–132), the garden of King Alkinoös on Scheria — fruit upon fruit, pear ripening on pear, never failing winter or summer — is kept in perpetual bearing because 'the breath of Zéphyros, ever blowing, causes some fruits to swell and others to ripen'. Homer needs no allegory here: the west wind simply is the climate of paradise, the mildest air imaginable, made divine.

zephyros.syncretism: The Romans called him Favōnius, from favēre, 'to favor' — the propitious wind — and married him to their own flower-goddess Flōra, whose festival, the Floralia, kept the Greek Chlōris-marriage alive in cult. Horace (Odes 1.4) sings winter loosening 'under the welcome west wind', and Virgil lets Favonius breathe through the Georgics as the air that unbinds the fields. Through Latin poetry the name passed intact into every European vernacular: the gentle west wind of Greece became the zephyr of the modern world.
zephyros.culturalLegacy: English zephyr — 'a soft, gentle breeze' — descends directly from his name through Latin zephyrus, and has been a staple of English verse since Chaucer opened the Canterbury Tales with 'Zephirus… with his sweete breeth' quickening the spring crops. The word also gave its name to a fine, light yarn and to anything featherweight. Few Greek wind-gods survive so completely: not as a character, but as the very word English reaches for when the air turns kind.
zephyros.extendedMeditation: The Greeks did not usually worship the winds with temples and myths of their own — they felt them, and feeling was enough. Zéphyros is the clearest case of a natural force crossing into personality precisely because it was pleasant: the storm winds stay brute daimones, but the wind that opens the flowers earned a wife, a marriage bed, and children. His ambivalence is quiet but real — the same wind that breeds Achilles's immortal horses also breeds the speed that carries the hero toward death. For the Greeks the west wind was proof that the divine could be gentle without ceasing to be power: a daimon you pray to by opening the orchard gate.
zephyros.archaeology: Zéphyros's most famous monument is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestēs, 1st c. BCE) in the Roman Agora of Athens, whose octagonal frieze personifies the eight winds — Zéphyros on the west face as a youth scattering flowers from his folded cloak. Pausanias (2.12.1) records a sanctuary with an altar of the Winds at Titanē in Sikyonia, where a priest sacrificed to them annually — one of the few attested cult sites for the Anemoi as a group. In Rome, his cult life ran through his bride: the temple of Flora near the Circus Maximus and the games of the Floralia.

pronunciation.note: Tier 1: the Greek original Χείρων carries both stress (the acute on ει) and long vowels (ει and ω). The restored form Cheírōn preserves both marks — the accent and the macron — that plain ASCII 'Cheiron' erases.

domains.title: The Most Just of Centaurs
domains.subtitle: Wisdom · Teaching · Heroes
domains.lead: Cheírōn is the exception among the wild κένταυροι: the immortal son of Kronos who dwells in a cave on Mount Pelion and turns raw princes into heroes. Where his kin are drunkards and rapine, Homer calls him δικαιότατος Κενταύρων — the most just of centaurs. He is the teacher: medicine for Asklepios, the lyre and the remedies for Achilles, the whole heroic craft for Iason and Herakles.

cards.name: The Tutor's Craft
cards.desc: He reared Achilles, Iásōn, and Asklepios on Mount Pēlion — “the most just of the Centaurs” (Iliad 11.832).

cards.name: The Healing Hand
cards.desc: He taught Asklepios the art of drugs, and was himself struck by Herakles’ hydra-venomed arrow that no healing art could cure.

cards.name: The Hunter's Art
cards.desc: From him the heroes learned the chase itself — tracking, coursing, and spear-work in the mountain wilds.

symbols.name: The Pelian Ash Spear
symbols.meaning: The great spear of ash wood that Cheírōn cut on Pelion's peak and gave to Peleus at his wedding — the same spear Achilles alone could wield (Iliad 16.143–144). The teacher's gift that arms the hero.

symbols.name: The Cave on Mount Pelion
symbols.meaning: His dwelling and school, the legendary academy of heroes where the gods themselves celebrated the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Pindar, Pythian 9.29–30).

symbols.name: The Lyre
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the education he gave Achilles, who in Iliad 9 (186–189) is found in his hut singing the glories of heroes to the lyre.

symbols.name: Herbs and Remedies (φάρμακα)
symbols.meaning: The healing lore he taught Asklepios and gave to Peleus's line; Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave his father' (Iliad 4.219, 11.831–832).

symbols.name: The Hydra-Poisoned Arrow
symbols.meaning: Herakles's stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, that struck his knee and gave the immortal an unhealable wound (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).

symbols.name: The Stars
symbols.meaning: Zeus set him in the sky — remembered as Centaurus or Sagittarius — after he surrendered his immortality and died (Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38).

mythology.lead: Cheírōn stands at the hinge of two orders: Titan-born yet honored by the Olympians, beast-bodied yet the very image of wisdom. His myths are the myths of transmission — what one generation hands to the next.

myths.title: Son of Kronos and Philyra
myths.text: Kronos lay with the Oceanid Philyra in the shape of a horse, and from that union was born a child of double nature — half god, half horse: Apollodorus, Library 1.2.4. Pindar likewise names him the son of Philyra and Kronos, making Cheírōn the half-brother of Zeus (Pythian 4.102–103). Abandoned by his mother, who in shame was changed into a linden tree in later telling, he was reared by Apollo and Artemis, from whom he learned the arts he would pass on. Thus the wisest of teachers begins as the child of deception and rejection.

myths.title: Tutor of the Heroes
myths.text: Pindar gives the roll of his pupils: in his cave Cheírōn reared Iason, gentle-handed Asklepios, whom he taught the craft of remedies, and Achilles, whom he fed on the marrow of lions and wild boars to make him fierce (Nemean 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the bond: Achilles carries remedies 'that Cheiron gave to his father in friendship' (Iliad 4.218–219), and is the man 'whom Cheiron taught, the most just of the centaurs' — δικαιότατος Κενταύρων (Iliad 11.831–832). Actaeon and Herakles also passed through his tutelage. In Pindar's grief for Hieron, the poet wishes Cheírōn still lived in his cave, that another healer might come to Sicily (Pythian 3.1–7).

myths.title: The Spear for Peleus
myths.text: When Peleus married the sea-goddess Thetis, the wedding feast was held on Pelion at Cheírōn's cave, and the centaur gave the bridegroom a spear of mountain ash cut from Pelion's peak (Iliad 16.143–144). That spear passed to Achilles, and at Troy no other Achaean could wield it — Patroklos himself left it behind when he donned Achilles's armor, 'heavy, huge, and strong.' The teacher's gift thus runs through the whole Iliad: it is the one weapon that marks the hero he made. The marriage it honored also produced the child Cheírōn would raise.

myths.title: The Immortal Who Chose Death
myths.text: When Herakles fought the wild centaurs at the cave of Pholos, one of his arrows — tipped with the hydra's incurable venom — struck Cheírōn's knee (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4). The poison that the great healer had no remedy for burned in his own flesh; immortal, he could neither heal nor die. Sophocles remembers the shaft as the one 'wherewith Cheiron was struck' (Trachiniae 714–716). At last he surrendered his immortality and was allowed to die, and Zeus set him among the stars — Ovid watches the father of heroes' education take his place in the sky (Fasti 5.379–414; cf. Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). The teacher's last lesson is mortality itself.

chiron.syncretism: Rome changed Cheírōn least of all the Greek figures: he keeps his name as Chiron in Latin, too singular to be merged with any Italian power. What Rome absorbed was his catasterism — Latin poets and star-cataloguers fixed him in the sky, debating whether the Centaurus or the Sagittarius was his (Ovid, Fasti 5; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). In later tradition he remains the named exception among his kind: Dante makes him chief of the centaurs who guard the violent in Inferno 12, still 'Chiron, who nursed Achilles.' The word 'centaur' (κένταυρος) traveled into every European language, but Cheírōn travels as himself.
chiron.culturalLegacy: His name lives in the sky: the minor planet 2060 Chiron, discovered in 1977 between Saturn and Uranus, was named for him and gave its class of objects — the centaurs, bodies orbiting among the giant planets — their collective name. Modern astrology adopted him as the emblem of the wounded healer, the one whose incurable hurt becomes the source of healing for others. Ancient herbalists named the plant centaury (κενταύριον, Centaurium) after the centaur's healing lore. And the old association of his name with χείρ, the hand, echoes — though by the word's own root, not by his name — in 'surgery,' from χειρουργία, 'hand-work.'
chiron.extendedMeditation: Cheírōn is the Greek answer to a question the centauromachy asks in stone at Olympia and on the Parthenon: can nature be educated? He is a κένταυρος — the very type of ungoverned appetite — who is instead called most just. That he is Kronos's son and Zeus's half-brother matters: he belongs to the older, Titan order, yet serves the new one by raising its heroes, as if the wild past could be redeemed only by becoming a teacher. His unhealable wound completes the thought — the master of remedies cannot master his own pain, and immortality becomes not a privilege but a sentence. That he must surrender deathlessness to find release is among the most quietly radical moments in Greek myth: even an immortal may long for the human portion.
chiron.archaeology: No great temple of Cheírōn is known; he is a daimonic tutor, not an Olympian with a state cult, though a cave above Portaria on Mount Pelion is traditionally identified as the Cheironeion, his school. His real monument is the art: Attic black- and red-figure vases repeatedly show Peleus handing the infant Achilles into the centaur's arms, and Roman sarcophagi of the 'education of Achilles' (2nd–3rd c. CE) show him teaching the lyre. The sculpted centauromachies — the Olympia west pediment and the Parthenon south metopes — preserve the wild centaur type against which his justice was defined.

Voiceless unaspirated retroflex affricate [ʈʂ] plus open central vowel [a], with Tone 1 (high level, ˥). Pinyin 'zh' denotes the retroflex series, not the English 'zh' of 'measure'.

pronunciation.approximation: NUH-jah — the first syllable rises like a question, the second stays high and level; keep the 'zh' retroflex, tongue curled back, closer to 'dr' than to 'j'.

pronunciation.note: 哪吒 is the settled transcription of a name that entered Chinese through Buddhist transmission from Sanskrit Nalakūvara, son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Nézhā: 吒 zhā (Tone 1) is the value recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard dictionaries, while 哪 carries here its special proper-name reading né (Tone 2), preserved only in this name and recorded as such in the standard dictionaries (Xiandai Hanyu Cidian, Hanyu Da Cidian); its ordinary interrogative reading is nǎ (Tone 3), the value given under kMandarin in the Unihan Database. Because the name is a medieval transcription of a foreign theonym rather than a native Chinese word, Old Chinese reconstruction does not apply.

domains.title: The Lotus-Born Rebel
domains.subtitle: Filial Sacrifice, Divine Weaponry, Unconquerable Youth
domains.lead:
Nézhā is the child who would not stay born. Third son of the garrison commander Li Jing, he came into the world after three and a half years of pregnancy — not as an infant but as a ball of flesh, which his father split with a sword to reveal a walking, talking boy. The immortal Taiyi Zhenren took him as a disciple and armed him as no child has ever been armed: the Universe Ring, the Red Armillary Sash, the Fire-Tipped Spear, and the Wind Fire Wheels on which he rides the sky.

What follows is one of the most harrowing arcs in Chinese myth: a boy who kills the Dragon King's son, returns his flesh to his father and his bones to his mother to spare them heaven's vengeance, and is rebuilt from lotus roots and blossoms — a body owed to no one. From there he becomes the vanguard of Jiāng Zǐyá's Zhou army in the Investiture of the Gods and, in Journey to the West, the celestial marshal sent to battle Sūn Wùkōng.

cards.name: The Universe Ring
cards.desc: Qiánkūnquān, the golden ring of heaven and earth, first of the weapons Taiyi Zhenren bestowed — a cosmic bracelet that strikes with the weight of the world it names.

cards.name: The Eastern Sea
cards.desc: Bathing in the sea, Nézhā stirred the waters with his sash until the Dragon King's palace shook — the act that killed Āo Bǐng and set the cycle of debt and sacrifice in motion.

cards.name: The Lotus Rebirth
cards.desc: His soul rebuilt from lotus roots and blossoms by Taiyi Zhenren, Nézhā returns in a body owing flesh to no parent — purity, renewal, and freedom from the debt of birth.

cards.name: The Wind Fire Wheels
cards.desc: Fēnghuǒlún, the paired wheels of wind and flame beneath his feet — the mount that carries the celestial vanguard faster than storm across the three realms.

symbols.name: Universe Ring (乾坤圈)
symbols.meaning: Cosmic sovereignty in miniature — heaven and earth bound into a single striking weapon

symbols.name: Red Armillary Sash (混天綾)
symbols.meaning: The seven-chi silk that churns seas and binds foes; the instrument of the East Sea upheaval

symbols.name: Fire-Tipped Spear (火尖槍)
symbols.meaning: Martial fire and unrelenting advance, the spear of the vanguard who never retreats

symbols.name: Wind Fire Wheels (風火輪)
symbols.meaning: Unstoppable motion — the storm itself harnessed as a vehicle for the young marshal

symbols.name: Lotus (蓮花)
symbols.meaning: Rebirth without debt: purity rising from the water, a body remade beyond blood and bone

mythology.lead: The Nézhā cycle is the great Chinese myth of the filial rebel — a story in which the most radical act of disobedience and the most extreme act of filial piety turn out to be the same act. Its canonical form was fixed in the Ming dynasty, above all in the Investiture of the Gods.

myths.title: The Flesh Ball
myths.text: Lady Yīn carries her third child for three years and six months. When the birth finally comes, what emerges is not an infant but a ball of flesh, and Li Jing, garrison commander of Chéntānguān, strikes at it with his sword, certain it is a demon. The ball splits open — and out steps a boy already able to walk and speak, a divine embryo sent down as the disciple of the immortal Taiyi Zhenren. The wrongness of the birth is the point: Nézhā enters the world already owing nothing to ordinary nature.

myths.title: The Dragon King's Third Son
myths.text: Bathing in the Nine-Bend River where it meets the East Sea, the boy dips his Red Armillary Sash in the water — and the sash, an instrument of cosmic order, churns the sea until the palace of the Dragon King Āo Guǎng trembles on its foundations. When the Dragon King's third son, Āo Bǐng, rises to punish the offender, Nézhā kills him. A child has bloodied the bureaucracy of the waters, and the Dragon King of the East Sea will have justice from heaven itself.

myths.title: Flesh to Father, Bone to Mother
myths.text: To spare his parents the Dragon King's vengeance, Nézhā takes his own life — and frames the deed as an accounting: he returns his flesh to his father and his bones to his mother, paying back the body they gave him so that his crime dies with him and no debt remains to be collected from his house. It is the most shocking sentence in Chinese popular mythology, filial piety pressed so hard it becomes separation. The motif is old — Chan Buddhist texts of the Song dynasty already speak of Nézhā rending flesh and bone to repay his parents.

myths.title: The Lotus Incarnation
myths.text: His wandering soul is gathered by Taiyi Zhenren, who rebuilds him from lotus roots for limbs and lotus blossoms for flesh — the lotus rebirth. Remade, Nézhā becomes what the old body never could be: a warrior free of the debt of birth. In the Investiture of the Gods he rides his Wind Fire Wheels as vanguard of Jiāng Zǐyá's Zhou army in the overthrow of the Shang; in Journey to the West he serves heaven as a celestial marshal, sent down to do battle with Sūn Wùkōng — one rebel conscripted against another.

nezha.syncretism: Nézhā is himself a product of transmission: the name enters Chinese through Buddhism as a transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, a son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa, and the earliest Chinese forms (那吒, read closer to Nata) preserve that foreign sound. As the figure was naturalized, the genealogy was rewritten — his father became the historical-flavored general Li Jing, who absorbed Vaiśravaṇa's iconography wholesale and became the pagoda-bearing Heavenly King (托塔天王) of the Chinese celestial court. Taoism then claimed the child outright: under the title Zhōngtán Yuánshuài, Marshal of the Central Altar, Nézhā became one of the most vividly worshipped protectors in the Chinese ritual pantheon. The figure traveled with the Chinese world — to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan (where he is Nataku) — but it is in the Sinitic ritual tradition, and above all in the temples and processions of Taiwan and the southeastern diaspora, that the lotus-born marshal remains a living god rather than a literary memory.
nezha.culturalLegacy: No Chinese deity has had a stronger twenty-first century. Nézhā's cult thrives in Taiwan and the diaspora, where the Marshal of the Central Altar dances in temple processions — in recent decades to electronic music, the 'techno Nézhā' of modern festival culture. On screen, the 2019 animated feature Ne Zha became the highest-grossing animated film in Chinese history, its defiant reading of the myth — fate is a rumor the child refuses — resonating with a generation; Ne Zha 2 (2025) went further, breaking global box-office records for animation. The rebel child who returned his body to his parents has become, arguably, the most popular Chinese deity of the modern era: an emblem of youth that will not be told what it owes.
nezha.extendedMeditation:
Nézhā teaches that the deepest bond and the deepest freedom can be purchased with the same act. He does not simply disobey his parents, as the Western rebel does; he pays them back — flesh for flesh, bone for bone — and discovers that what remains after the debt is settled is not nothing but everything: a self made of lotus, owing its shape to no one's expectation. The myth refuses the easy lesson. His sacrifice is genuinely filial and genuinely annihilating; his rebirth is genuinely free and genuinely owed to a master's compassion.

To name a domain Nézhā is to claim that paradox: the right to begin again without denying where you came from. The lotus does not pretend it was never in the mud. It rises out of it, blooms above the water, and carries the memory of the depths in every petal — the child of the East Sea who became the vanguard of heaven, still riding the wind on wheels of fire.

sources.name: Wu Cheng'en, Xīyóujì (Journey to the West)
Ao Guang, Dragon King of the East Sea (encyclopedia entry)

nezha.archaeology: Nézhā is a textual rather than an archaeological figure, and his attestation history tracks the Buddhist transmission itself. The name first appears in Tang-dynasty Buddhist translations as 那吒 (Nata), a transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa, whose cult flourished in Tang China and whose iconography — armor, spear, and reliquary pagoda — later passed to Nézhā's literary father, Li Jing. By the Song dynasty the flesh-and-bone-returning motif was current in Chan literature, and Yuan-era drama gave the child a stage life. The canonical narrative was fixed in the Ming novels: the Investiture of the Gods supplied the full cycle from flesh ball to lotus rebirth, and Journey to the West installed him as a marshal of the celestial court. Material attestation is chiefly cultic — temple statuary of the Marshal of the Central Altar, a wheel-riding, ring-bearing youth, across southeastern China, Taiwan, and the diaspora.
nezha.originalScriptNote: The original script is 哪吒, identical in traditional and simplified Chinese. Pinyin Nézhā combines the special proper-name reading né (Tone 2) of 哪 — preserved only in this name, the ordinary interrogative reading being nǎ — with 吒 zhā (Tone 1), as recorded in the standard dictionaries and the Unihan Database. The name is a medieval transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, so no Old Chinese reconstruction applies. The tone-marked restoration Nézhā maps directly to the registrable domain form: the display keeps both diacritics (é and ā, both registrable IDN characters), and no apostrophe is required anywhere in the name.

Open syllable with close-mid back unrounded vowel [ɤ] and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'e' in isolation corresponds to IPA [ɤ].

pronunciation.approximation: CHAHNG-UH — both syllables rise in tone, as in a questioning intonation; 'ch' is an aspirated retroflex with the tongue curled back, and 'é' is close to the vowel of 'her' with the r removed.
