Only the capital distinguishes the temple's form from the input; the name's fame, like Baldr's, vastly outruns its orthography.

domains.title: The Exalted One
domains.subtitle: Poetry, Smithcraft, Healing — and the Undying Flame of Kildare
domains.lead: Brigit, daughter of the Dagda, is the triple hearth of the Irish gods: Cormac's Glossary gives her two sisters of the same name — Brigit the smith and Brigit the leech beside Brigit the poet — so that the one name covers the forge, the well, and the word. Her feast is Imbolc, the first of February, when the ewes come into milk; and at Kildare a fire burned for her, Giraldus says, that no man might approach and no night ever saw go out.

cards.name: The Sacred Flame
cards.desc: The perpetual fire of Kildare, tended by nineteen nuns in turn — on the twentieth night, Giraldus says, it was left to Brigid herself.

cards.name: The Anvil
cards.desc: Smithcraft, one of the three provinces Cormac assigns to the sisterhood of Brigits — the forge where Goibniu's art and mortal craft meet.

cards.name: The Poet's Harp
cards.desc: The first of her provinces in the Glossary — Brigit banfhiled, Brigit the woman-poet, patroness of the learned craft of filidecht.

cards.name: The Rush Cross
cards.desc: St Brigid's cross, woven of rushes on Imbolc eve — the small loom on which the goddess's feast was carried into the saint's day.

symbols.name: The flame of Kildare
symbols.meaning: The fire that neither dies nor accumulates ash — patronage that outlasts the night-watch of its keepers

symbols.name: The anvil and the forge
symbols.meaning: Smithcraft, the making province — skill that transforms raw metal the way poetry transforms raw speech

symbols.name: The holy well
symbols.meaning: Healing drawn from the ground — the countless wells of St Brigit where the leech-sister's province is still visited

symbols.name: Fea and Femen, the two oxen
symbols.meaning: The Dagda's daughter's beasts, who gave their names to plains of Ireland — wealth and the working land

symbols.name: Imbolc
symbols.meaning: The first of February, the milk returning to the ewes — the year's first hinge, kept as her day

mythology.lead: Irish tradition gives Brigit few long tales but a peculiar density of testimony: the great pseudohistory of the Lebor Gabála knows her genealogy, the battle-tale Cath Maige Tuired gives her the first keening heard in Ireland, and Cormac's Glossary preserves the triad that made her three goddesses in one name.

myths.title: The Dagda's Daughter
myths.text: The Book of Invasions places Brigit firmly in the family of the Túatha Dé Danann: Brigit the poetess, daughter of the Dagda, the good god who owns the cauldron and the club. The same tradition marries her to Bres, the half-Fomorian king whose beautiful face and niggardly rule nearly undid the Túatha Dé Danann, and gives her a son, Ruadán — so that the exalted one stands, by marriage and blood, on both sides of the great conflict of Irish myth. The Lebor Gabála is pseudohistory, written by Christian scholars ordering the gods into an ancestry, but its genealogies are the tradition's own filing system: Brigit belongs to the Dagda's house.

myths.title: Three Sisters, One Name
myths.text: Cormac mac Cuilennáin's glossary, compiled around 900, preserves the tradition's clearest statement of her triple nature. Brigit, it says, is the poetess, daughter of the Dagda — and she had two sisters, Brigits also: Brigit the woman of smithcraft and Brigit the female physician, from whose names all the Irish used to call a goddess Brigit. Three crafts, three sisters, one name: from this single entry comes the familiar picture of the triple goddess of poetry, smithcraft, and healing. Whether the triad records three genuinely distinct figures or one goddess's three provinces arranged in the Irish love of threes, the Glossary is the witness every later account follows.

myths.title: The First Keening in Ireland
myths.text: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired gives Brigit her one moment of action, and it is grief. Her son Ruadán, sent by his Fomorian kin to spy on the Túatha Dé Danann, hurls a spear at the smith Goibniu; the smith draws it from his own wound and casts it back, and Ruadán goes to his father to die. Brigit comes to the field and bewails her son — and the text says she wept and shrieked over him, the first keening and the first whistling for grief that was heard in Ireland. The inventor of lamentation is a terrible dignity: the goddess of the word is the one who first taught Ireland what a mother says at a grave.

myths.title: The Fire at Kildare
myths.text: Writing about 1188, Gerald of Wales describes the wonder of Kildare with a traveller's precision: a fire hedged round with a circular fence of brushwood, which no male may cross — any man who tries, he says, does not escape Brigid's vengeance. Nineteen nuns tend the flame, one each night, each adding fuel; on the twentieth night the last nun lays the wood and says, 'Brigid, guard your fire, it is yours.' In the morning the fire is found still burning, and its ashes, Gerald marvels, never increase though the wood is always consumed. He records it as a marvel of the saint's church; scholarship has never doubted that the hedge, the number nineteen, and the unashing flame belong to a far older hearth.

myths.title: Imbolc, the Ewe's Milk
myths.text: Her feast stands at Imbolc, the first of February, one of the four great hinges of the Irish year beside Beltaine, Lugnasad, and Samain. Cormac's Glossary explains the word itself as oimelc, 'ewe's milk' — the season when the sheep come into milk and the year's hunger begins to turn. The old texts keep the day as Brigit's own; the keening, the forge, and the word all gather at the one date, when the light is just beginning to return and the flocks give their first milk. It is the oldest continuously observed fact about her: whatever else changed, the first of February stayed hers.

brigid.syncretism: Brigit's syncretic life runs in two directions. Across the water, her name is one with the goddess Brigantia of Roman Britain, honoured in inscriptions from the Wall country and portrayed on the Birrens relief with Minerva's globe and spear — the interpretatio romana pairing the exalted one with the Roman goddess of craft and war-wisdom; the tribal Brigantes and the Gaulish Brigindu carry the same name-element, and the old comparison with Sanskrit bṛhatī, 'the high, exalted one', shows how deep the root runs. Within Ireland, the identification is Christian: Brigit of Kildare, the sixth-century saint whose feast falls on Imbolc, whose church kept a perpetual fire, and whose wonder-tales in Cogitosus's Life echo the goddess's provinces. Whether saint succeeded goddess, goddess was Christianized into saint, or two figures fused in one name, the sources do not let us decide — and Mac Cana and Koch both counsel holding the question open. What is certain is the continuity of the name: the Exalted One never left Ireland's calendar.
brigid.culturalLegacy: No Celtic deity has a longer unbroken afterlife. Imbolc is still celebrated as St Brigid's Day — Lá Fhéile Bríde — and since 2023 it has been a public holiday in the Republic of Ireland, the first named for a woman. Rushes are still woven into Brigid's crosses on the eve of the feast and hung above doors; hundreds of holy wells bear the saint's name, and the clootie and cure customs at them preserve the leech-sister's province in folk practice. Modern paganism and Celtic Reconstructionism restored the goddess explicitly, keeping Imbolc as the feast of the returning light and of the three crafts; poets, smiths, and healers alike claim her patronage. And the name itself — Brigid, Bridget, Bríd — never ceased to be given to Irish daughters, carrying the Proto-Celtic word for exaltation into every generation since the Iron Age.
brigid.extendedMeditation: Brigit is the rare goddess whose three provinces are one act seen from three sides. The smith and the poet do the same thing: they take what is raw — ore, breath — and by heat and pressure give it a form that outlasts them. The healer does it too, coaxing the broken body back toward the shape it was made for. Cormac's three sisters are really a single lesson: that making is sacred wherever it happens, at the anvil, on the tongue, or at the sickbed. Her fire at Kildare, hedged and watched and never consumed, is the emblem of that lesson — a flame tended by nineteen keepers that still belongs, on the twentieth night, to the name itself. Craft, kept in common, does not go out.
brigid.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Brigit — already plain ASCII in its modern scholarly spelling, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover (hence Tier 2 by the mechanical rule). The medieval manuscripts wrote the name in Insular script, the Irish hand of the Latin alphabet; in the older Ogham alphabet it would have been notched ᚁᚏᚔᚌᚔᚈ (B-R-I-G-I-T), a normalized reconstruction only — no Ogham stone records the theonym. Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: brigid.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

brigid.archaeology: Brigit herself is unattested in pre-Christian Irish material: no Ogham stone, votive, or image names the goddess, and Ireland's Iron Age left no cult sites securely hers. Her name's material record lies across the water: Romano-British inscriptions honour Brigantia from the Wall country — most famously the relief from Birrens (Dumfriesshire), where the goddess stands with Minerva's globe, spear, and crown — and a Gaulish inscription from Volnay (Côte-d'Or) invokes Brigindu, the same name-element on the Continent. In Ireland the evidence is ecclesiastical and hydronymic: the monastic site of Kildare (Cill Dara, 'church of the oak'), with its round tower and its memory of the perpetual fire Giraldus describes, and the hundreds of holy wells dedicated to St Brigit, whose rag-trees and cure customs are the living deposit of the leech-sister's province.

phonemes.desc: Voiced dental stop [d], broad (velarized) before a; as in English 'day' but with the tongue on the teeth.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief.
Voiced velar fricative [ɣ], the lenited g of Old Irish between vowels — the soft gargle of Spanish 'lago', never the hard g of 'go'.
Voiced dental fricative [ð], the lenited d — the soft 'th' of English 'this' — closing on a short final [a].

pronunciation.approximation: 'DAH-ghah' — stress the first syllable; let the g melt into a voiced gargle and the d into the soft 'th' of 'this'. Modern Irish 'an Dagda' keeps the same shape.

The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the god's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The Good God of All Arts
domains.subtitle: The Club of Life and Death, the Cauldron of Plenty, the Harp of the Three Strains
domains.lead: The Dagda — Eochu Ollathir, the All-Father — is the great father-figure of the Túatha Dé Danann: their king for eighty years, master of every art, and owner of three wonders no other Irish god can match — the club whose one end kills nine men at a blow while the other restores them, the cauldron from which no company ever went away unsatisfied, and the harp that leaps to his hand from the enemy's wall and plays the world to tears, to laughter, and to sleep.

cards.name: The Great Club
cards.desc: So heavy it had to be dragged on a wheel; one end kills nine men at a stroke, the other brings the slain back to life.

cards.name: The Cauldron
cards.desc: The fourth treasure, brought from the city of Murias — the pot of plenty from which no company ever went away unthankful.

cards.name: The Harp of the Three Strains
cards.desc: Daur Da Bláo, the Oak of Two Greens; Coir Cethar Chuir, the Four-Angled Music — it killed nine men coming to his hand, then played tears, laughter, and sleep.

cards.name: Eochu Ollathir
cards.desc: 'The All-Father' — father of Óengus, Midir, Bodb Derg, and Brigit; the Túatha Dé Danann's provision and, for eighty years, their king.

symbols.name: The great club
symbols.meaning: Life and death hung on opposite ends of one tool — power that answers for both

symbols.name: The cauldron of Murias
symbols.meaning: Plenty that no company can exhaust — abundance as a standing fact, not a lucky day

symbols.name: The harp and its three strains
symbols.meaning: Weeping, laughing, sleeping — the whole register of feeling under a master's hand

symbols.name: The porridge pit
symbols.meaning: The Fomorians' mock-feast swallowed whole — insult converted into endurance

symbols.name: Brú na Bóinne
symbols.meaning: The Brug on the Boyne, his Otherworld house — the mound his son Óengus won for a day and a night

mythology.lead: The Dagda's dossier is the largest of any Túatha Dé Danann god: he is king, laborer, glutton, lover, harper, and father, and Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's two strangest set-pieces — the porridge pit before the battle and the harp on the enemy's wall after it.

myths.title: The Cauldron from Murias
myths.text:
When the Túatha Dé Danann came to Ireland, the tradition says, they came from four cities of the north of the world — Falias, Gorias, Finias, and Murias — and each city yielded a treasure. From Murias came the Dagda's cauldron, and the poem of the four jewels fixes its fame in one line: no company ever went away from it unthankful.

The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, then gives him the longest reign of the divine kings: Eochu Ollathir, that is the Dagda, held the kingship for eighty years — and it records his death at the Brug, his mound on the Boyne, from the wound that Cethlenn, Balor's wife, had dealt him at Mag Tuired.

myths.title: The Builder of Bres' Forts
myths.text:
When the half-Fomorian Bres was made king and laid the Túatha Dé Danann under tribute, the greatest of them were put to work like serfs: Ogma carried the firewood, and the Dagda was set to building raths around Bres' stronghold, laboring every day at the forts of a usurper. There the satirist Cridenbél found him, and demanded the three best bits of the Dagda's ration every night — for a satirist's curse could raise blisters on a king's face, and no one dared refuse him.

The Dagda's health failed under the tax until his son Óengus took a hand. On Óengus's counsel the Dagda asked Bres for the pick of the cattle of Ireland as his wages, and hid three gold coins in the porridge meant for Cridenbél's portion. The satirist swallowed greed and gold together and died of it; when Bres demanded the Dagda's death for the killing, Óengus's plea turned the case — the gold found in the dead man's belly was itself the proof of his greed. The episode is the tradition's slyest portrait of the god: a king enduring serfdom, rescued not by force but by a father's patience and a son's wit.

myths.title: The Porridge Pit and the Tryst at the Ford
myths.text:
On the eve of the second battle of Mag Tuired the Dagda went to the Fomorian camp to win a truce, and the Fomorians, who knew his love of food, prepared a mock-feast to kill him with: eighty measures of new milk and the same of meal and fat, with goats and sheep and swine boiled into it, all poured into a great pit in the ground. Eat it all, they told him, or die — for to him death was no worse than leaving the porridge. He took his ladle, big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the hollow of it, ate to the scraping of the pit, and walked away with his belly dragging on the ground while the Fomorians roared with laughter — and the truce was won.

That Samain night he met the Mórrígan at the ford of the Unius in Connacht, where she stood washing with one foot on either side of the water. They lay together at the ford — the place was afterward called the Bed of the Couple — and she pledged herself to the Túatha Dé Danann's cause: she told him where the Fomorians would land, and promised to bring him the hearts of their fighting-men and the blood of their king Indech. The glutton the Fomorians mocked came home from the truce with the war-goddess's promise in his hand.

myths.title: The Harp on the Wall
myths.text:
After the battle the Fomorians had carried off the Dagda's harper, Uaithne, and the harp itself hung on the wall of the hall where Bres feasted — the harp the Dagda called Daur Da Bláo, the Oak of Two Greens, and Coir Cethar Chuir, the Four-Angled Music, in which he had bound the melodies so that they would not sound until he summoned them. Lugh, the Dagda, and Ogma pursued the retreating host and came to that hall, and the Dagda called the harp to him. It sprang from the wall and came through the hall to his hand, killing nine men in its path.

Then he played the three strains that Irish music ever after took as its whole art. First the goltraí, the weeping-strain, until their women wept; then the gentraí, the laughing-strain, until their youths and maidens laughed; last the suantraí, the sleeping-strain, until the whole host slept — and the three of them walked out of the hall through sleeping enemies. When the harpers of Ireland later divided their music into three kinds, they were naming the Dagda's set.

myths.tag: Tochmarc Étaíne / De Gabáil in t-Sída
myths.title: The Day and the Night
myths.text:
The Dagda's most famous fatherhood begins with a deception of time itself. He desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand; and to hide what followed, the tales say, he held the sun fast in the sky for nine months, so that the child Óengus was conceived and born within a single day — whence the boy was called mac ind Óc, the son of the young.

Years later, when the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the defeated Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home and asked his father for land, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his house back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent — and kept the greatest mound in Ireland on a quibble. The All-Father lost the argument, and one suspects he meant to.

dagda.syncretism: The Dagda's clearest cross-border witness is not Welsh but Gaulish. The Mabinogion and the whole Welsh corpus know no counterpart of him — the Brythonic silence is total, and no scholar has repaired it convincingly. The comparison the handbooks prefer runs to Gaul: the god Sucellos, 'the Good Striker', shown on altars with his long-shafted mallet in one hand and a pot in the other, often beside his consort Nantosuelta. Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both set Sucellos beside the Dagda — the good god with the enormous club and the vessel of plenty — as two regional faces of one Celtic figure-type: the all-providing father whose tool serves both ends of life. The Christian scribes who preserved him euhemerized him in their own way, demoting the god to an ancient king mighty in magic and druidry; the medieval glossaries kept his name's meaning anyway, and Cormac's Glossary was already printing 'good god' around the year 900.
dagda.culturalLegacy: The Dagda rode the Celtic revival better than almost any Irish god. Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired into English — porridge pit, ford, and harp complete — and made him the genial giant of a generation's reading, the counterweight to Yeats's more ethereal Sidhe. Twentieth-century scholarship gave him his modern standing: Mac Cana's Celtic Mythology made him the type-case of the Celtic all-skilled father, and the Sucellos comparison fixed him in the pan-Celtic frame. Modern Druidry and Celtic pagan practice honor him as god of plenty, craft, and fatherhood; and Brú na Bóinne — Newgrange, the most visited prehistoric monument in Ireland — keeps his mythic address, the Brug of the Dagda that his son won for a day and a night. In Irish itself the name never went anywhere: an Dagda has meant the same large, shrewd, inexhaustible father of the gods for twelve hundred years of the written language.
dagda.extendedMeditation:
The Dagda is the god of competence, and his name says so: the 'good' of the Good God is the goodness of the craftsman, not the confessor — he is good at things, all the things, and the tradition loves him for it without ever making him solemn. He is the only great god in the Irish corpus whom the myths allow to be ridiculous: belly dragging, porridge-smeared, out-argued by his own son, set to digging forts by a usurper. And every one of those scenes ends the same way — the job finished, the pit scraped clean, the truce won, the satirist buried by his own greed.

His three treasures are really one treasure in three keys. The club settles accounts at both ends of life; the cauldron makes sure the table never runs out; the harp keeps feeling itself in order — grief, joy, and rest, each in its strain. Provision, power, and harmony: the whole duty of a father, enlarged to divine scale. The Dagda asks the question every household answers daily — not whether you are good, but whether you are good for something, and whether there is enough.
dagda.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Dagda — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: dagda.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. R. A. S. Macalister — the eighty-year kingship; his death at the Brug from Cethlenn's wound

dagda.archaeology: The Dagda is a textual god: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses are exact — Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, which is the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the Book of Leinster and its sister codices. His mythic address, by contrast, is one of the most famous pieces of architecture in Europe: Brú na Bóinne, the Bend of the Boyne, where the passage tomb of Newgrange (c. 3200 BCE) has stood for five thousand years on the site the tales call the Dagda's Brug and Óengus's síd. The nearest material kin of his iconography is Gaulish: the altar from Sarrebourg showing Sucellos with his mallet and pot beside Nantosuelta is the standard comparison for the good god with the club and the vessel — comparative evidence, never identification.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar stop [k] — Gaulish c is always hard — plus short open [e] and trilled [r]; the horn-root *karno- lies underneath.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], short back [u], and the doubled nasal [n.n] across the syllable boundary, as the Latin capitals ERNVNNOS spell it.
Short [o] and final voiceless [s]; the Gaulish nominative ending the inscription preserves in full.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ker-NOON-nos' — every c is hard, the double nn is fully sounded, and the final -os is crisp, not anglicized to '-us'.

kin.label: Gaulish
kin.form: [C]ERNVNNOS — the single epigraphic attestation, on the Pillar of the Boatmen, Paris (1st c. CE)

kin.label: Proto-Celtic
kin.form: *karnon, 'horn' — the root beneath the name (Matasović, EDPC)

kin.form: Old Irish corn and Welsh corn, 'horn, drinking-horn' — the same word, worn smooth

kin.form: Conall Cernach, the Ulster Cycle hero whose epithet has been linked to the theonym since the nineteenth century — proposed, never proven

pronunciation.note: Cernunnos is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the attested Gaulish form is already plain Latin letters — ERNVNNOS in the capitals of the Paris inscription — with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The restoration differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital. The etymology 'the horned one' is the standard reading (Delamarre, Matasović), though the details of the suffix formation remain debated and the connection with Conall Cernach is conjecture, not consensus.

domains.title: Wilderness, Animals, Fertility
domains.subtitle: The Antlered Lord Between the Wild and the Otherworld
domains.lead: Cernunnos is the horned god of Gaul: named once in stone at Paris, pictured across the Celtic world as the cross-legged, antlered lord who holds the torc of rank in one hand and the ram-horned serpent of the underworld in the other, with the beasts of the wild gathered at his back.

cards.name: The Antlers
cards.desc: The stag's crown the single inscription illustrates: the name means 'the horned one', and the Paris stone shows exactly that.

cards.name: The Torc
cards.desc: The gold neck-ring of rank — held in the god's hand on the Gundestrup plate, hung from the antlers on the Paris pillar.

cards.name: The Ram-Horned Serpent
cards.desc: The hybrid creature of Gaulish art — serpent's body, ram's horns — coiled in the god's left hand on the cauldron plate.

cards.name: The Cross-Legged Seat
cards.desc: The seated posture of the Gundestrup figure, echoed at Reims and Saintes: the stillness of the lord of animals.

symbols.name: The antlers
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over the wild, written into the name itself — the horn made godhead

symbols.name: The torc
symbols.meaning: Rank and offering at once: the wealth the lord of beasts holds, wears, and dispenses

symbols.name: The ram-horned serpent
symbols.meaning: The underworld's animal, held bare-handed — the chthonic power no other Gaulish figure touches so calmly

symbols.name: The gathered beasts
symbols.meaning: Stag, boar, and the beasts of the deep wood: the retinue that answers to him and to no one else

mythology.lead: Cernunnos has no mythology in the literary sense — no tale, no genealogy, no surviving word of his deeds. Gaul wrote no epics down. What survives is a dossier of stone, silver, and bronze: one inscription that names him and a gallery of images that show him, and the whole tradition must be read from those.

myths.title: The Name on Stone
myths.text: Under the choir of Notre-Dame, in 1711, workmen uncovered the monument the boatmen's guild of the Parisii — the nautae Parisiaci — had raised to Jupiter in the reign of Tiberius, early in the first century CE. Among its carved gods, one block shows a balding, bearded head wearing antlers, with a torc hanging from each antler, and above the figure runs the inscription [C]ERNVNNOS. The first letter is lost and restored by convention, but the reading has held for three centuries of scholarship: this is the only text in the world that names the horned god. Everything else called Cernunnos is an identification argued from this single stone.

myths.title: The Cross-Legged Lord
myths.text: In 1891 a peat-cutter's spade struck silver in the Rævemosen bog at Gundestrup in Jutland: a great gilded vessel of thirteen plates, the masterpiece of Celtic metalwork, now in the National Museum of Denmark. On one interior plate sits the figure the whole world now pictures when it hears the name — cross-legged, antlered, a torc gripped in the right hand and a ram-horned serpent in the left, while a stag with matching antlers stands beside him and the animals of the wild close round: boar, bull, and a wolfish beast padding toward him. No inscription names him, and honest scholarship marks the identification as inference — but the face, the horns, the torc, and the serpent are the Paris pillar's figure seated in full.

myths.title: The Antlered Lords of Gaul
myths.text: The figure recurs across the Roman Gaulish world without ever being named again. At Reims an altar shows an antlered, cross-legged god seated between Apollo and Mercury, emptying a sack of grain or coin over a bull and a stag — the horned one as the source of abundance. At Saintes a relief gives the cross-legged figure his serpents again. In the rock carvings of Val Camonica in northern Italy a standing antlered figure with torcs on his arms was cut perhaps four centuries before the Paris pillar — the oldest of all the horned images, and the proof that the type long predates the name's one surviving attestation.

myths.title: Conall Cernach and the Insular Echo
myths.text: Insular Celtic literature preserves no Cernunnos — but it preserves a name that has tempted scholars since the nineteenth century. Conall Cernach, the Ulster Cycle hero who stands beside [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] as the second champion of Ulster, bears the epithet cernach, and the possibility that his name continues the same horn-root as the Gaulish god has been argued from Vendryes to Mac Cana. The honest verdict is suspension: the philology permits the connection, the sources never confirm it, and Mac Cana himself counsels caution. The horned god of Gaul may have an Irish cousin in the hero-lists — or the resemblance may be the oldest false friend in Celtic studies.

cernunnos.syncretism: Rome met the horned god the way Rome met every god: by pairing him with her own. The Reims altar seats the antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury — a Roman frame built round a native centre — and the Pillar of the Boatmen itself is dedicated to Jupiter, with the Gaulish gods carved in attendance. The deepest Roman comparison is inferential: Caesar reports (De Bello Gallico 6.18) that all the Gauls claim descent from Dis Pater, father of the underworld, and since the nineteenth century scholars have wondered whether the antlered lord with his serpent and his cross-legged stillness is the god Caesar's informants meant. The identification is suggestive, never provable, and the best handbooks — Mac Cana, Green, Koch — keep it filed under hypothesis. His closest kin inside the lexicon are the other lords of the Celtic otherworld: [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], who hunts with white red-eared hounds, and [[dagda|the Dagda]], the good god whose cauldron never empties.
cernunnos.culturalLegacy: Cernunnos has the strangest afterlife in the lexicon: a god named once in antiquity who became, two millennia later, the most famous horned figure in modern religion. Margaret Murray's The God of the Witches (1931) made him the prime exhibit of her pan-European witch-cult — a thesis academic history has since dismantled (Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon is the standard autopsy) — but the image outlived the theory. Gerald Gardner placed the Horned God at the centre of modern Wicca, and 'Cernunnos' became his conventional name in contemporary pagan practice worldwide. The Gundestrup plate did the visual work: that cross-legged, antlered silhouette is now one of the most reproduced images of the ancient world, from album covers to fantasy games. A god with no surviving myth became the emblem of every wild thing that refuses to be tamed.
cernunnos.extendedMeditation: Cernunnos is the god built from evidence alone. No hymn, no saga, no genealogy — one word on a Paris stone, one silver plate from a Danish bog, and a scattered congregation of images that agree with each other across six hundred miles and four hundred years. He asks a different kind of attention than the storied gods: not 'what did he do?' but 'what did they see, that they carved him so carefully and wrote his name so rarely?' The answer the monuments give is always the same: the still one in the middle of the animals, holding rank in one hand and the underworld in the other, entirely at peace. Some gods are known by their stories. This one is known by his posture — and the posture has proved enough.
cernunnos.originalScriptNote: The name is attested exactly once, in Roman capitals on the Pillar of the Boatmen: [C]ERNVNNOS — the initial letter lost and restored by convention, the double NN and final -OS certain. Gaulish was also written in the Greek alphabet elsewhere in Gaul, but this name survives only in the Latin-letter epigraphic tradition; no native Celtic script attests it. The form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: cernunnos.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

cernunnos.archaeology: Cernunnos is the most materially grounded name in the Celtic lexicon and the most textually impoverished: his entire attestation is archaeological. The Pillar of the Boatmen, raised by the boatmen's guild of the Parisii under Tiberius (14–37 CE) and rediscovered beneath Notre-Dame in 1711, carries the name's only inscription, [C]ERNVNNOS, above the antlered head with torcs; it stands today in the Musée national du Moyen Âge, Paris. The Gundestrup cauldron, cut from the peat at Rævemosen, Jutland, in 1891 and dated to around the first century BCE or CE, shows the cross-legged antlered figure with torc and ram-horned serpent on its most famous interior plate; it is the treasure of the National Museum of Denmark. The supporting gallery is wide: the Reims altar with its antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury, the cross-legged relief from Saintes, the horned figure with serpents from Cirencester in Roman Britain, and the fourth-century BCE antlered carving of Val Camonica — the oldest horned image in the Celtic world.

phonemes.desc: Broad alveolar nasal [n̪ˠ], the plain 'n' of Old Irish initial position, unlenited.
Long close back [uː] gliding into open [a]; the two vowels of Nuadu fall across a syllable boundary.
Lenited d, the voiced dental fricative [ð] — the soft 'th' of 'this', which medieval Irish scribes wrote simply as d.
Short back [u], the final vowel of the Old Irish nominative form Nuadu.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NOO-ah-oo' — stress the first syllable, hold the 'oo' long, soften the middle d toward the 'th' of 'breathe', and finish on a short 'oo'. Modern English speakers usually say 'NOO-uh-duh'.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Nudd, and Lludd Llaw Eraint, 'Lludd of the Silver Hand', king of Britain in Lludd a Llefelys

kin.form: Nodens (also Nodons, Nudens), the god of the temple at Lydney Park in Gloucestershire

pronunciation.note: Nuada is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the attested Old Irish form carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, so plain ASCII loses nothing. The etymology is honestly uncertain: one proposal reads the name as 'cloud-maker', from a root behind Welsh nudd 'mist'; another, argued by Tolkien for the Gaulish Nodens, connects it to a root meaning 'to catch, acquire' — a fisher or hunter — which would suit the sea-and-hounds imagery of the Lydney temple. Neither is settled, and the temple says so.

domains.title: War, King of Tuatha
domains.subtitle: The Silver-Handed King of the Tuatha Dé Danann
domains.lead: Nuada Airgetlám is the first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland — the ruler who lost his arm at the First Battle of Mag Tuired, lost his throne to the law that a blemished man cannot be king, and won both back through the physicians' craft: first the silver arm that named him, then the living arm that restored him. His sword from Findias was one of the Four Treasures of his people, and he died at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye.

cards.name: The Silver Hand
cards.desc: Dian Cécht's silver arm, made with Credne the brazier, moved in every joint — and gave the king his name, Airgetlám.

cards.name: The Sword from Findias
cards.desc: One of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann; once it was drawn from its sheath, no one escaped it.

cards.name: Mag Tuired
cards.desc: The plain of the two battles: against the Fir Bolg, where the arm was lost; against the Fomorians, where the king fell.

cards.name: The Unblemished Throne
cards.desc: Irish kingship law held that no man with a blemish could rule; Nuada's wound cost him Tara, and his healing restored him.

symbols.name: The silver arm
symbols.meaning: Wholeness made by craft when nature failed — the prosthesis that kept a king king in all but law

symbols.name: The sword of Nuada
symbols.meaning: The irresistible weapon from the city Findias, one of the Four Treasures brought to Ireland

symbols.name: Tara (Temair)
symbols.meaning: The seat of the kingship of Ireland, which a blemished man could not lawfully hold

symbols.name: The physician's craft
symbols.meaning: Dian Cécht's silver-work and Miach's flesh-work — healing as the instrument of sovereignty

symbols.name: Dog and fisherman (as Nodens)

mythology.lead: Nuada's story is the Irish tradition's great parable of kingship and the body: a ruler can be unmade by a single wound and remade by healing, and the law watches both. The record runs from the Lebor Gabála Érenn through the two battles of Mag Tuired, and his Welsh and Gaulish cognates carry the same silver-handed name across the Celtic world.

myths.title: The First Battle of Mag Tuired
myths.text: When the Tuatha Dé Danann came to Ireland, Nuada had been their king for seven years. They demanded the country from the Fir Bolg, and the two peoples met at Mag Tuired in Connacht. In the battle Nuada fought Sreng, champion of the Fir Bolg, and Sreng struck off his right arm at the shoulder — yet the Tuatha Dé Danann won the field, and the Fir Bolg king Eochaid mac Eirc was driven to his death. The victory that made the Tuatha Dé Danann masters of Ireland cost their king the wholeness the kingship required.

myths.title: The Silver Hand and the Hand of Flesh
myths.text: Because a blemished man could not hold the kingship, Nuada yielded the throne to Bres. The physician Dian Cécht, with Credne the brazier, made him a full arm of silver that moved in every joint — whence his byname Airgetlám, Silver-hand. But Dian Cécht's own son Miach went further: he set the severed arm to the stump and healed it 'joint to joint and vein to vein' in thrice nine days. Jealous that the son had outdone the father, Dian Cécht struck Miach dead; from the young healer's grave grew three hundred and sixty-five herbs, which his sister Airmed sorted by their virtues — and which Dian Cécht scattered, so that their full knowledge died with him. Healing, in this cycle, is never free of the wound of envy.

myths.title: Bres, the Satire, and the Restoration
myths.text: Bres mac Elatha, half Fomorian by blood, ruled badly: the warriors of Ireland were set to menial labour, hospitality failed, and the poet Cairbre mac Etaine composed against him what the tradition calls the first satire ever made in Ireland — and Bres's face broke out in blotches. The same law that had unseated Nuada now unseated Bres, for a blemished king could not stand; and with his arm made whole by Miach, Nuada took back the kingship and held it until the war with the Fomorians came. The symmetry is exact: one king falls by the body's wound, the other by the wound of the word.

myths.title: The Second Battle and the King's Death
myths.text: At Tara, on the eve of the war, a stranger came to Nuada's hall claiming every skill at once — harpist, warrior, smith, poet, healer — and Nuada, testing Lugh and finding him unmatched, gave the young god his own seat, the champion's seat, to lead the counsel of war. The Second Battle of Mag Tuired was fought against the Fomorians, and there Nuada Airgetlám and Macha his wife fell together at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye. The first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland died in the victory that secured his people's rule; the sword of Findias passed into memory as the measure of a weapon that cannot be withstood.

nuada.syncretism: Nuada belongs to one of the clearest pan-Celtic name families. In Welsh he is Nudd and, in full form, Lludd Llaw Eraint — 'Lludd of the Silver Hand' — the king of Britain in Lludd a Llefelys, whose byname renders Airgetlám word for word (llaw 'hand', eraint 'silver'). In Gaulish he is Nodens (also Nodons, Nudens), worshipped at the great temple at Lydney Park in Gloucestershire, where Roman dedicants equated him with Mars and where the imagery — hounds, fishermen, the sea — suggests a healer and hunter as much as a warrior. The Romano-British curse tablet of Silvianus, asking 'Lord Nodens' to deny health to the thief of his ring, shows the god working as an enforcer of justice. Scholars (Mac Cana, Koch) reconstruct a Common Celtic *Noudont- or *Noudo- behind all three, though the root's meaning — 'cloud-maker' or 'catcher, fisher' — remains genuinely debated.
nuada.culturalLegacy: Nuada's afterlife runs through scholarship into fantasy. When R. E. M. and T. V. Wheeler published their excavation of the Nodens temple at Lydney Park in 1932, the young philologist J. R. R. Tolkien contributed the appendix 'The Name Nodens', tracing the god's name to a root of catching and acquiring — a fragment of Tolkien's scholarly life that fans of his fiction still chase. In modern Irish the name survives as Nuadha, and Maynooth University's old arms carried Nuada's sword. In popular culture the silver-handed king rides again as Prince Nuada Silverlance in Hellboy II: The Golden Army (2008), and the motif of the magical prosthetic hand — from A Song of Ice and Fire to Japanese fantasy — descends, knowingly or not, from Airgetlám. Modern Celtic pagans honour Nuada as a god of rightful rule, healing, and sovereignty restored.
nuada.extendedMeditation: Nuada is the king of the necessary surrender. The Irish law of the unblemished king looks cruel — a man maimed in his people's victory loses his throne — but the myth refuses both easy readings. It does not mock the law: Bres, who takes the throne, is judged by the same standard and falls to a blemish of the face raised by satire. And it does not abandon the wounded: the whole craft of the physician-gods bends itself to making Nuada whole, first in silver, then in flesh. What the cycle teaches is that sovereignty is not possession but fitness, and fitness can be lost and restored. The silver hand is the emblem of every function that has to be rebuilt after catastrophe: it moves in every joint, it does the work, and it is not the thing it replaces — until Miach's deeper healing shows that even that distinction can be overcome. The king who rules again is not the king who fell. He is the king who was remade.
nuada.originalScriptNote: The attested Old Irish form is Nuadu (later Nuada), written by medieval Irish scribes in the Insular Latin bookhand of the great vellum codices; in the Ogham letter-row the name would have been notched ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ (N-U-A-D-A), though no Ogham stone yet found carries it. Because the name is already plain ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: nuada.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

nuada.archaeology: Nuada is textual in Ireland — no inscription names him there — but his Gaulish cognate has one of the best-excavated cult sites in Roman Britain. At Lydney Park, Gloucestershire, overlooking the Severn estuary, a temple complex of the late third and fourth centuries CE was dedicated to Nodens: the Wheelers' excavations (1928–29, published 1932 with Tolkien's philological appendix) uncovered mosaic floors, inscribed slabs reading DEVO NODENTI and D M NODONTI ('to the god Mars Nodens'), bronze dog figurines, a fisherman plaque, and pins and bracelets left as votives — the material of a healing-and-hunting cult. The famous curse tablet of Silvianus, asking Nodens to withhold health from whoever stole his ring until it was returned 'to the temple of Nodens', was found on the site; a gold ring inscribed SENICIANE VIVAS IN DEO, plausibly the very ring, surfaced at Silchester. On the Irish side, the texts are the evidence: the Second Battle of Mag Tuired survives in the sixteenth-century British Library Harley MS 5280, the First Battle in a single late vellum copy edited by Fraser, and the Lebor Gabála in its medieval recensions.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar trill [r̥] — the Welsh digraph rh, an r sounded with breath; English has no equivalent, so 'hr' is the usual crutch.
Short close front [i], the light first syllable; Welsh stress has not yet fallen.
Open [a] in the stressed penult — Welsh words stress the next-to-last syllable, so the weight of the name lands here.
Alveolar nasal [n], open-mid [ɔ] (the Welsh o), final [n]; the unstressed ultima closes quietly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'hree-AH-non' — begin with a breathy, whispered r, and put the stress on the middle syllable, the Welsh penult.

pronunciation.note: Rhiannon is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The etymology is a scholarly reconstruction rather than an attested form: Celticists derive the name from Common Celtic *rīgan- 'queen' plus a divine suffix, 'Great Queen', a reading that fits the figure precisely but must be labelled as what it is.

domains.title: The Rider No Horse Can Catch
domains.subtitle: Horses, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Rhiannon is the Great Queen of the Mabinogi: the lady of the Otherworld who rides past Gorsedd Arberth on a pale horse at a slow, even pace that the fastest mounts of Dyfed cannot close — the goddess who chooses her own king, bears a false charge with unbroken dignity, and endures the penance of the horse-collar without bending.

cards.name: Gorsedd Arberth
cards.desc: The mound above Narberth where wonders are seen: whoever sits there receives blows — or sees a marvel. Pwyll saw her ride past.

cards.name: The Uncatchable Pace
cards.desc: She rides a pale horse at a slow, steady walk, and the swiftest riders in Dyfed cannot close the distance — until she is asked to stop.

cards.name: The Birds of Rhiannon
cards.desc: Adar Rhiannon: three birds whose song, though heard far over the sea, is as clear as if they sang beside you — sweeter than any earthly song.

cards.name: The Horse-Block
cards.desc: The marble mounting-block at the gate of Arberth, where she sits out her penance and offers to carry every guest to court on her back.

symbols.name: The pale horse
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty arriving at its own pace — the mount no pursuit can overtake, because the rider alone decides when to stop

symbols.name: The three birds
symbols.meaning: Adar Rhiannon, whose song crosses the boundary between the living and the dead — the Otherworld made audible

symbols.name: The horse-block
symbols.meaning: Dignity under a false sentence: the queen who carries her guests rather than break under the charge she did not earn

symbols.name: The bottomless bag
symbols.meaning: The cleverness that out-plots a forced marriage — Gwawl's undoing, and the game of Badger in the Bag

symbols.name: The collars of asses

mythology.lead: Rhiannon is the strongest female figure in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and the tales give her a complete arc: the uncatchable rider who chooses her husband, the accused mother who bears her penance, the captive of the enchantment who comes home still a queen. Every word of her story is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts.

myths.title: The Rider on the Pale Horse
myths.text: Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, goes up to Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where a man either suffers blows or sees a wonder, and there he sees a lady in shining gold brocade riding past on a great pale horse — at a slow, even pace. He sends his swiftest rider after her; the faster the pursuit, the farther she draws ahead. Day after day it happens, with Pwyll's own horse and Pwyll himself, until at last he calls out: 'Maiden, for the sake of the man you love best, wait for me.' She stops at once: 'I will wait gladly — and it would have been better for the horse had you asked me that long ago.' She is Rhiannon, daughter of Hefaidd Hên, and she has come of her own will: she is being given to a man she does not want, and she has chosen Pwyll instead.

myths.title: The Bag That Would Not Fill
myths.text: At the wedding feast, Pwyll grants a request before he hears it — and the petitioner is Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused, who claims her by the promise. Rhiannon is not dismayed; she devises the counter-plot. A year later Pwyll comes to Gwawl's feast disguised as a beggar, asking only that a certain small bag she has given him be filled with food. The bag cannot be filled: it will never be full, she has told him, unless a true lord treads the food down with his feet and declares that enough has been put in. Gwawl rises and treads it down — and Pwyll draws the bag shut over him, blows his horn, and his war-band falls on the hall. Each man strikes the bag and asks what is in it; 'a badger,' comes the answer, and from that night the Welsh played the game called Badger in the Bag. Gwawl buys his release with sureties and a renounced claim, and Rhiannon marries the man she chose.

myths.title: The May-Eve Vanishing and the Penance
myths.text:
After three childless years the nobles of Dyfed press Pwyll to take another wife; he begs one year more, and Rhiannon bears a son. On the night of the birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep, and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own child. Pwyll will not put her away, but a penance is imposed: she is to sit beside the horse-block at the gate of Arberth, tell her story to every traveller who comes, and offer to carry guests and strangers to the court on her back. She accepts the sentence she did not earn, and she bears it without breaking.

The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the boy as Gwri Wallt Euryn, Gwri of the Golden Hair — who grows with uncanny speed and bears, year by year, the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. Rhiannon looks at him and says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. From that word the boy is named Pryderi, and the penance ends.

myths.title: The Enchantment of Dyfed and the Collars of Asses
myths.text:
After Pwyll's death, Rhiannon is given in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr, and the four of them — Rhiannon and Manawydan, Pryderi and his wife Cigfa — return to Dyfed. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, the land is emptied: not a person, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. For two years the four live by hunting; then they try their hand at saddlery, shield-making, and shoemaking in the towns of England, and each time the local craftsmen drive them out for making work too good to allow. Back in empty Dyfed, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before; Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain, and is rooted to the spot, struck dumb. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is trapped beside him — and fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish.

Manawydan undoes the spell by patience. Sowing wheat, he watches three ripe fields stripped bare by mice on successive nights, and on the third he catches one slow, heavy mouse and condemns it to hang as a thief. A clerk, a priest, and a bishop come one after another to beg it off, each offering more than the last, and Manawydan names his price: Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, transformed with all his household; Llwyd had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud. Pryderi comes home with the gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers — the second humiliation she has worn like a queen, and the second she survives.

myths.title: The Birds of Rhiannon
myths.text: Rhiannon never steps on stage in the Second Branch, but her birds do. When the seven survivors of the Irish war come back over the sea bearing the wounded head of Brân the Blessed, they feast at Harlech for seven years, and there come three birds — the Birds of Rhiannon, Adar Rhiannon — that begin to sing to them. Every other song seems unlovely beside it; and though the birds must be gazed at far out over the sea, their singing is as clear as if they sang in the hall. At Gwales in Penfro the company feasts on for eighty years with the uncorrupted head, in the presence of the birds' song, until the door toward Cornwall is opened and memory and sorrow return. Later Welsh tradition says of the Adar Rhiannon that their song wakes the dead and lulls the living to sleep — the music of a world that does not end.

rhiannon.syncretism: The great comparative debate pairs Rhiannon with Epona, the Gaulish horse-goddess whose dedications — more than two hundred inscriptions from Britain to the Balkans — make her the best-attested Celtic deity of the Roman west. A queenly rider whose whole story is bound to horses, whose name the handbooks reconstruct as 'Great Queen', looks very like an insular reflex of the mare-goddess; Mac Cana and others have argued the parallel, and Koch registers it as the standard comparison — but no inscription names Rhiannon or *Rīgantonā, and the identification remains typological, not epigraphic. The second frame is sovereignty: Mac Cana reads the First Branch against the Irish pattern in which the land's queen chooses and validates the king, so that Pwyll's marriage to Rhiannon is his investiture as much as his wedding. The third is Macha, the Irish sovereignty figure forced to race the king's horses: horse, humiliation, and queenship cluster around both women, and the handbooks have compared them for a century. None of these parallels is an identity; together they map the kind of goddess the Welsh prose is remembering.
rhiannon.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Rhiannon out of the Welsh manuscripts and into the English-speaking world, and the Victorian Celtic revival made her one of the best-known figures of Welsh tradition. Evangeline Walton's twentieth-century retellings of the Four Branches kept her before modern readers, and in 1975 Fleetwood Mac's 'Rhiannon' — written by Stevie Nicks, who found the name in a novel and only afterwards learned it belonged to a Welsh goddess — made the name famous worldwide; the given name Rhiannon, already living in Wales, spread across the English-speaking world in the song's wake. In modern Druid and pagan practice she is honoured as a goddess of horses, sovereignty, and endurance under injustice, and scholars of the Mabinogi rank her among the most fully realized women in medieval European literature — a figure whose dignity the prose never once allows to slip.
rhiannon.extendedMeditation: Rhiannon cannot be caught because she has already decided where she is going. The fastest horses in Dyfed gallop themselves to exhaustion behind a rider who is barely trotting — and the moment she is asked, she stops, because stopping was always hers to give. That is the secret the First Branch teaches about power: the pace of a sovereign is not set by her pursuers. The rest of her story tests the lesson. Falsely accused, she does not rage or plead; she sits down by the horse-block and carries her guests, one by one, until the truth walks home on its own legs. Trapped in the enchantment, she endures the collars of asses and comes out still the Great Queen. Endurance, in her telling, is not passivity — it is the refusal to let an unjust sentence write your name. She waits, she carries, she outlasts; and the land is hers again.
rhiannon.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Rhiannon — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: rhiannon.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/rhiannon/ in the meantime.

rhiannon.archaeology: Rhiannon is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the reconstructed *Rīgantonā has no epigraphic attestation anywhere in the Celtic world. Her evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales themselves are dated by debate rather than document, most often to the later eleventh or early twelfth century. The geography of her story is real — Arberth, the court of Dyfed, stands by modern Narberth in Pembrokeshire — but no sanctuary of hers is known. The nearest material horizon is comparative, not hers: the two hundred and more dedications to the Gaulish horse-goddess Epona recovered across the Roman west, against which scholars have long read the rider of Arberth.

pronunciation.approximation: GWID-yon — the gw is a single lip-rounded consonant, the y sounds like the i of 'kin', and the stress falls on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Gwydion (Gwydion uab Dôn) is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The etymology is honestly debated: a derivation from the Celtic root *widu- 'wood, forest' has often been proposed (compare Welsh gwydd 'trees', Old Irish fid, Gaulish vidu-), but the connection is not proven and the standard handbooks mark it uncertain.

domains.title: Magic, Poetry, Trickery
domains.subtitle: The domain of Gwydion
domains.lead: In the celtic tradition, Gwydion governed magic, craft, vengeance. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.name: The Enchanted Swine
cards.desc: Disguised as a poet, Gwydion conjured illusory stallions, hounds, and shields to trade for Pryderi's otherworld pigs — the first swine in Wales — and started a war with a vanishing herd.

cards.name: Math's Wand
cards.desc: The wand that transformed Gwydion and Gilfaethwy into deer, boars, and wolves for three years — and that later struck Lleu from eagle back into man.

cards.name: The Flower-Maiden
cards.desc: With Math, Gwydion fashioned Blodeuwedd from the flowers of oak, broom, and meadowsweet — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed.

cards.name: The Eagle on the Oak
cards.desc: When Lleu was struck into eagle-shape, Gwydion followed a sow to the oak, sang three englynion to bring him down, and turned vengeance into restoration.

symbols.name: The magic wand
symbols.meaning: Math's wand of transformation — punishment, testing, and restoration carried in a single rod

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet
symbols.meaning: The three flowers from which Blodeuwedd was made by enchantment

symbols.name: The illusory horses and hounds
symbols.meaning: Gwydion's conjured wealth, real for a day and gone by morning — craft as currency

symbols.name: The eagle on the oak
symbols.meaning: Lleu wounded into bird-shape, rotting flesh feeding a sow beneath the tree

symbols.name: The sow
symbols.meaning: The beast Gwydion followed through the valley to find his foster-son

symbols.name: The shoemaker's disguise
symbols.meaning: The craft under which Gwydion tricked Arianrhod into naming her own son

mythology.lead: Gwydion fab Dôn is the enchanter of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math fab Mathonwy': nephew of Math the king of Gwynedd, brother of Gilfaethwy, and the foremost magician of medieval Welsh literature. He is poet, trickster, foster-father, and avenger in one figure — the man who makes illusions that pass for wealth, who pays for his crimes in animal skins, and who ends the tale as the careful hand that puts a broken world back into shape.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
King Math of Gwynedd could live only with his feet in the lap of a virgin, except in time of war, and the maiden Goewin held that office. When Gilfaethwy desired her, Gwydion devised the remedy: war. He went to Pryderi of Dyfed in the guise of a poet and asked for the swine — the hobeu, the first pigs ever brought to Wales, a gift from Arawn of Annwfn. Refused, he conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, and traded the apparitions for the herd. By the time Pryderi's glamour faded, Gwydion was gone, and Pryderi came north with an army.

While Math marched to meet him, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demanded single combat, 'for it was because of me that the hosts came'; at Maenor Penard, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed went home under tribute. The victory is real and so is its cost: Gwydion's finest trick is also his crime, and the Fourth Branch never lets the two be separated.

myths.title: The Punishment of the Brothers
myths.text:
Math's justice is the strangest in the Mabinogi. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand and turned them into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year their offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — were sent to the court, baptized, and raised.

After the third year Math struck them back into their own shapes: 'You have had punishment enough, and you have been greatly shamed.' The punishment is exact and even-handed — the brothers suffer in the flesh what they did, and when the debt is paid the king takes them back into honour. It is the Fourth Branch's doctrine of justice in miniature: transformation as sentence, restoration as mercy.

myths.title: The Naming and Arming of Lleu
myths.text:
When Gwydion proposed his sister Arianrhod as Math's new footholder, she stepped over the wand for the virginity test and dropped a yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who made for the sea — and 'something small' that Gwydion hid in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest came the boy who would be Lleu. Gwydion fostered him, and Arianrhod, shamed, laid three tynghedau upon him: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth.

Gwydion undid the destinies by craft. Disguised as a shoemaker with the boy at his side, he came beneath Caer Arianrhod, and when Lleu flung a stone and knocked a wren's leg askew, Arianrhod cried that the fair one had struck it with a skilful hand — and so named him Lleu Llaw Gyffes. For the arms, Gwydion conjured a phantom fleet against the castle until Arianrhod herself armed the defenders. The magician wins not by force but by arranging the world so that his opponent speaks the words he needs.

myths.title: The Flower-Maiden and the Eagle
myths.text:
For the third tynged there was no earthly answer, so Gwydion and Math took their wands and made one: from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet they fashioned the fairest woman anyone had seen, and named her Blodeuwedd, 'Flower-face'. She married Lleu — and betrayed him with Gronw Pebr of Penllyn, drawing from her husband the secret of how he could be killed, so that Gronw's spear struck him at the impossible meeting of conditions. Lleu flew off in the shape of an eagle, screaming.

Gwydion searched Gwynedd and Powys until he followed a sow to an oak where rotten flesh and maggots fell to her snout, and in the top of the tree sat the eagle. He sang three englynion down the years of the bird's perches until Lleu came to his knee, then struck him with the wand back into human shape — skin and bone, a man to be nursed back with doctors and good care. The vengeance that followed was as crafted as the rescue: Blodeuwedd he would not kill, but turned into an owl, 'the shape hated by all the birds', renamed Blodeuwedd, 'Flower-face' become 'Owl'; and Gronw, standing where Lleu had stood, took Lleu's spear-cast through the slab at Llech Gronw and died. Maker of the woman, finder of the man, instrument of the sentence: the whole of Gwydion's domain is in this last movement.

myths.title: The Battle of the Trees
myths.text: Outside the Mabinogi, the Book of Taliesin preserves Gwydion's other great fame: Kat Godeu, 'The Battle of the Trees', in which he enchants the trees of the forest to march as an army against Arawn of Annwfn — alder at the front, oak in the thick of it. The poem's voice, Taliesin, boasts that he was there when Gwydion 'made the sally of the trees'. In the later tale-tradition around the poem, Gwydion also guesses the hidden name of the opponent's champion from the alder twigs in his hand — the same gift of naming-by-craft that the Fourth Branch shows in the wren scene. Whether the poem preserves older myth or learned fancy is debated, but its Gwydion is unmistakably the Mabinogi's: the magician whose weapons are other things' natures.

gwydion.syncretism: Gwydion is the Welsh trickster-enchanter, and comparative scholarship has set him beside the other shape-changing cunning figures of Europe: [[loki|Loki]], whose disguises and bargains Gwydion's deceptions recall; [[hermes|Hermês]], the poet-thief of the Greek pantheon; and Óðinn in his sorcerer's aspect. Mac Cana treats him as one of the great magician-figures of the Celtic world, and the comparison holds at the level of motif — illusion, disguise, the hidden name, the shape-shifting punishment — not of borrowing. The deeper kinship is insular: Irish tradition is full of druidic shape-shifters, and Gwydion's transformations of and by Math belong to a shared Celtic idiom of magic as metamorphosis. Scholars have also long linked the Fourth Branch's otherworld material — Arawn's swine, the phantom fleet — to the mythology of [[manawydan|Manawydan]] and the First and Third Branches.
gwydion.culturalLegacy: Gwydion's afterlife runs from Welsh tradition into modern letters. Later Welsh usage named the Milky Way Caer Gwydion, 'Gwydion's fortress' — the enchanter's castle written across the night sky — and the antiquarian bards kept his tree-battle in the poetic canon. In the twentieth century he entered world literature twice over: Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) rebuilt the Blodeuwedd tragedy as a haunting that repeats itself down the generations of a Welsh valley, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain gave young readers a Prince Gwydion fab Don, heir of Math, drawn directly from the Fourth Branch. Evangeline Walton's retellings of the Mabinogion made his punishment and restoration the moral hinge of her Fourth Branch volume. In scholarship he remains the standard exhibit of the Welsh magician: Ifor Williams's edition, Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi, and Koch's Celtic encyclopedia all treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose and Gwydion as its animating intelligence.
gwydion.extendedMeditation: Gwydion is what a culture makes of cleverness when it refuses to call cleverness innocent. His illusions win a war and buy a rape; the tale answers by putting him, for three years, into the bodies of beasts, one year for each shape of the debt. But the same hands that tricked a king out of his swine later coax a dying god out of a tree, one verse at a time, and the same wand that punishes him he is finally trusted to hold. The Fourth Branch's calm is that magic and justice are one craft: to know the true shape of a thing — a name, a name-day, a wound, a woman made of flowers — is to be able to change it, and to be answerable for the change. Gwydion is the enchanter who learns, and teaches, that power over forms is a form of responsibility.
gwydion.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Gwydion (the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest), and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain gwydion.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

sources.name: Ifor Williams, Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi
John T. Koch, Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia

gwydion.archaeology: Gwydion is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), in which the Fourth Branch survives, and the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth 2, early 14th c.) for Kat Godeu. The tale's geography is walkable real terrain — Gwynedd, Dyfed, Penllyn, the river Cynfael — and a holed stone traditionally pointed out as Llech Ronw, 'Gronw's stone', the slab Lleu's spear pierced, stands in the Cynfael valley; the identification is local tradition rather than proof, but it shows how early and how firmly the story was mapped onto the Welsh landscape.

phonemes.desc: Long close back vowel [oː], the Old Irish ó that opens the name; the later spellings Aengus and Angus record its long drift toward a diphthong and then a plain vowel.
Voiced velar nasal [ŋ], the n drawn back before g — the ng of English 'singer', never a hard en-g split.
Voiced velar stop [g], kept hard after the nasal; the lenition that softens intervocalic g in Irish does not touch this cluster.
Short back [u] with voiceless [s], the unstressed final syllable — the masculine -us ending of the o-stem name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OHN-gus' — one long open 'oh', the ng of 'singer', a hard g, and a short unstressed 'us'. Modern Irish Aonghus and Scottish Aonghas have worn it toward 'AYN-guhs' — the Anglicized Angus.
