pronunciation.note: Aengus is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple form is plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to rescue. The normalized Old Irish Óengus does carry a fada, but the project follows the unaccented Middle Irish Aengus, and the mechanical rule judges the restored form, not the manuscript one. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the god's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Love, Youth, Poetry
domains.subtitle: The Mac Óc — the Son of the Young, god of Brú na Bóinne
domains.lead: Aengus — Old Irish Óengus, the mac ind Óc, 'son of the young' — is the ever-young god of the Túatha Dé Danann, son of [[dagda|the Dagda]] and Bóand, the goddess of the Boyne. His dossier is the strangest kind of power in the Irish corpus: not the club or the spear, but the dream, the bargain, and the unaging house. He was conceived and born in a single day the sun was made to hold still; he won the greatest mound in Ireland on a quibble of grammar; he loved a girl he had seen only in sleep, and found her by searching every lake in Ireland for a year. Where his father's strength is provision, his is patience: the young god who waits out time itself.

cards.name: The Dream
cards.desc: In the Aislinge Óenguso a maiden comes to him in sleep with music; he sickens for love of a woman he has never seen awake, and the dream must be hunted like a quarry.

cards.name: The Swan
cards.desc: Caer Ibormeith lives one year as a girl and one as a swan among a hundred and fifty swans on Loch Bél Dracon; to win her, Óengus takes the swan-shape himself.

cards.name: Brú na Bóinne
cards.desc: The Brug on the Boyne — síd in Broga, the mound the world calls Newgrange — his Otherworld house, won from the Dagda for 'a day and a night' and kept ever since.

cards.name: The Day and the Night
cards.desc: Asked when he would surrender the mound lent 'for a day and a night', he answered that the whole world is spent in days and nights — and the answer has never been overturned.

symbols.name: Brú na Bóinne
symbols.meaning: The Brug on the Boyne, his unaging house — the síd the tales call síd in Broga and the world calls Newgrange

symbols.name: The swan-shape
symbols.meaning: The form he takes at Samain on Loch Bél Dracon to win Caer Ibormeith — love answered in kind, shape for shape

symbols.name: The dream (aisling)
symbols.meaning: The maiden's nightly visit with her timpán — desire that arrives before its object, and must be pursued into the waking world

symbols.name: The day and the night
symbols.meaning: The quibble that holds the Brug forever — time itself parsed as a loan without a term

symbols.name: The crystal bower
symbols.meaning: The grianán he built at the Brug for Étaín in her fly-shape — shelter given to a hunted woman when no one else could hold her

mythology.lead: Aengus's mythology is a study in winning without fighting. The three great set-pieces — his birth inside a stopped day, his taking of the Brug, and the dream-quest for Caer Ibormeith — are all victories of time: time held still, time parsed, time waited out. Cath Maige Tuired and Tochmarc Étaíne add the counselor and the host: the son whose wit saves his father, and the keeper of the Brug who shelters Étaín when the whole of Ireland has no safer room.

myths.title: The Day the Sun Stood Still
myths.text:
The Dagda desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand to Bres. To hide what followed, the tale says, the Dagda made the sun stand still: nine months passed, and the world reckoned it a single day — so the child was conceived and born within one day, and Elcmar came home none the wiser. They named the boy Óengus, but the story gave him the name that stuck: mac ind Óc, 'the son of the young', because young was the day that bore him.

The episode fixes the god's signature before he can speak: he is a child of bent time. Bóand, the Boyne itself made goddess, is his mother; the Dagda, the All-Father, his sire; and his first house is the river-bend his father stole a day to give him. The fosterage that followed — with Midir of Brí Léith — placed him among the proudest of the Túatha Dé Danann and set up every tale that came after.

myths.title: A Day and a Night
myths.text:
When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home to claim his share, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne — the Dagda's own house — for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his Brug back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent, and so the grant had no end. The All-Father lost the argument, and the greatest mound in Ireland passed to the son who had read the fine print.

The tale is told with a straight face, but its logic is the logic of the síd itself: the Otherworld does not run on mortal clocks. A god born inside a single stretched day is the natural owner of a house held on a day without a term. Irish law prized the exact word; Óengus's first deed makes etymology into real estate.

myths.title: The Dream of Óengus
myths.text:
A maiden came to Óengus in sleep, playing a timpán, the sweetest music he had heard; for a year she came, and for a year he could not touch her, and when she ceased to come he wasted with love-sickness. The physicians of the Túatha Dé Danann could not cure him, for his sickness was a woman who existed somewhere in the world. Bóand his mother searched Ireland for a year and found nothing; the Dagda searched a year and found nothing; then Bodb Derg, king of the síd of Munster, searched, and at the year's end found her: Caer Ibormeith, daughter of Ethal Anbuail of síd Uaman in Connacht.

But Caer lived under a rhythm no bargain could break: she spent one year in girl's shape and one as a swan, among nine score swans on Loch Bél Dracon, and the change came at Samain. Óengus went to the lake at Samain and saw them, each pair of swans linked by a silver chain, Caer's own chain of gold about her neck. He called to her, and she answered that she would go with him only if he took the swan-shape beside her. He entered the water, became a swan, and they flew three times around the lake — and their music put every listener to sleep for three days and three nights — then away to Brú na Bóinne, where the singing of the two swans became part of the mound's music ever after.

myths.title: The Bower of the Purple Fly
myths.text:
When the jealous Fuamnach struck Étaín with a rod of scarlet quicken-tree and made her a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly, the fly that was Étaín came at last to Brú na Bóinne, to the hall of Óengus. He knew her — the fly's music and its radiance were hers — and he built her a grianán, a sun-bower of crystal filled with healing herbs and the bloom of every field, and she stayed with him there, and the window of the bower let her pass in and out as she pleased.

It could not last. Fuamnach followed the rumor of the fly's good fortune and raised a magic wind that swept Étaín out of the bower and across Ireland for seven years, until she fell into the cup of Étar's wife at the Bay of Cíú and was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth. Óengus's shelter is one of the gentlest episodes in the cycle: the young god keeping one hunted woman safe in the safest house in Ireland, against a malice even his Brug could not finally exclude.

myths.title: The Satirist's Three Gold Coins
myths.text:
Under the tyranny of Bres the Dagda was set to building the usurper's forts, and the satirist Cridenbél taxed him the three best bits of every ration, until the greatest of the gods was failing from hunger — for no one dared refuse a satirist whose curse raised blisters on the face. Óengus came to his father and gave him the counsel that turned the trap: demand of Bres the pick of the cattle of Ireland as wages, and hide three gold coins in the porridge portion meant for the satirist. Cridenbél swallowed greed and gold together and died of it; and when Bres demanded the Dagda's death for the killing, the dead man's own belly gave the verdict — cut open, it held the gold, proof that greed and not the Dagda had killed him.

The episode is the tradition's clearest pairing of father and son: the Dagda's patience carrying the labor, Óengus's wit carrying the case. The young god does not raise a weapon in the whole of Cath Maige Tuired, and does not need to — his contribution to the war that freed the Túatha Dé Danann was a sentence spoken at the right fireside.

aengus.syncretism: The comparison the handbooks prefer for Óengus runs to Gaul and Wales rather than to Rome. The Gaulish Maponos, 'the Divine Son' — known from dedications to Apollo Maponus in the Roman north of Britain and from the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi — is the same figure-type: the ever-young son of a greater divine parent. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt set Maponos beside both Óengus and the Welsh Mabon ap Modron, 'Son son of Mother', the hunter-youth of Culhwch ac Olwen whose name is built on the same Proto-Celtic words *makwos, 'son', and *mātīr, 'mother'. The popular handbooks go further and call Óengus 'the Irish Eros'; the medieval texts give a stranger and more specific figure — a god of dream, youth, and cunning whose love-story is won by patience and shape-changing rather than by arrows. The comparisons are structural and instructive; no inscription identifies him, and the identification of Maponos with Mabon is itself a scholarly argument, not a fact.
aengus.culturalLegacy: No Irish god had a better literary afterlife than the young one. W. B. Yeats made him a byword for longing itself in 'The Song of Wandering Aengus' (1899) — the hazel wand, the fire in the head, the glimmering girl with apple blossom in her hair who called his name and ran — a poem that poured the Aislinge into the bloodstream of modern English verse. James Stephens gave him speaking parts and moods in The Crock of Gold (1912), where Angus Og wanders the Irish countryside being wise and young. In the later Gaelic tradition he never faded: the Fenian tale of Diarmaid and Gráinne keeps him at Brú na Bóinne as Diarmaid's fosterer and protector, and Irish folklore kept the Brug as his house into the modern period. His name took a second, quieter path: worn to Angus, it became one of the most familiar masculine names in Scotland — a theonym hiding in plain sight on every map of Angus and in every roll of Scottish kings. And his address became the most visited prehistoric site in Ireland: Newgrange, where five thousand winters of sun have entered the chamber the tales assigned to the son of the young.
aengus.extendedMeditation:
Aengus is the god of the interval — the stretch of time between wanting and having, and his whole dossier asks what can be done with it. His father held the sun still for nine months to make a day large enough to be born in; the son learned the lesson and spent his career proving that time is a text to be parsed, not a wall to be stormed. A loan of a day and a night is forever, if you read it right. A dream that comes nightly for a year is an address, if you are willing to search every lake in Ireland for it. The name says the same: óen-gus, one vigor, a single strength held undivided — no club, no cauldron, no host, just the one force applied without distraction.

That is why his love-story is the corpus's gentlest. Every other divine wooing in Irish myth is a raid, a riddle, or a revenge; Óengus's is a search. He does not seize Caer Ibormeith; he finds her, asks her, accepts her condition, and meets her in her own shape — a god who becomes a swan because the girl is one. The music the two swans make, which puts the world to sleep for three days, is the dream coming back around: the aisling that began as a haunting ends as a harmony. Youth, in this mythology, is not the season of appetite. It is the season before resignation — the one vigor that has not yet learned to stop looking.
aengus.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Óengus, written in the Insular Latin script of the medieval manuscripts, with a síneadh fada marking the long Ó; the Middle Irish spelling Aengus drops the accent, and the temple follows that unaccented form. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: aengus.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

aengus.archaeology: Aengus is a textual god — no ogham stone names him and no votive inscription invokes him — but his mythic address is the single most famous piece of prehistoric architecture in Ireland. Brú na Bóinne, the palace of the Boyne, is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and the passage tomb of Newgrange (c. 3200 BCE), older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, has been identified with the tales' síd in Broga, Óengus's Brug, since the medieval topographical tradition. The mound's roof-box, which admits the rising sun into the chamber on the mornings around the winter solstice, was excavated and documented by Michael J. O'Kelly (1962–1975), who observed the phenomenon in 1967 — a real alignment behind the mythology of a god born of a stopped sun. The witnesses to the texts are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre and later manuscripts; Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's edition. For the comparative figure, the material record is Romano-British: altars dedicated to Apollo Maponus from the military north, including the Corbridge series, with the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi completing the map of the Divine Son's cult — comparative evidence, never identification.

phonemes.desc: Short open back unrounded [ɑ], stressed as the first syllable of every Old Norse word; brief, not the long á.
Alveolar nasal [n] followed by a fully voiced stop [d]; in runic carving the d would be written with the t-rune, which underspecifies voicing.
Voiced labiodental [v] as in English 'very', a second short [ɑ], trilled [r], and a short close [i]; the name is a weak masculine and carries no added nominative -r.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AHND-vah-ri' — three even syllables, stress on the first, the v soft as in 'very', the r trilled, the ending a short 'ih' as in 'bit'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Andvari, the dwarf of Andvarafors; beside the proper name stands the common noun andvari, 'care, solicitude, watchfulness'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛅᚾᛏᚢᛅᚱᛁ (a-n-t-u-a-r-i) — the sixteen-rune Viking-Age rendering, with ᛏ writing the voiced d and ᚢ writing v.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Andvari — the name revived as the title of the learned journal of the Icelandic Literary Society, founded 1874.

pronunciation.note: Andvari is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the ASCII alphabet loses nothing in copying it. The dwarf's fame rides on his ring, not on his orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Dwarf, Guardian of Gold
domains.subtitle: The Careful One of the Waterfall
domains.lead: Andvari is the dwarf who lived in the waterfall Andvarafors in a pike's shape, sweeping his gold about him with his fins — the most careful hoarder in the northern corpus, and the owner of the ring Andvaranaut. When Loki caught him in Rán's net and stripped him of everything to pay the otter's ransom, Andvari spoke the curse that made his gold a death sentence for every hand that held it after him: Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, and the whole line of the Gjúkungar.

cards.name: Andvarafors
cards.desc: The waterfall that was his hall — the stream where he swam in a pike's shape and kept his gold, named for him in Reginsmál's prose.

cards.name: Andvaranaut
cards.desc: 'Andvari's jewel' — the last ring of the hoard, hidden in his hand, taken by force, and answered with the curse that every owner would find death in it.

cards.name: Rán's Net
cards.desc: The sea-queen's net that Loki borrowed to drag the waterfall — the tool that turned a fishing into an extortion.

cards.name: The Pike-Shape
cards.desc: The fish-form in which he swept his hoard through the water — the careful one's disguise, netted all the same.

symbols.name: Andvaranaut
symbols.meaning: The ring taken last and cursed first — a treasure that kills every hand it passes through

symbols.name: Andvarafors
symbols.meaning: The waterfall named for its keeper — a hoard-hall that flows and cannot be locked

symbols.name: Rán's net
symbols.meaning: Borrowed catching-power — the gods paying a blood-debt with a fisherman's trick

symbols.name: The pike-shape
symbols.meaning: The disguise of the careful — a form made for guarding, not for fighting

symbols.name: The otter's ransom
symbols.meaning: The wergild that had to cover a dead otter's skin from the inside — gold counted out hair by hair

mythology.lead: Andvari's dossier is a single episode and its long echo: one afternoon's extortion at a waterfall, and a curse that runs through the rest of the Völsung cycle like poison through water. Reginsmál's prose, Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, and Völsunga saga all tell the catching; everything after — Fáfnir's dragon, Sigurðr's sword, the gold sunk in the Rhine — is the curse working itself out.

myths.title: The Otter's Ransom
myths.text:
Óðinn, Loki, and Hœnir were traveling when they came to a waterfall, and there they saw an otter eating a salmon on the bank, its eyes shut. Loki killed it with a stone and boasted of a double catch — otter and fish at one cast. But the otter was Ótr, son of the farmer Hreiðmarr, a shape-shifter who took a pike's or otter's form to fish the falls. That night the gods sought lodging at Hreiðmarr's house and showed their catch; Hreiðmarr called his sons Fáfnir and Reginn, and the three seized the gods and bound them. The wergild was set by the skin itself: the otter's hide was to be filled with red gold, and then covered with gold from the outside until not a hair showed. Óðinn sent Loki to get the gold, and Loki went down to the world of the black-elves to find it where it lay — in the keeping of a dwarf at a waterfall.

Snorri tells the same in Skáldskaparmál as the explanation of gold's kennings: this is why poets call gold the otter's ransom, the forced payment of the Æsir. The episode exists in the tradition to gloss poetry — a myth doing the work of a dictionary.

myths.title: The Net of Rán
myths.text:
Völsunga saga gives the fullest account of the catching. Loki went to Rán, the sea-queen who drowns sailors, and borrowed her net, then came to the waterfall called Andvarafors. There lived the dwarf Andvari, who kept a pike's shape in the water and swept his gold about him, guarding everything. Loki cast the net and caught him, and demanded the ransom: all the gold in the waterfall, or Andvari's head.

The dwarf paid over the hoard — but he kept one ring back, a small thing, hidden in his hand. Loki saw it and took that too, despite Andvari's plea that with the ring kept he could breed gold again and would not beggar himself entirely. Loki answered that one coin would be too many to leave him, and went up out of the water with the whole of it. Reginsmál's prose tells the same catching more briefly: Loki got Rán's net, cast it before the pike, and the dwarf paid the otter's ransom from his own keeping.

myths.title: The Curse on the Ring
myths.text:
Stripped of everything, Andvari did the only thing left to a dwarf with nothing: he spoke. Reginsmál's prose preserves the curse as the tradition's own words: the gold that Gustr had owned — Gustr, 'Gust', the other name the prose gives the dwarf — would be the death of two brothers, and would bring strife to eight of the kin-line — eight ættlingar — and no man would ever have joy of his wealth. Völsunga saga gives the same sentence over the ring itself: it would be the death of every man who owned it.

The ring got a name from its first owner's loss: Andvaranaut, 'Andvari's jewel'. Nothing in the corpus says the curse was magic in the modern sense; it needs none. What the careful one laid on the gold was a prophecy any listener could verify, because the gold itself was now worth killing for — and the story spends the rest of its length proving him right, owner by owner.

myths.title: Fáfnir's Bed of Gold
myths.text:
The gods filled the otter-skin and covered it, and the last hair was covered with Andvaranaut itself — Loki had kept the ring back from Hreiðmarr until that final hair, so that even the last coin of the hoard went into the ransom. The gods went free. But Hreiðmarr refused his sons any share of the gold, and the curse began its work at once: Fáfnir killed his father sleeping, took all the treasure, and refused Reginn a share in turn. He carried the hoard out to the heath called Gnitaheiðr, and there he brooded on it until he became the worst of serpents — a dragon lying on his gold, wearing the helmet of terror.

Reginn, cheated, went to the court of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to Sigurðr of the Völsung line. He reforged the sword Gram from the shards of Sigmund's blade and egged the young man to the heath. Sigurðr dug a pit in the dragon's path, stabbed up into the belly as Fáfnir crawled over him to drink, and then — warned by the nuthatches that Reginn meant him harm — cut off his foster-father's head. He ate of the dragon's heart and understood the speech of birds; he loaded the hoard, Andvaranaut and all, on Grani's back. The careful one's gold had a new owner, and the third owner of the ring was the greatest hero of the North. The curse did not care.

myths.title: The Gold in the Rhine
myths.text:
From Sigurðr the treasure passed as blood-price and dowry into the house of the Gjúkungar — Gunnar, Högni, and their sister Guðrún, whom Sigurðr married. When Sigurðr was murdered in his bed over Brynhildr's vengeance, the hoard was the Gjúkungs' alone, and it drew King Atli, Brynhildr's brother, who invited his brothers-in-law to his hall to take it from them. Gunnar and Högni rode knowing the invitation was death, and before they crossed the Rhine they did the last careful thing anyone does with Andvari's gold: they sank the whole hoard in the river, in deep water, where no one would have joy of it — the dwarf's sentence carried out by its victims themselves.

Atli's men cut Högni's heart out and cast Gunnar living into a pit of serpents, where he played the harp with his toes until an adder struck him to the heart; the hoard he died to keep lay at the bottom of the Rhine, ownerless. Atlakviða ends the account with the river itself as the treasure's last keeper: the Rhine shall hold the strife-metal of the Niflungar. Two brothers dead, eight princes at strife, no man the happier — Reginsmál's prophecy closed like a hand. Andvari was avenged on everyone, which is to say on no one in particular, which is exactly what a curse is.

andvari.syncretism: Andvari needs no foreign counterpart to be understood — the cursed-hoard complex is native Germanic and runs through the whole North: treasure extorted is treasure poisoned. The corpus itself supplies the sharpest contrast in another dwarf-ring: Draupnir, forged freely by [[brokkr|Brokkr]] and [[sindri|Sindri]] for the gods, which drips eight new rings every ninth night — the given ring multiplies, the taken ring kills. Continental heroic tradition keeps the same stratum: the hoard of the Nibelungenlied, sunk in the Rhine and deadly to its holders, is the southern telling of the Andvaranaut complex, and scholars from Lindow onward treat the Norse and German versions as one inheritance rather than borrowings. The dwarf caught in fish-shape also has a family resemblance to the water-spirits of later folklore, but the Eddic Andvari is a smith and hoarder first; his pike-form is camouflage, not nature.
andvari.culturalLegacy: Andvari's afterlife is one of the largest in all mythology, under another name. Wagner's Alberich in Das Rheingold — the dwarf of the water's depth who is robbed of his gold, lays a curse on the ring forged from it, and watches it destroy owner after owner through four operas — is built substantially on the Andvari of Reginsmál and Völsunga saga, crossed with the Nibelungenlied's hoard; the curse-motif that drives the entire Ring cycle is the sentence spoken at Andvarafors. William Morris's Sigurd the Volsung (1876) kept the original name before English readers, and the Nibelungenlied's Rhine-gold carried the same hoard into German memory. In Iceland the name itself was revived with no curse attached: Andvari is the title of the learned journal of the Icelandic Literary Society, founded in 1874 — the careful one finally keeping something that multiplies without killing. Modern fantasy's treasury of cursed gold, from dragons' hoards onward, runs downhill from his waterfall.
andvari.extendedMeditation: His name is care itself — andvari, watchfulness, the quality of mind that checks the locks twice. And the myth is merciless to it: the most careful keeper in the corpus is caught in an afternoon, by a borrowed net, in his own water, and stripped to the last hidden ring. Care could not save him, because care guards against theft and what came for him was law — a wergild, a debt, a skin that had to be covered hair by hair. What he had left was speech, and he used it like a dwarf: precisely, vindictively, and with perfect aim. The curse is the one thing he made that nobody could take, because it was already given. Everything after is arithmetic — two brothers, eight princes, no joy — and the myth lets the numbers run for four generations to teach a single lesson the North never tired of: gold that is taken by force does not change owners; it changes victims. Andvari in his waterfall is the small still beginning of the Völsung tragedy, the moment the hook was set. The careful one's revenge on the careless world was simply to tell it the truth about what it had just picked up.
andvari.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Andvari — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛅᚾᛏᚢᛅᚱᛁ (a-n-t-u-a-r-i, the t-rune writing d and úr writing v). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: andvari.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Reginsmál, prose introduction (the killing of Ótr, Rán's net, the ransom, and the curse: 'the gold that Gustr owned shall be the death of two brothers and bring strife to eight of the kin-line; no man shall have joy of my wealth')
Poetic Edda: Fáfnismál (Sigurðr and the dying dragon on the hoard) and Atlakviða (the Gjúkungs, the sunken gold, the Rhine as last keeper)
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál (the otter's ransom and the kennings for gold — 'forced payment of the Æsir', 'Fáfnir's bed', 'metal of Gnitaheiðr')

andvari.archaeology: Andvari himself is a purely literary figure: no runestone, votive deposit, or named image records him. But the cycle his gold sets in motion is the best-attested narrative in Viking-Age art. The Ramsund carving in Södermanland (Sö 101, c. 1030) cuts the whole Fáfnir episode into a rock face — Sigurðr thrusting up through the serpent's body, the slain Reginn with his smith's tools, Grani loaded with the treasure, and the birds whose speech the dragon-heart taught — and the Gök stone (Sö 327) weaves the same scenes through a runic inscription. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) shows Sigurðr stabbing the serpent, and related scenes appear on the Isle of Man and in English stone sculpture as far west as the Halton cross in Lancashire, tracking the cycle along the Norse sea-roads. The manuscript witnesses are thin in the usual way: Reginsmál and its narrative prose stand in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda, Snorri's account in the codices of the Prose Edda, and Völsunga saga in the paper manuscript NKS 1824 b 4to (c. 1400), the saga's only complete medieval copy.

phonemes.desc: Short open [a], stressed on the first syllable as in most Welsh words; the 'a' of 'cat' opened slightly.
Geminate alveolar nasal [nː], written double and held longer than a single English n.
The letter w is here a full vowel: short high back rounded [ʊ], the 'oo' of English 'put' — never a consonant.
Final alveolar nasal [n], closing the second syllable cleanly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AN-oon' — two syllables, stress on the first; the w is sounded as a short 'oo', so the name rhymes with 'cannon' said with Welsh vowels.

kin.form: Annwfn, the spelling of the manuscripts — the f is the voiced [v] of lenited final -m, and the word was often understood as an- + dwfn, 'the deep, the abyss'

The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the realm's fame in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Otherworld, Underworld
domains.subtitle: The Deep, the Abyss — realm of the feast and the hunt
domains.lead: Annwn is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry — a realm of plenty where the feast never fails, ruled in the First Branch by [[arawn|Arawn]], and hunted across by Gwyn ap Nudd, whom God set over the demons of Annwn lest they destroy this world. Its cauldron, borne home from its fortresses at terrible cost, is the oldest quest of Arthurian tradition.

cards.name: The Cauldron of the Head of Annwn
cards.desc: Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, it will not boil a coward's food — the prize of Arthur's voyage in Preiddeu Annwfn.

cards.name: The Hounds of Annwn
cards.desc: Arawn's pack — gleaming white with red ears, the colours the Welsh tradition gives every creature from the Otherworld.

cards.name: Prydwen
cards.desc: Arthur's ship on the voyage to the fortresses of Annwn — three full loads went in; except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.

cards.name: The Hunt of Gwyn ap Nudd
cards.desc: The son of Nudd rides with the hunt of Annwn; in Culhwch ac Olwen, God set him over its demons lest they destroy this world.

symbols.name: The cauldron of Pen Annwn
symbols.meaning: Plenty that will not serve the coward — abundance that answers only to courage

symbols.name: White hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colours of the Otherworld made flesh — beauty that marks the boundary crossed

symbols.name: Caer Sidi and the fortresses
symbols.meaning: The revolving castle and its sister fortresses — the Otherworld as architecture that must be won, not visited

symbols.name: Prydwen
symbols.meaning: Arthur's ship — the voyage into the deep from which only seven returned

symbols.name: The year's exchange
symbols.meaning: Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes and kingdoms — the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face

mythology.lead: Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself.

myths.title: The Year in Annwn
myths.text:
Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before.

Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn.

myths.title: The Spoils of Annwn
myths.text:
The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back.

The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned.

myths.title: Gwyn ap Nudd and the Demons of Annwn
myths.text:
The great hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen names its most uncanny huntsman: Gwyn ap Nudd, son of Nudd — 'God has set him over the demons of Annwn, lest this world be destroyed.' The hunt of the boar Twrch Trwyth cannot be accomplished without him, and so Gwyn rides out of Annwn at Arthur's muster: the Otherworld's own power, conscripted to keep its worst inhabitants leashed.

The same tale gives Gwyn his famous quarrel. He had carried off Creiddylad, daughter of Lludd, from her father's house, and Gwythyr ap Greidawl raised a host and took her back; Arthur judged between them — the maiden to remain with her father, and the two to fight for her every May Day until the Day of Judgment, when the winner takes her for good. Gwyn's hunt is therefore not seasonal sport but a standing order: Annwn's violence rides out under a king who is himself a covenant.

myths.title: The King on Glastonbury Tor
myths.text:
The Welsh Life of St Collen gives Annwn its most local address. Collen, keeping his hermitage under Glastonbury Tor, hears two men say that Gwyn ap Nudd — king of Annwn and of the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Folk — holds his court above. Collen answers that the hosts of the air are demons; a summons follows, and on the summit he finds a castle of the utmost splendour, the king on a golden chair, and a banquet of dishes he has never seen the like of.

Collen sprinkles his holy water over the food, and the whole vision dissolves — castle, court, and king gone as if they had never been, leaving the saint standing on the green Tor. The tale is late and Christian, but it keeps the old facts in place: Gwyn is king of Annwn, his hall is a feast beyond earthly measure, and the Otherworld can open on a hillside in Somerset and close again without a trace.

annwn.syncretism: Annwn's clearest kin are Irish: the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann, where the feast likewise never fails — the Dagda's cauldron of Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standing comparison for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and Mac Cana sets the two vessels side by side as one Celtic figure-type. The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach, lands 'without grief, without sorrow, without death' — matches Annwn's profile point for point: plenty, beauty, and the suspension of age and sickness. Yet the Brythonic tradition is not a copy of the Gaelic one: no Irish text knows the name Annwn, and the Welsh corpus built its Otherworld on its own geography — the ford at Glyn Cuch, the revolving fortresses of the Taliesin poem, the Tor at Glastonbury. The Christian redactors left the structure intact while re-labelling its inhabitants: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's splendid court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour without surrendering one detail of the feast.
annwn.culturalLegacy: Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the Otherworld fortresses is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the Head of Annwn's cauldron — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root. The name kept working in Welsh: Annwn remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later Welsh folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death. Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman and psychopomp of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Restoring Annwn in Unicode costs nothing and fixes something: the canonical spelling of the deep, held against the drift of anglicized spellings like Annwvyn and Annwyn.
annwn.extendedMeditation:
Annwn is the rare Otherworld whose name tells you where it is: an- + dwfn, the un-deep, the very deep — not a land over the sea or under a hill but the depth beneath the world, the place the surface world is the skin of. The tradition never pretends it is far away. Pwyll stumbles into it on an ordinary hunt by breaking an ordinary courtesy; it lies a year's shape-shift away, close enough for two kings to trade faces and governments across it.

And its gifts all carry a price exacted in courage. The feast is boundless, but the cauldron will not boil a coward's food; the voyage is possible, but except seven none returned; the hunt rides out, but it rides to keep the demons of the deep leashed for the world's sake. Annwn is the Celtic imagination's answer to the question of what lies underneath: plenty without limit, behind a door that only opens once — and a word for it, five plain letters, that still means the deep.
annwn.originalScriptNote: Welsh has been written in the Latin alphabet throughout its manuscript history, and the normalized form Annwn is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The manuscripts spell the name Annwfn (Middle Welsh f writes the voiced [v]); the modern normalized spelling is Annwn. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: annwn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed (First Branch of the Mabinogi) — the meeting at Glyn Cuch, the year's exchange, the defeat of Hafgan, the title Pen Annwn; ed. Ifor Williams, Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930); trans. Sioned Davies, The Mabinogion (2007)

Preiddeu Annwfn (The Spoils of Annwfn), Book of Taliesin — Arthur's voyage in Prydwen, the fortresses, the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn, 'except seven, none returned'; ed. and trans. Marged Haycock, Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (2007)
Culhwch ac Olwen — Gwyn ap Nudd set over the demons of Annwn; the May Day fight with Gwythyr for Creiddylad; ed. Rachel Bromwich and D. Simon Evans (1992)
Buchedd Collen (The Life of St Collen) — Gwyn ap Nudd's court on Glastonbury Tor and the banquet dispelled by holy water
Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru / A Dictionary of the Welsh Language, s.v. annwfn ('the otherworld, the abyss')

Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology; Koch, Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, s.v. Annwfn; MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology, s.v. Annwn (lexicon authorities for this entry: Mabinogion, MacKillop)

annwn.archaeology: Annwn is a wholly textual realm: no inscription invokes it, and the Romano-British epigraphy of Wales is silent on the Otherworld by name. Its manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Mabinogi survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two great codices of medieval Welsh prose; Preiddeu Annwfn is preserved uniquely in the Book of Taliesin (National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century); and Culhwch ac Olwen comes down in a White Book fragment and the full Red Book text. The one site the tradition ties to Annwn is Glastonbury Tor, Gwyn ap Nudd's seat in Buchedd Collen: excavations on the Tor in the 1960s found sub-Roman and early medieval occupation beneath the ruins of St Michael's church — real archaeology on the hill, though none of it speaks to the Otherworld, whose only true location is the text.

phonemes.desc: Unstressed short open [a], the light first syllable; Welsh stress has not yet fallen.
Trilled or tapped [r] followed by the Welsh diphthong aw [aʊ] — the 'ow' of English 'town'; this is the stressed penult that carries the whole weight of the name.
Final alveolar nasal [n], closing the stressed syllable cleanly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'a-ROWN' — the aw sounds like the 'ow' of 'town', and the stress falls on the second syllable, the Welsh penult.

kin.form: Arawn, king of Annwn in Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed, the First Branch of the Mabinogi.

kin.form: Aaron — the derivation proposed by Ifor Williams and registered as a possibility by the modern handbooks.

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Arawn, a rare but living given name.

kin.label: Welsh folklore
kin.form: Master of the Cŵn Annwn, the white red-eared hounds of the Otherworld — a folk elaboration of his Mabinogi pack.

pronunciation.note: Arawn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The lexicon's traditional gloss is 'silver-tongued', but the etymology is genuinely unsettled: scholars have proposed a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron (a suggestion going back to Ifor Williams) as well as native Celtic derivations, and no derivation commands consensus (Koch; GPC, s.v. Arawn).

domains.title: The King of Annwn
domains.subtitle: Otherworld, Annwn
domains.lead: Arawn is the king of Annwn, the Welsh Otherworld: the lord whose white, red-eared hounds bring down a stag in Pwyll's hunting-ground at Glyn Cuch, and whose answer to the insult is the strangest exchange in the Mabinogi — a year and a day in which two kings trade faces, thrones, and beds, so that honor may be tested where no one is watching.

cards.name: The White Hounds
cards.desc: Arawn's pack, shining white with red ears — the colour of the Otherworld, a sight Pwyll had never seen on any hound of his own.

cards.name: The Exchange of Shapes
cards.desc: A year and a day in which Arawn takes Pwyll's form in Dyfed and Pwyll takes Arawn's in Annwn — and neither court suspects.

cards.name: The Ford
cards.desc: The appointed meeting-place where Pwyll must face Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn — with one blow and no more.

cards.name: The Untouched Bed
cards.desc: Arawn's queen, the fairest woman Pwyll had ever seen — with whom he shares a bed for a year and never turns his face to her.

symbols.name: The white hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colour of the Otherworld — a hunt that arrives from the far side of the boundary

symbols.name: The exchanged shape
symbols.meaning: Kingship as a trust held for another: the year Arawn's face ruled two realms

symbols.name: The single blow
symbols.meaning: Restraint as the condition of victory — strike once, or not at all

symbols.name: The untouched bed
symbols.meaning: Honor kept in the dark, where no one would ever have known

symbols.name: The ford
symbols.meaning: The meeting-place between realms, where debts are paid and blows are counted

symbols.name: The yearly gifts
symbols.meaning: Friendship renewed in kind — horses, greyhounds, hawks, and treasure

mythology.lead: Arawn's whole dossier is one story, and it is the opening movement of the Mabinogi: the hunting-debt at Glyn Cuch and the year-long exchange that turns an insult into the strongest friendship in Welsh prose. Every word of it is preserved in the First Branch, Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.

myths.title: The Wrong at Glyn Cuch
myths.text: Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, goes hunting at Glyn Cuch, and there he sees a sight he has never seen: a pack of hounds shining white with red ears bringing down a stag. He drives them off and sets his own hounds on the kill — and the stranger who rides up is Arawn, king of Annwn, and it was his hunt. Arawn names the discourtesy plainly: he will not take revenge, but a man who feeds his hounds on another's kill has wronged him, and Pwyll offers to buy back his friendship at whatever price. Arawn names it. He has a rival, Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn, who wars on him without end; let Pwyll take Arawn's shape and his place for a year and a day, and meet Hafgan at the ford at the year's turning.

myths.title: The Exchange of Shapes
myths.text: Each king takes the other's form and goes to the other's court, and neither realm suspects. Arawn rules Dyfed so well that there had never been so good a year in it. Pwyll enters Annwn in Arawn's likeness, and that first night he is led to the bed of Arawn's wife — the fairest and most comely woman he had ever seen. He turns his back to her, and he does so every night of the year: he speaks to her with courtesy by day, and in the bed he never once turns his face toward her. The queen never knows. The whole test of the tale is here, in the dark, where no one could have seen the difference.

myths.title: The Single Blow at the Ford
myths.text: Arawn's instructions were exact: Hafgan — the name suggests 'Summer-White' — can be slain by one blow, and only one; strike him a second time and he will rise as strong as before and fight again the next day. At the appointed time the two kings meet at the ford, and at the first clash Pwyll strikes Hafgan one blow that shears through his shield and armour, and Hafgan knows he is dead. 'For God's sake,' he begs, 'finish me' — and Pwyll refuses: the stroke he gave is all Hafgan will have from him. Hafgan's nobles declare their king lost, and Pwyll takes the submission and hostages of Hafgan's realm, so that the two kingdoms of Annwn are made one under Arawn's crown.

myths.title: The Restoration and the Title
myths.text: The two kings meet again at the ford where they had arranged it, each in his own shape, and embrace and go home. Arawn's queen, rejoicing at his return, remarks that he has not spoken to her as he does tonight for a whole year — and Arawn praises God for a friend so true. In Dyfed, Pwyll's court hears the story and tells him he did well to make such a friend. From that time the two realms send each other gifts every year: horses and greyhounds and hawks, and every kind of treasure they think will please. And because Pwyll had ruled Annwn and joined its two kingdoms in one, he was called from then on Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll Head of Annwn — in place of Pwyll lord of Dyfed.

myths.title: The Hounds and the Spoils of Annwn
myths.text: The Mabinogi never brings Arawn back on stage, but his world keeps growing. The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwn', preserved in the Book of Taliesin, sends Arthur's men to raid the Otherworld for the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — Pen Annwfn, the very title the First Branch gives Pwyll's honour — and only seven come home. The poem never names Annwn's king, and honest scholarship leaves it unnamed. Later Welsh folklore knows the Cŵn Annwn, the Hounds of Annwn — white with red ears, exactly Arawn's pack — whose baying across the night sky was heard as a death-omen, and folk tradition gave their mastery to Gwyn ap Nudd rather than to Arawn. The hounds outgrew their first master; the year of the exchange did not.

arawn.syncretism: Arawn's comparisons are almost all inward, and the Welsh corpus itself supplies them. His clearest rival for the kingship of the Otherworld is Gwyn ap Nudd, whom Culhwch ac Olwen says God set over the demons of Annwn — a second king of Annwn in a second text, and the folklore gave Gwyn the hounds that the Mabinogi gave Arawn. The structural reading runs deeper: commentators since Mac Cana have read the Annwn adventure as the proving of Pwyll's character before the coming of [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] — the hero tested in honor and restraint in the Otherworld before the Otherworld's queen chooses him in this one. The name itself may be the tale's one foreign guest: Ifor Williams proposed that Arawn is a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron, carried into Welsh by Latin learning, and the handbooks register the possibility without deciding it. No Gaulish or Irish counterpart of Arawn has ever been convincingly proposed; the exchange-of-kings motif is the Mabinogi's own.
arawn.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Arawn out of the White and Red Books and into English, and the white red-eared hounds entered the stock of Celtic imagery from that day. In the twentieth century the figure found his widest audience inverted: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'Arawn Death-Lord of Annuvin' the arch-villain of five children's novels, and Disney's The Black Cauldron (1985) kept the dark-lord version on screen — a long way from the most honorable king in Welsh prose, but the reason the name is known worldwide. The Cŵn Annwn meanwhile never left Welsh folklore, still baying as a death-omen in folk memory into the modern period. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours Arawn as lord of the Otherworld and patron of kept faith, and the name survives in Wales as a rare living given name.
arawn.extendedMeditation: Arawn sets the one test that cannot be cheated: he gives a stranger his face, his throne, and his bed, and waits a year to learn what the stranger is. Everything Pwyll does in Annwn is invisible — no one in either kingdom can tell the kings apart, and no one will ever know what passed in the bed unless the doer confesses it. That is exactly the point. Honor, the First Branch argues, is what a man does when the only witness is himself. The tale rewards it without sentimentality: the kept faith becomes an unbroken friendship, an otherworld alliance, the title Pen Annwfn, and a court that tells its lord he chose his friend well. Arawn's kingdom is the far side of the world, but his question is asked everywhere: who are you when no one is watching?
arawn.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Arawn — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: arawn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/arawn/ in the meantime.

arawn.archaeology: Arawn is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of the tale is real: Glyn Cuch, where the insult happens, is identified with the valley of the River Cych on the Pembrokeshire–Carmarthenshire border, inside the Dyfed the story governs. The nearest material echo of the Otherworld hunt is literary: the Book of Taliesin, the manuscript that preserves Preiddeu Annwfn, is a fourteenth-century Welsh codex (NLW Peniarth MS 2).

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], broad (velarized) before a; as in English 'bay', with the tongue already set for the wide vowel.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the single syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief.
Lenited [ð], the voiced dental fricative of English 'this', running into lenited final [β], a soft bilabial v — both consonants melt in speech though the spelling keeps them whole.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-dhuv' — one short syllable; let the d soften into the 'th' of 'this' and the final b melt into a light v. Modern Irish badhbh keeps the softening, and English ears often hear the word as something like 'bave'.

domains.title: Battle, Death, Crow
domains.subtitle: The Scald-Crow of the Battlefield
domains.lead: Badb is the Irish war-goddess whose name is her shape: badb, the scald-crow — the grey-and-black hooded crow that walks the battlefield when the spears have done their work. She is one of the three of war whom the Lebor Gabála calls the daughters of Ernmas — Badb, Macha, and Anand, the Morrígan — and the Táin gives her its most terrible sound: the shriek over the marching hosts that kills men with fear before a blow is struck. She never fights; she foretells, she panics, and she gathers what the battle leaves.

cards.name: Badb Catha
cards.desc: 'Crow of battle' — her standing title in the texts: the bird that haunts the field and the goddess who owns it are one word.

cards.name: The Shriek over the Hosts
cards.desc: At Gáirech and Irgáirech, the Táin says, Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above the armies until a hundred warriors fell dead of fright.

cards.name: The Ford
cards.desc: The boundary water where the war-goddess stands washing — the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius, the washer of the doomed in the later Gaelic tradition.

cards.name: The Daughters of Ernmas
cards.desc: Badb, Macha, and Anand — the triple face of Irish war, three sisters of one mother whom the sources also call by the single name Morrígan.

symbols.name: The scald-crow
symbols.meaning: The hooded crow, grey and black — her name, her shape, and her retinue on every field

symbols.name: The shriek
symbols.meaning: Panic as a weapon: the sound that kills men with fear before the spear is thrown

symbols.name: The ford
symbols.meaning: The boundary between bank and bank, living and dead — the water where the doomed are read

symbols.name: The triad
symbols.meaning: Badb, Macha, Némain: the three of war, one terror in three voices

symbols.name: The washing of spoils
symbols.meaning: The harness and garments of the soon-dead, rinsed in the ford before the battle that will bloody them

mythology.lead: Badb's dossier is genealogy, sound, and omen rather than adventure: she is the sister in the list, the voice over the army, the bird on the pillar-stone. The Lebor Gabála fixes her family, the Táin fixes her weapon, and the death-tales fix her posture — and the commentators have spent a century and a half working out where she ends and her sisters begin.

myths.title: The Daughters of Ernmas
myths.text:
The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, gives the war-goddesses their pedigree: 'Badb and Macha and Anand, of whom are the Paps of Anu in Luachair, were the three daughters of Ernmas the she-farmer.' The verse recension sings the same family in another key — 'Badb and Macha, greatness of wealth, Morrígu, springs of craftiness, sources of bitter fighting, were the three daughters of Ernmas' — so that the tradition itself is of two minds: sometimes the Morrígan is the third sister, sometimes the single name for all three.

The same book marries her into the house of the war-god. Neit son of Indui, the god of battle, had two wives — Badb and Nemain — and the pedigree records the slaying of the three of them at Ailech by the Fomorians. Cormac's Glossary had already fixed the marriage in the language of record: Neith, the god of battle among the pagan Gael, and Nemon his wife. Badb is never an isolated figure; she is a sister and a wife in a family whose whole business is war.

myths.title: The Shriek over the Hosts
myths.text:
When the men of Ireland march under [[medb|Medb]] for the brown bull of Cooley, the Táin marks the nights of the hosting with the sound of the war-goddesses: 'Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above them that night in Gáirech and Irgáirech, so that a hundred of their warriors fell dead of fright.' It is the battle's true opening — the killing has begun before a single spear is cast, and its instrument is a voice.

The passage tells you everything about her method. She does not wound; she announces. The shriek over the column is prophecy delivered as noise, the knowledge of the field's end injected into the march at its beginning — and the Irish phrase for the whole business of battlefield terror, badb catha, the crow of battle, is simply her name at work as a common noun.

myths.title: The War-Goddess at Mag Tuired
myths.text:
The Second Battle of Mag Tuired, the war the Túatha Dé Danann fight against the Fomorians, runs on the war-goddess's work from its eve to its aftermath. On Samain night [[dagda|the Dagda]] met the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius in Connacht, where she stood washing with one foot on either bank; they lay together at the ford, and she pledged herself to the Túatha Dé Danann's cause, promising to bring the hearts of the Fomorian host and the blood of their king Indech.

After [[lugh|Lugh]]'s sling-stone felled [[balor|Balor]] and the Fomorians broke, it was the Morrígan who proclaimed the battle and the rout to the royal heights of Ireland and its síd-hosts, and who uttered the great prophecy — 'Peace up to heaven, heaven down to earth, earth beneath heaven' — and then its darker twin, the vision of the world's ending. The commentators note that the texts keep the sisters' voices interchangeable: what the manuscript gives to the Morrígan, the tradition hears also in Badb's register, and the Lebor Gabála had already made them one family.

myths.title: The Crow on the Pillar-Stone
myths.text:
Cú Chulainn's death-tale, Brislech Mór Maige Muirthemni, gives the crow-goddesses the last word over the greatest of the Ulster heroes. Mortally wounded at Muirthemne, [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] lashed himself to a pillar-stone so that he would die on his feet, and for three days his enemies would not close in, uncertain whether he lived. Then the battle-goddess Morrígu came with her sisters in the form of scald-crows and settled on his shoulder — and Erc said, 'That pillar is not wont to be under birds,' and only then did the host dare approach and take the hero's head.

It is the emblematic scene of her whole dossier: the scald-crow is the signature of death itself, the field's first and final reader. The living man keeps her off; the dead man is her perch.

myths.title: The Washer at the Ford
myths.text:
The medieval texts give the war-goddess her washing-place — the Morrígan washing at the ford of the Unius on the eve of Mag Tuired — and the later Gaelic tradition gives the figure her full shape: the washer at the ford, the woman seen at the boundary water rinsing the blood-stained garments and harness of those about to die in battle. In Scottish Gaelic folklore she is the bean nighe, the washerwoman whose sight foretells death, and the commentators, Mac Cana among them, treat her as the folk continuation of the Badb's own figure.

The washing is prophecy, not threat. The doom is already written — the garments in her hands belong to men still alive and armed — and she merely launders the evidence. No Irish figure holds the moment before death so patiently: not the blow, not the battle, but the foreknowledge, rinsed clean in running water.

badb.syncretism: Badb's clearest cross-border witness is Gaulish, and it is exact. An altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicates to Cathubodua — *catu-*bodwā, 'battle-crow' — the precise reverse compound of Irish badb catha. Delamarre and Koch treat the two names as one formation across the Celtic languages: the crow of battle named in stone on the continent and in saga in Ireland. The Welsh corpus, by contrast, is silent on her — no figure of the Mabinogi continues the name, and the Brythonic silence is recorded rather than repaired. Typological comparison has set her beside the Norse valkyries, the raven-feeding choosers of the slain; the handbooks note the parallel without claiming descent. Within the lexicon her closest kin are her own sisters, [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]] and [[macha|Macha]], and the war she prophesied binds her to [[dagda|the Dagda]], [[lugh|Lugh]], and [[nuada|Nuadu]].
badb.culturalLegacy: The crow of battle rode the Celtic revival in English dress. W. M. Hennessy's 'The Ancient Irish Goddess of War' (Revue Celtique, 1870) had already gathered the Morrígan material for scholars, and Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired and its war-goddesses to a wide reading public, crow-form and prophecy complete. Modern fantasy and games have made the war-goddess's crow-shape one of the stock images of the genre, and contemporary pagan practice honors Badb among the three of the Morrígan. In the Irish language the word never needed reviving: badhbh has meant the hooded crow all along, and the grey bird on the battlefield needed no gloss for any Irish hearer. Across the water, the Scottish bean nighe kept her folk shape washing at the ford deep into the era of the great folklore collections.
badb.extendedMeditation:
Badb is the rare theonym that refuses to be a metaphor: the word for the bird and the name of the goddess are one, and the medieval writers never felt the need to choose between them. To name her is already to say what she does. Other gods have attributes; she has a species — the grey scald-crow that comes down to the field when the field is finished, and the texts simply ask us to understand that the bird knew all along.

Her power is the moment before. In no surviving text does she strike a blow: she shrieks over the marching column, washes at the boundary water, settles on the pillar-stone — the goddess of foreknowledge and of aftermath, of everything in a battle except the fighting. That is not a small dossier but a strange and exact one: she is what war feels like to those who already know its end. The name keeps the question open in every grey bird on a fence-post: if you could see the end of the day at its beginning, what would you do with the hours between?
badb.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Badb — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: badb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

badb.archaeology: Badb is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses are exact. The Táin Bó Cúailnge survives in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (Royal Irish Academy, c. 1100), and in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; Lebor Gabála Érenn likewise rests on the Book of Leinster and its sister codices; and Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition. The nearest epigraphic witness is continental: the altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicating to Cathubodua, 'battle-crow', is the standing proof that the crow-of-battle compound is old Celtic and not an Irish literary invention — comparative evidence across the water, never an identification.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], broad (velarized) before a; as in English 'bay' but with the back of the tongue raised.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief.
Broad (velarized) lateral [l̪ˠ], the dark Irish l with the tongue toward the teeth and the back raised — never the light l of English 'leaf'.
Short [o] closing on a broad trilled or tapped r [rˠ]; the second syllable unstressed, as in all Old Irish words stressed on the first.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-lor' — stress the first syllable hard, keep the l dark and broad, and let the final r stay tapped. Modern Irish 'Balor' keeps essentially the same shape.

domains.title: The King of the Evil Eye
domains.subtitle: The Venomed Gaze, the Fomorian Tribute, the Fortress of Tory, the Grandson's Stone
domains.lead: Balor — Balor Béimnech, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows' — is king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors of medieval Irish tradition, and owner of the most feared weapon in the whole corpus: a single eye so venomed by the fumes of a druids' brew that no army could stand before its gaze. Grandfather of Lugh and doomed by that very grandson's sling-stone at Mag Tuired, he is the Irish tradition's great figure of destructive sovereignty — power that poisons its possessor and is answered, in the end, by his own blood.

cards.name: The Venomed Eye
cards.desc: One eye, poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew; any army it looked upon was worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

cards.name: The Fomorian Tribute
cards.desc: Under Balor and Indech the Fomorians taxed Ireland from the sea, and set the very gods to serf-work until Mag Tuired broke the yoke.

cards.name: The Tower of Tory
cards.desc: In the Donegal oral tradition, the sea-girt tower where Balor prisoned his daughter Eithne against the prophecy of a grandson's hand.

cards.name: The Grandson's Stone
cards.desc: Lugh's sling-stone at Mag Tuired drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that its own gaze blasted the Fomorian host.

symbols.name: The venomed eye
symbols.meaning: A weapon the owner cannot aim without an army to raise the lid — power that outgrew its possessor

symbols.name: The polished lid-lifter
symbols.meaning: Four men with a handle passed through the eyelid — kingship reduced to machinery, a gaze other men must operate

symbols.name: The tower of Tory
symbols.meaning: The sea-girt prison built against a prophecy — the fortress that made the doom it feared

symbols.name: The Glas Gaibhnenn
symbols.meaning: The grey-green cow Balor stole from Cian in the oral tradition — the theft that set the grandson's birth in motion

symbols.name: The sling-stone
symbols.meaning: The small, aimed answer to the vast, unaimed gaze — the grandson's hand the druids foretold

mythology.lead: Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's revenge, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that medieval manuscripts only glance at.

myths.title: Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét
myths.text:
The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, and it was her spear, or the wound she dealt at Mag Tuired, that killed the Dagda at the Brug years later — the Lebor Gabála records the All-Father's death from Cethlenn's blow as the long-settled price of Balor's war.

His daughter was Ethniu, and she was given to Cian, son of Dian Cécht the healer; their son was Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer — the genealogy that the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns on.

myths.title: How the Eye Was Poisoned
myths.text:
Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it. Any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime.

myths.title: The Tower and the Prophecy
myths.text:
The medieval manuscripts know that Ethniu was Balor's daughter and Lugh's mother; how that came to be is told by the oral tradition of the north-west, collected in the nineteenth century on and around Tory Island — Balor's sea-girt fortress off the Donegal coast. A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson, and the king answered the prophecy with masonry: he locked his daughter Eithne in a tower on the rock, with twelve matrons to keep every man from her sight.

The doom came in by the usual door. Balor coveted the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and stole her across the water; Cian crossed to Tory for redress, and with the help of the druidess Biróg won into the tower in woman's dress and to Eithne's side. When the child was born Balor had him cast into the sea — but the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger called Lugh came to Nuadu's court at Tara and was asked what art he practiced. The question the Fomorians could not answer had been growing up under their own doom all along.

myths.title: The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired
myths.text:
At the second battle of Mag Tuired the armies broke each other all day, and then Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering. He commanded that the lid of his eye be raised, so that he might blast the enemy with its look — and the four men set the polished handle to the lid.

It was then that Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it. Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners — and the battle turned with the eye. Afterward the Túatha Dé Danann took the tribute back from the defeated host, and the power of the Fomorians over Ireland was broken for good.

balor.syncretism: Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so many of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological. First, the Greek Acrisius: the king who prisoned his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same — the Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the Polyphemus pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the evil eye itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine.
balor.culturalLegacy: Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's Early Irish History and Mythology (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king, a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short. The second was the folklore itself: the Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century and never stopped being retold, and 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address; the Irish language never lost his name.
balor.extendedMeditation:
Every part of Balor's story is about containment failing. The eye is contained — cloaked, lidded, lifted only by machinery — and containment is the whole catastrophe: a gaze so dangerous it must be operated by four other men is no longer a weapon but an occupation, a king reduced to the caretaker of his own poison. The daughter is contained in a tower against a prophecy, and the tower is the prophecy's instrument: no tower, no Cian, no Lugh. Balor is the tradition's purest study of power that can only destroy — he is given no craft, no counsel, no feast, no children worth the having, nothing but the eye and the tax it enforces.

And the answer the tradition gives him is exact. Not a bigger eye, not a stronger king, but a sling-stone: small, aimed, and thrown by the one hand the whole machinery existed to forestall. The venom that could wither an army is turned in a single instant into the Fomorians' own epitaph — it was his own host that looked into it. That is the Irish judgment on the evil eye, and on every power built to wither rather than to make: it ends by looking inward. The grandson does not defeat the weapon. He simply turns it around.
balor.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Balor — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: balor.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.
