domains.title: Giant, Owner of Cauldron
domains.subtitle: The Host at Heaven's End, the Ox-Head Bait, and the Cup Broken on a Giant's Skull
domains.lead: Hymir is the sea-giant of Hymiskviða: the fierce host at the eastern edge of heaven whose herd feeds his hall, whose fishing-ground is the cold reach of the Élivágar, and whose treasure is the one thing the gods lack — the mile-deep cauldron in which Ægir could brew ale for all the Æsir at once.

cards.name: The Mile-Deep Cauldron
cards.desc: The roomy, hard-forged kettle Týr says his fierce father owns — a mile deep, the only vessel large enough to brew for all the gods.

cards.name: The Ox-Head Bait
cards.desc: The head of the black bull Himinbrjótr, torn off by Þórr for bait — the offering that drew the Miðgarðsormr up from the sea-floor.

cards.name: The Crystal Cup
cards.desc: Hymir's unbreakable drinking-cup, which no pillar could crack — smashed at last on the one thing harder: the giant's own skull.

cards.name: The Hall of Cattle
cards.desc: The giant's byre at heaven's end, where Þórr devoured two of the three oxen at supper and beheaded the finest for the fishing.

symbols.name: The mile-deep cauldron
symbols.meaning: The vessel of plenty the giants keep and the gods must win — hospitality's measure in the Eddic world

symbols.name: The ox-head bait
symbols.meaning: The price of the catch: the herd's finest head traded for the serpent that girdles the world

symbols.name: The cup broken on the skull
symbols.meaning: The giant's own hardness turned against his treasure — strength answering strength

symbols.name: The nine-hundred-headed grandmother
symbols.meaning: The monstrous ancestry of the giant-house, set against the golden-browed mother who hides the guests

mythology.lead: Hymir lives in one great poem and its prose retelling: Hymiskviða, the comic and terrible lay of the cauldron-quest, and Gylfaginning 48, where Snorri tells the fishing-trip for the Miðgarðsormr with all its sea-cold detail. It is Þórr's most famous adventure, and the giant is its immovable setting.

myths.title: The Demand for the Cauldron
myths.text: The Æsir had hunted and taken auguries from the blood, and saw that Ægir — called also Gymir — had brew-stuff in plenty. Þórr ordered the sea-giant to brew ale for the gods, and Ægir, to be rid of the demand, set an impossible price: first let them bring a cauldron a mile wide. Týr knew where one stood: east of the Élivágar lives the shrewd Hymir at heaven's end, and "my fierce father owns the roomy kettle, a mile deep." So Þórr and Týr drove to the giant's hall. There they met Týr's grandmother, loathsome, with nine hundred heads — and another woman, golden-browed, Týr's mother, who hid the guests under the great cauldron, for her husband was often cruel to visitors.

myths.title: The Host Comes Home
myths.text: Hymir came in from the hunting with the ice rattling in his beard. The pillar he looked toward burst apart; eight cauldrons crashed from the broken beam, and one hard-forged kettle came down whole. The guests came out, and the hall fed them: three oxen were slaughtered, and Þórr alone ate two before he slept. In the morning the giant eyed his thinned herd and told his guest they must fish for the next day's meal — Þórr might row out with him, if the little fellow dared the cold and the long pull to his fishing-ground.

myths.title: The Fishing for the Miðgarðsormr
myths.text: Asked for bait, Þórr went to the herd and wrenched the head from the black bull Himinbrjótr — Snorri calls him Himinhrjóðr. Hymir rowed hard, then harder, and still Þórr matched him, past the giant's own grounds into water he said was unsafe, where the serpent lies. Hymir pulled up two whales at once on his hooks; Þórr cast the ox-head overboard. The Miðgarðsormr gaped on the bait, the hook caught, and Þórr braced his feet through the bottom of the boat and hauled the serpent's head to the gunwale — the two glaring, the sea foaming, the boat nearly swamped — until the hammer struck and the serpent sank back into the sea. Hymir rowed home in gloomy silence.

myths.title: The Cup, the Skull, and the Carrying-Off
myths.text: Back on land Hymir demanded proof of strength, and set his crystal cup: break that, and be counted mighty. Twice Þórr hurled it through the stone pillars, and twice it came back to the giant's hand unbroken — until the fair counsellor whispered to strike it on Hymir's own skull, harder than any cup. The cup shattered. Hymir mourned it with the formula of loss: he could no longer say over it "ale is brewed." Then, sullen, he yielded the wager — take the cauldron, if you can carry it out. Týr heaved twice and could not shift it; Þórr hoisted it over his head and strode off with the rim ringing at his heels. They had not gone far before he looked back and saw Hymir coming east from the caves with a troop of many-headed giants; he set down the cauldron, raised Mjöllnir, and slew the whole host. One of Þórr's goats went lame on the road — Loki's doing, the poem says — but the cauldron came to Ægir, who brews ale in it for the Æsir ever after.

hymir.syncretism: Hymir's poem has drawn comparatists for a century because the cauldron-quest is one of the old travelling stories of the North Atlantic: a vessel of plenty, kept by a grudging power beyond the sea, won for the feast of the gods. Scholars since Dumézil have set Hymiskviða beside the Celtic cauldron-quests — the Welsh Preiddeu Annwfn, where Arthur sails for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and the Irish cauldrons that no company leaves unsatisfied — and beside Vedic parallels for the winning of the gods' drink. The fishing scene has its own comparative trail: the thunder-god's combat with the sea-serpent belongs with the wide Indo-European dragon-fight. Inside the Norse corpus the neater tension is genealogical: Hymiskviða makes the giant Týr's father, while Snorri elsewhere counts Týr among Óðinn's sons — two filiations the tradition never reconciled.
hymir.culturalLegacy: Hymir's afterlife is carried almost entirely by the fishing-trip, which became the most retold of all Þórr's adventures: Victorian mythographies made it a set-piece, modern handbooks open their Þórr chapters with it, and every popular retelling keeps the ox-head, the glaring serpent, and the giant rowing home in silence. In scholarship the poem holds a double distinction — it is both the fullest portrait of a giant household in the Edda and the standing exhibit in the debate over the cauldron-quest's Celtic kin. The name itself stayed where the þulur put it: a giant-name, rarely borrowed, carried into modern fantasy and games chiefly as the surly host of the world's most famous fishing story.
hymir.extendedMeditation: Hymir is the Edda's portrait of hospitality under strain: the host who feeds his guests two oxen and counts the cost, who rows farther than he means to because pride will not let him ship his oar first, who wagers his treasures on contests he frames himself — and loses both. The poem never makes him a monster; it makes him a householder with a monstrous ancestry and a mile-deep kettle, and lets the comedy and the cold do the work. What the story measures is not his failure but the difference between keeping plenty and sharing it: the cauldron that brews for all the gods spent its best years in a hall where even a guest's supper was tallied.

hymir.archaeology: Hymir is a textual figure: his attestations are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), which alone preserves Hymiskviða, and the manuscripts of Snorri's Edda; the þulur keep his name among the giant-heiti. The myth's antiquity is proven by skaldic verse: Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrápa (9th c.) describes the fishing-scene on a painted shield — the ox-head bait, the hooked serpent, the hammer raised — with the giant aboard conventionally identified as Hymir. The picture-record follows: the Altuna runestone (U 1161, Uppland) shows Þórr with his foot braced through the boat's bottom and the serpent on the line, and the Gosforth Cross fishing-panel shows two figures in the boat — the angler and his giant companion. No cult site, toponym, or inscription names Hymir himself.

kin.form: Kay — Sir Kay the seneschal, Arthur's foster-brother

pronunciation.note: Kai is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: Middle Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters, so there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the hero's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The Steward of Arthur's Hall
domains.subtitle: The Nine Days' Breath, the Fire in His Hands, and the Sword No Physician Can Heal
domains.lead: Cei son of Cynyr is the first companion Arthur assigns to Culhwch: the tall man of the Mabinogion's oldest Arthurian tale, who could hold his breath nine nights and nine days under water, go nine nights and nine days without sleep, deal a wound no physician could heal, grow as tall as the tallest tree in the forest, and carry so much heat in his body that rain dried a handbreadth above and below his hand and his companions lit their fires from him in the cold. Centuries of romance would remember him as the steward of the court — the seneschal Kay.

cards.name: The Nine Days' Breath
cards.desc: Nine nights and nine days under water; nine nights and nine days without sleep — the Mabinogion's measure of the tall man's endurance.

cards.name: The Fire in His Hands
cards.desc: His heat kept his hand dry a handbreadth in the hardest rain; in the bitterest cold he was fuel for his companions' fire.

cards.name: The Unhealable Sword
cards.desc: A wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal — and the sword of Wrnach the giant came into Arthur's hand by Cei's trickery.

cards.name: The Seneschal's Office
cards.desc: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Caius dapifer — steward of Arthur's household, given Anjou, buried at Chinon: the office the later romances never let him leave.

symbols.name: The nine days' breath
symbols.meaning: Endurance past the human limit — the hero who outlasts water and sleep alike

symbols.name: The fire in his hands
symbols.meaning: Heat as provision: the companion who keeps the whole company warm, dry, and fed with fire

symbols.name: The unhealable sword
symbols.meaning: A stroke beyond remedy — the oldest stratum's mark of the warrior, before romances made him a steward

symbols.name: The beard of Dillus
symbols.meaning: The quest accomplished by cunning — and Arthur's mocking englyn that ended the fellowship

symbols.name: Cei Hir, 'the Tall'
symbols.meaning: Tall as the tallest tree in the forest when it pleased him — stature as the visible sign of the older, larger hero

mythology.lead: Kai's mythology lives in the oldest stratum of Welsh Arthurian tradition: Culhwch ac Olwen gives him the tale's largest dossier after Arthur himself, and the fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur remembers exploits the prose never told. The later Latin and French traditions kept the man and quietly spent the magic.

myths.title: The First Companion
myths.text: When Culhwch comes to Arthur's court to win Olwen daughter of Ysbaddaden Chief Giant, Arthur grants him help, and the first companion named is Cei son of Cynyr. The warrior-list fixes his peculiarities in one breath: nine nights and nine days he could be under water; nine nights and nine days he could go without sleep; a wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal. Cei the Tall — when it pleased him he could make himself as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. And the list adds the attribute the whole fellowship depended on: when the rain was heaviest, whatever he carried in his hand stayed dry for a handbreadth above and below, so great was his heat; and when the cold was hardest on his companions, he was fuel to them to light their fire. The list also preserves his mother's prophecy that his heart would be cold — the oldest trace of the coldness the later romances turned to mockery.

myths.title: The Salmon and the Sword
myths.text: Two of the hardest anoethau — the 'things hard to get' that Ysbaddaden sets as the bride-price — fall to Cei. To free Mabon son of Modron from his prison at Caer Loyw, the company follows the oldest animals to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, and Cei and Bedwyr ride up the Severn on the salmon's shoulders; while Arthur's men assault the fort from the front, Cei carries Mabon away on the salmon's back. And when Arthur's band comes to the hall of Wrnach the giant, whose sword is needed to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth — no guest had ever left that hall alive — Cei claims to be a master polisher of swords. Admitted, he burnishes the giant's blade, asks to hold it to test the work, and strikes Wrnach's head off with his own sword; the company destroys the fortress. The wonder-hero's greatest feats in the tale are won with a craftsman's hands, not a charge of horse.

myths.title: The Beard of Dillus and the Englyn
myths.text: The beard of Dillus the Bearded was wanted to make a leash for the whelp Drudwyn, and Cei and Bedwyr found the giant alone. Cei dug a pit, tricked Dillus into it, plucked his beard out with wooden tweezers, and killed him afterward — and Arthur, watching, sang an englyn mocking Cei for making a leash from a living beard he could never have taken from a healthy man. Cei answered nothing, but the tale records the consequence in a line: because of that englyn there was enmity between Cei and Arthur ever after, and Cei took no part in the hunt of Twrch Trwyth. The tale's closing tally keeps the ending: Gwyddog son of Menestyr slew Cei, and Arthur slew Gwyddog and his brothers to avenge him — the rift repaired only in vengeance.

myths.title: Nine Witches and the Cat of Anglesey
myths.text: The fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur yv y Porthaur?, preserved in the Black Book of Carmarthen, shows Arthur and the gatekeeper Glewlwyd Mighty-grasp trading boasts, and the boasts are Cei's: Cei pierced nine witches, and Cei the Fair went to Anglesey to destroy the monster the Welsh called Cath Palug — the gigantic cat that the triads say was born of the sow Henwen and raised by the sons of Palug as one of the island's plagues. The poem breaks off in the middle of that account, and scholars read the torn ending as the oldest trace of Cei's own death-fight. The early verse remembers him where the prose does not: as the champion sent against the things no one else would face.

myths.title: Caius Dapifer
myths.text: Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, Latinizes him as Caius dapifer — Kay the steward — and gives him the seneschal's office and the province of Anjou at Arthur's plenary court at Caerleon, while Bedwerus the cupbearer receives Normandy. In Geoffrey's Roman war Kay fights as duke, is mortally wounded in the great battle against Lucius, and dies; Geoffrey says he was buried at Chinon, the castle he himself had built, mourned by the whole army. The magic is gone — no nine days' breath, no fire in the hands — but the office Geoffrey fixed to the name proved more durable than any peculiarity: from this book onward, Kay is the steward of Arthur's court in every language that tells the story.

kai.syncretism: Kai is less a figure who absorbed other gods than one whom each retelling rewrote. The Welsh stratum gives a wonder-hero: the tall, fire-handed, sleepless companion whose attributes belong to the oldest legendary stock of Britain. Geoffrey of Monmouth euhemerizes him into Caius dapifer, a duke and steward of recognizable twelfth-century type; Chrétien de Troyes turns the steward's sharpness into Keu's venomous tongue, the court's mocker who is always wrong; and Malory resolves the long arc into Sir Kay, Arthur's foster-brother — loyal, loud, and forever outmatched. Scholars have long paired him with Bedwyr, his constant companion in Culhwch ac Olwen, as the two oldest members of Arthur's band; and Mac Cana and others note that the tale-patterns around the pair — the raid on a giant's stronghold, the hunt of the enchanted boar — have close Irish analogues, though no Irish cycle preserves Cei himself. The transformation of the tall man into the seneschal is the tradition's own syncretism: one name, four costumes, and the office outlasting the magic.
kai.culturalLegacy: The steward outlived the giant-killer. Malory's Sir Kay — the foster-brother who claims he drew the sword from the stone, confesses, and is made seneschal at Arthur's coronation — fixed the English image: blunt, envious, brave enough, and indispensable to the household. Chrétien's Keu had already made him the court's satirist, and the romances of every language kept that register. T. H. White's The Sword in the Stone made Kay the human counterweight to the Wart, the brother who gets the crown's shadow instead of the crown. In Welsh the name never left: Cai remains a living given name, and the Mabinogion's Cei Hir is still the tall man of the oldest Arthurian tale. Modern scholarship treats the arc from wonder-hero to comic steward as one of the great case-studies in how the Arthurian legend domesticated its oldest figures.
kai.extendedMeditation:
Kai is the patron of the unglamorous power: the one who keeps the fire, the stores, the hall — the office that lets everyone else be heroic. His oldest attributes are a steward's attributes written in mythic scale. He does not merely endure the cold; he is fuel for the company's fire. He does not merely keep dry; whatever he carries stays dry a handbreadth around. The seneschal of the romances is the same figure after the magic has been spent: the man who knows where everything is kept, who answers the gate, whose sharp tongue is the friction of service worn into habit.

And the tradition is honest about the cost. His mother's prophecy said his heart would be cold; Arthur's englyn mocked the feat no one else could perform; the fellowship ended in a vengeance taken too late. Kai asks the question every household and every court must answer: what do you owe the one who keeps the fire — and what does keeping it do to the heart?
kai.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Cei, with the spelling variants Kei and Kai — plain Latin letters in Insular script, c. 12th–14th c. CE, in the Black Book of Carmarthen, the White Book of Rhydderch, and the Red Book of Hergest. No diacritic and no distinctive letter is involved: the normalized form is already ASCII, and the restoration Kai differs from the input only by its capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: kai.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

kai.archaeology: Kai is a literary figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or Romano-British dedication names him, and Welsh tradition generally left texts rather than cult monuments for its heroes. His manuscript witnesses are exact and early. The dialogue poem Pa Gur survives in the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), the oldest substantial manuscript of Welsh verse; Culhwch ac Olwen survives in a fragmentary copy in the White Book of Rhydderch (Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and complete in the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425); and the Otherworld-raid poem Preiddeu Annwn, the companion witness to this stratum, is preserved in the Book of Taliesin (Peniarth 2, early 14th c.). Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) and Lifris of Llancarfan's Vita Cadoci (c. 1100) carry the Latin attestations. The places of the tales — Caer Loyw on the Severn, the Anglesey of Cath Palug — remain on the map, but the tall man himself left nothing in stone.

phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar lateral [l], unchanged from Proto-Germanic; the name opens as cleanly as English 'low'
Short mid back [o], as in English 'lot'; the Old Norse vowel is short, never the diphthong of English 'low'
Voiced velar fricative [ɣ] — the soft, gargled medial g of Spanish 'lago', not the hard stop of English 'go' — followed by short close front [i]; a light second syllable closed by the vowel

pronunciation.approximation: 'LOH-yi' — two short, even syllables with the weight on the first; keep the o short and round, and let the medial g soften to a voiced friction in the throat, as in modern Icelandic logi.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: logi, m., 'flame, blaze' — the common noun borne as a proper name

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: logi — still the everyday word for a flame, from hearth-talk to weather reports

kin.label: Word-family
kin.form: log n. 'flame' and loga v. 'to burn with a flame, blaze' — the same root at work and at rest

kin.label: Fornjótr's son
kin.form: Logi, brother of Hlér (the sea, called Ægir) and Kári (the wind) in Skáldskaparmál and Hversu Noregr byggðist

kin.label: Distinct figure
kin.form: Loki Laufeyjarson shares the sound, not the word: the old equation of Loki with logi 'flame' is abandoned, and Snorri stages the two as opponents

pronunciation.note: Old Norse Logi is a common noun made person: logi, m., 'flame, blaze', beside log, n., 'flame', and the verb loga, 'to burn with a flame'. The restoration and the ASCII form are the same word — the manuscripts write four plain letters and the ASCII alphabet loses nothing — so Logi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule. The etymology is transparent in the North; the old scholarly difficulty was never the word's meaning but its neighbor: nineteenth-century philology equated the god Loki with logi, 'flame', on the strength of the similar sound, an equation now abandoned — the vowels differ in kind, the figures never merge in the texts, and Gylfaginning itself stages Logi as the opponent who out-eats Loki at Útgarðr. Attestation and lexicography follow Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. logi; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. logi; and de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch (1962), s.v. logi.

domains.title: Fire, Flame, Giant
domains.subtitle: The Trough, the Wildfire, and the Sons of Fornjótr
domains.lead: Logi is the Norse name for flame itself — the common noun logi, 'blaze', walking on two legs into the greatest hall of giants the mythology knows. In Útgarða-Loki's court he is served a trough of meat against the god Loki, and when the two eaters meet in the middle, Logi has consumed the meat, the bones, and the trough besides: wildfire does not chew, it consumes. He is catalogued in the norse pantheon under the domain "Fire, Flame, Giant", and his meaning is the plainest in the lexicon — "Flame".

cards.name: The Trough
cards.desc: The full-length feeding-trough set on the hall floor; Loki clears the meat from the bones — Logi clears everything.

cards.name: The Eating Contest
cards.desc: The one fair contest of Útgarðr: no enchantment was needed — the opponent was fire.

cards.name: Villieldr
cards.desc: 'Wildfire', the unmasking word: what sat down to eat with Loki was flame itself.

cards.name: Hlér and Kári
cards.desc: His brothers in the Fornjótr genealogy: the sea and the wind — an elemental triad with fire between them.

symbols.name: The feeding-trough
symbols.meaning: Appetite made measurable: the only scoreboard in mythology that fire ever emptied

symbols.name: The eaten bones
symbols.meaning: The line between hunger and combustion: Loki strips the bone, Logi strips the question

symbols.name: The flame (logi)
symbols.meaning: The common noun kept as a name — fire called by the very word the hearth already knew

symbols.name: The brothers Hlér and Kári
symbols.meaning: Sea and wind: the family that makes fire one element among three, not a freak among persons

mythology.lead: Logi has one great scene and one great family. The scene is the eating contest in Útgarða-Loki's hall, the showpiece of Þórr's eastern journey in Gylfaginning; the family is the Fornjótr genealogy, which makes him fire brothered to sea and wind. Between them the mythology says everything it has to say about him: he is not a character with a history but an element with a name — and his single appearance is constructed to prove exactly that.

myths.title: The Road to Útgarðr
myths.text: Þórr sets out east for Jǫtunheimr with Loki for company, and at a peasant's farm takes the children Þjálfi and Rǫskva as his servants. On the road they meet the giant who calls himself Skrýmir: they sleep, unknowing, in the thumb of his dropped glove, and Þórr's three hammer-blows in the night — which the giant greets as a leaf, an acorn, and a bird's dropping — will be explained only later. Skrýmir points them to Útgarðr, a stronghold so vast the travellers must tilt their heads back to see the top of it, and vanishes. Every step of the journey is a setup: by the time the company reaches the hall, the story has already taught the reader that nothing here is what it is called.

myths.title: The Eating Contest
myths.text: Útgarða-Loki, the giant-king, declares that no one may stay in his hall who is not master of some art or accomplishment beyond other men. Loki, travel-hungry and never at a loss, speaks first: no one in the hall can eat faster than he can. The king accepts the challenge and calls from the far bench a man named Logi. A trough full of meat is set down on the floor between them; Loki takes one end, Logi the other, and they eat toward each other. They meet in the middle — and there the verdict lies in plain sight. Loki has eaten every shred of meat from the bones; but Logi has eaten the meat, and the bones, and the trough as well. 'And it now seemed to everyone,' Snorri says, 'that Loki had lost the game.'

myths.title: The Unmasking
myths.text: The rest of the evening fails the same way: Þjálfi is outrun by Hugi, Þórr cannot drain the drinking-horn, cannot lift the grey cat, and is forced to one knee by the old foster-mother Elli. In the morning Útgarða-Loki walks the company outside — and when he has told the truth and they turn back, the stronghold is gone. Skrýmir was himself; the glove was the hall; the blows fell on three mountain-valleys. The horn's end stood in the sea, and the tide now answers to Þórr's drinking; the cat was the Midgard Serpent; Elli was old age, whom no one out-wrestles; Hugi was the king's own thought. 'And he who contended with Loki in the eating-contest was wildfire itself' — villieldr — and it was no wonder he made short work of the trough. Fire against hunger was never a contest of the same kind.

myths.title: The Sons of Fornjótr
myths.text: Logi's other attestation is genealogical. Skáldskaparmál, teaching the kennings for wind, names Kári as Fornjótr's son and his brothers as Hlér and Logi; Hversu Noregr byggðist, the legendary preface to the Norwegian settlement preserved in the Flateyjarbók, gives the triad its famous form: Fornjótr had three sons — Hlér, 'whom we call Ægir', Logi, and Kári. Sea, fire, and wind as one old giant's household: the genealogy is not narrative but classification, the North keeping its elements in a family tree, with the sea Logi's brother and the wind his kin.

myths.title: The Flame That Goes Out
myths.text: The word's longest echo is eschatological. When Óðinn asks the giant Vafþrúðnir who will survive the world's burning, the answer keeps Víðarr and Váli in the gods' sanctuaries 'when Surtr's flame dies down' — þá er sloknar surtalogi. The compound welds Logi's common noun to Surtr's name: the fire that ends the world and the flame that eats the trough are one word at two scales. Even eschatology, in Old Norse, is written in the vocabulary of the hearth.

logi.syncretism: Logi's cross-cultural life begins with a mistake and ends with a commonplace. The mistake is famous: nineteenth-century philology, from Grimm onward, heard the fire-word in the god Loki and made Loki a fire-god; the equation is now abandoned — the vowels differ in kind, the figures never merge in the texts, and Snorri stages them face to face across a trough, which is about as far apart as two beings can sit. Its monument survives in art rather than scholarship: Wagner's Loge, the flame-cynic of the Ring cycle, is the conflation set to music. The commonplace is older than any comparison: every tradition that watches fire discovers that it eats. The Vedic hymns give flame a mouth and a priesthood in Agni, the devourer who carries the sacrifice to heaven; the Norse kept the same observation at the scale of a common noun, logi, and personified it once, brilliantly, as the unbeatable guest. Within the corpus his kin are elemental: Surtr of Múspellheimr, whose sword-fire burns the world; Ægir, the sea his own genealogy calls brother; and Loki, the god his name was once wrongly spent to explain.
logi.culturalLegacy: The eating contest is one of the most retold scenes of the Norse revival: the Kearys' The Heroes of Asgard (1857) made Útgarða-Loki's hall a set-piece for English-reading children, and every handbook since keeps Logi's trough beside Hugi's running and Elli's wrestling as the triad of unwinnable contests — fire, thought, and age, the three things no champion beats. The nineteenth century's false etymology had an afterlife of its own: Wagner's Loge, and a long tail of fire-trickster Loki in popular fiction, are children of the conflation scholarship has buried. In Iceland the name never needed reviving: logi remains the everyday word for flame, and Logi persists as a given name. Modern retellings and games cast him as he was written — fire wearing a face, the one opponent in Útgarðr who cheated by being exactly what he was.
logi.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Logi compresses the oldest observation the North made about fire: it has appetite. The myths give every god a hunger — Óðinn for knowledge, Þórr for food and fight — and then stage one contest where hunger meets its master. Loki is the gods' own appetite, the mouth of the company, and he eats well; no shame attaches to losing as he lost. The lesson the hall teaches is a taxonomy, not a moral: some appetites are animal, and some are elemental, and the two are not the same kind of thing. Unicode restoration has nothing to rescue here — the name arrived whole, four letters the scribes and the ASCII machines spell exactly alike — and that plainness suits him: a word so common the hearth used it nightly, set in capital letters and given a bench in the hall of giants.

logi.archaeology: Logi is a textual figure in the strictest sense: his attestations are the Snorra Edda manuscripts — Codex Regius (GKS 2367 4to), Codex Wormianus, Codex Upsaliensis — together with the þulur, the rhymed name-lists appended to the Prose Edda, which keep the common noun logi among the heiti for fire, and the Fornjótr genealogy of Hversu Noregr byggðist in the Flateyjarbók. No runic inscription names him, no place-name is securely his, and no cult could attach to a figure who is, by definition, an element rather than a person. His material context is the fire itself: the hearth-centered longhouse, the cremation pyres of the Late Iron Age, and the wildfire of the northern forests — the villieldr Snorri names as the truth behind the illusion.
logi.originalScriptNote: The Old Norse form is Logi — the common noun logi, 'flame', borne as a proper name — attested throughout the Gylfaginning manuscripts with a short o and no diacritic; the normalized spelling and the ASCII spelling are identical. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the Younger Futhark, the name would be rendered approximately ᛚᚢᚴᛁ (l-u-k-i) — the sixteen-rune row writes both k and g with ᚴ, so the runes of Logi and Loki are the same — but no runic inscription preserves the figure's name, so the manuscript form remains the primary witness. Because the restoration preserves no distinctive feature the ASCII form loses, Logi is a Tier-2 name: the plain-ASCII logi.com is the philologically complete form — and it is registered to a third party, held outside the PuniCodex collection, and watched for release. The temple is served at /sites/logi/ in the meantime; no owned domain is claimed for this entry.

phonemes.desc: Broad (velarized) bilabial nasal [m], before a; as in English 'mother', with the tongue already set for the wide vowel.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief; Old Irish stresses the first syllable throughout.
Voiceless velar fricative [x] — the rasp of Scottish 'loch' or German 'ach', never the hard k of 'cat'; lenited c, written ch, is a fricative in Old Irish.
Short open final [a], lightly sounded; two matching syllables, the second unstressed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAHKH-ah' — two short open a's, stress on the first, and let the ch rasp like the end of Scottish 'loch'. Modern Irish keeps the sound: Eamhain Mhacha is said with the same fricative.

kin.form: Macha — the theonym and the woman's name are the same word; the texts know several bearers, all of whom the commentators treat as one goddess wearing several stories

The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the goddess's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: War, Sovereignty, Horses
domains.subtitle: The Woman Who Outran the King's Horses
domains.lead: Macha is the sovereignty figure of the Ulster Cycle: the otherworld woman who came to the door of the widower Cruinniuc and made his house prosper, and who — when her husband boasted at the assembly that she could outrun the king's horses — was brought out pregnant to the racetrack, outran the horses of Conchobar mac Nessa at the finish, gave birth to twins on the field, and laid on the men of Ulster the curse that shapes the whole Táin: in their hour of greatest need, the pangs of childbirth.

cards.name: The Race at the Assembly
cards.desc: Nine months gone, she begged for delay until she had given birth; the Ulaid refused. She raced the king's chariot-horses and beat them at the line.

cards.name: The Debility of the Ulaid
cards.desc: Her curse, the ces noínden: for five days and four nights, in every generation to the ninth, the men of Ulster would lie in the pangs of a woman in labor — whenever the province needed them most.

cards.name: Emain Macha
cards.desc: 'Macha's twins' — the boy and girl born at the finish line named the royal seat of Ulster, the Navan Fort that still stands outside Armagh.

cards.name: Macha Mongrúad
cards.desc: The red-maned queen of the Lebor Gabála who seized the kingship of Ireland in her own right and traced the rampart of Emain with the brooch of her neck.

symbols.name: The king's horses
symbols.meaning: Conchobar's unmatched chariot-pair — the boast that forced the race and the measure she outran

symbols.name: The twins
symbols.meaning: Emain, the boy and girl born on the racetrack — the naming of Ulster's royal seat and the price of its pride

symbols.name: The debility
symbols.meaning: Five days and four nights of a woman's labor-pangs, laid on a warrior people for nine generations — the curse that left Cú Chulainn to fight the Táin alone

symbols.name: The brooch of the queen
symbols.meaning: Macha Mongrúad marked the circuit of Emain with her eo-muin, her neck-brooch — sovereignty drawing the boundary of its own seat

symbols.name: Macha's mast
symbols.meaning: Mesrad Machae, 'Macha's crop' — the Táin's kenning for the severed heads of the slain, the war-goddess's harvest

mythology.lead: Macha's dossier is one great tale and a family of namesakes: the Debility of the Ulstermen gives her the race, the twins, and the curse; the Táin harvests the consequences; the Lebor Gabála remembers her as Nemed's wife and as the red-maned queen; and the genealogies fold her into the three of war beside [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]].

myths.title: The Woman at Cruinniuc's Door
myths.text:
Cruinniuc mac Agnomain was a rich farmer of the Ulaid, a widower with sons, and one day a woman he had never seen walked into his house, set about the work of it without a word, and lay with him that night. She stayed, and under her hand everything prospered — the house, the cattle, the table — and she told him the one condition of their life together: he must never speak of her, never boast of her. It is the old compact of the otherworld wife, and it held as long as he kept his mouth shut.

The tale that tells this — Noínden Ulad, 'The Debility of the Ulaid', one of the fore-tales of the Táin — is a sovereignty story before it is anything else: the land's own woman comes to the man of the land, and her condition is silence about the source of the plenty. Cruinniuc kept it until the day of the great assembly of the Ulaid, when the talk turned to the king's horses and there was nothing in the world faster.

myths.title: The Race, the Twins, and the Curse
myths.text:
At the assembly Cruinniuc forgot the condition and boasted: his wife could outrun the king's chariot-horses. Conchobar had him seized, and sent for the woman — who was nine months gone with twins. She begged the gathering for delay until she had given birth, 'for a mother bore each of you'; the Ulaid refused. She was set against the horses and raced them, and she beat them at the line — and at the line the pangs took her, and she was delivered of a boy and a girl on the field.

Then she cursed them: as she had been given no mercy in her labor, so the men of Ulster, in their hour of greatest straits, would suffer the pangs of a woman in childbirth — five days and four nights, for nine generations, every man save the boys and the women. And in most recensions she died there. The twins gave the royal seat of Ulster its name: Emain Macha, 'Macha's twins'. It is the most economical curse in Irish literature — one wrong, answered in exact kind, for nine generations.

myths.title: The Debility in the Táin
myths.text:
The curse is the engine of the greatest Irish epic. When [[medb|Medb]] of Connacht marches into Ulster for the Donn Cúailnge, the men of the province are down in the ces noínden, gripped by the pangs Macha laid on them — the curse spared the boys and the women, and it spared [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], who stands alone against the host of Ireland while the warriors of Emain writhe. The whole boyhood-deeds section of the Táin is narrated against the debility: one boy holding a province because a goddess was made to race in labor.

The Táin keeps her name in the language of battle as well. Its phrase for the harvest of heads is mesrad Machae, 'Macha's mast' — the crop the war-goddess gathers from the field. And the Lebor Gabála had already counted her among the three daughters of Ernmas: [[badb|Badb]] and Macha and Anand, 'of whom are the Paps of Anu' — the triple face of Irish war, the sisters the sources also gather under the one name [[morrigan|Morrígan]].

myths.title: The Queens and the Naming of Emain
myths.text:
The book of invasions remembers two earlier Machas. The first is Macha wife of Nemed, who came with the Nemedians in the days before the Túatha Dé Danann; she died in Ireland, and Ard Macha — Armagh, 'Macha's height' — and Mag Macha, 'Macha's plain', the country around it, are named from her grave.

The second is Macha Mongrúad, the red-maned daughter of Áed Rúad. When her father and his brothers Díthorba and Cimbáeth had held the kingship of Ireland in rotation, seven years each, and Áed died, the brothers refused the daughter her turn. She took it by war: she married Cimbáeth, defeated Díthorba's five sons — after going to them, the tale says, in the guise of a leprous hag — and held the kingship herself. It was she who marked out the rampart of Emain Macha with the brooch of her neck, her eo-muin, and made the captives dig it. The dindsenchas keeps both etymologies side by side — Macha's twins and Macha's brooch — and the tradition never chose between the goddess of the race and the queen of the fort.

macha.syncretism: Macha's clearest cross-border witness is Welsh, and it is the standard comparison of the handbooks: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] of the First Branch of the Mabinogi, the otherworld woman on the horse no rider can overtake, who — falsely accused and shamed — is sentenced to sit at the horse-block and offer to carry guests on her back like a beast of burden. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt both set the two figures side by side: the sovereignty woman bound to horses, wronged by the men of the court, and made to bear an equine humiliation. Behind both stands the Gaulish horse-goddess Epona, whose altars run from Britain to the Danube — the one Celtic deity with a festival in the Roman calendar — the continental anchor of the comparison, cited as type, never as identity. Within the Irish corpus her structural kin are [[medb|Medb]], the sovereignty queen whose favor makes kings, and her own sisters of war, [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]], with whom the Lebor Gabála shares a mother.
macha.culturalLegacy: Macha rode the Celtic revival as the first wrong of the Ulster Cycle. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) opens the epic with her — 'The Curse of Macha' — and made the race and the debility the gateway through which two generations of English readers entered the Táin. Thomas Kinsella's The Táin (1969) kept the fore-tale at the head of the epic, and the twinned figures of the wronged woman and the war-goddess have made Macha a standing subject in the study of Celtic sovereignty myth. On the ground, her names never went anywhere: Emain Macha is Navan Fort, one of the royal sites of Ireland and the ceremonial capital of Ulster, and Ard Macha — Armagh, the ecclesiastical primacy of Ireland, founded by Patrick in the fifth century — still carries her name in every address in the county. Modern scholarship from Mac Cana to Koch treats the race as the type-case of the Irish sovereignty goddess, and contemporary Celtic pagan practice honors her among the three of war.
macha.extendedMeditation:
Macha is the goddess of the exact answer. The Ulaid would not wait for her labor, so their labor is her labor: the pangs she suffered alone on the racetrack become the pangs of every fighting man in the province, whenever the province needs its men. Nothing in the curse is arbitrary; it is the wrong replayed on the body politic for nine generations, precise as a mirror. The Irish called it ces — the debility — and built their greatest epic inside it: a whole war fought by one boy because an assembly of men could not grant a pregnant woman a postponement.

Her name, if the etymologists are right, is simply 'field' — Mag Macha, Macha's plain, is the ground of Armagh itself. That is the sovereignty doctrine in a single word: the goddess is the land, the race is run on her, the fort is drawn by her brooch, and the men who rule there hold their strength on her sufferance. Macha asks the question every power eventually answers: what does it cost to use the land — and its women — as though they had no claims of their own?
macha.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Macha — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: macha.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

macha.archaeology: Macha is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses are exact: Noínden Ulad survives in the Yellow Book of Lecan and its sister codices (Hull's edition in Celtica 8 rests on them), the Táin in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (c. 1100), and the twelfth-century Book of Leinster, and the Lebor Gabála in the Book of Leinster and its companions. Her mythic address, by contrast, is one of the most instructive monuments in Atlantic Europe: Emain Macha is Navan Fort, Co. Armagh, where Waterman's excavations (1961–71) uncovered beneath the mound a forty-metre timber structure — a ring of great posts around a central oak — that dendrochronology dates to 95 BC, built in a single episode, filled with a stone cairn, burned, and buried under the mound still visible today. A building raised to be unmade is a ritual statement, not a residence; the standing interpretation, Lynn's, is a one-time ceremonial monument at the very seat the Ulster Cycle calls Macha's. No artifact names her; the identification of the fort with Emain Macha rests on the early medieval record, beginning with the annals and the Book of Armagh.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], as in English 'might'; Old Norse initial m is unchanged.
Short open back unrounded [ɑ], held brief — Old Norse short a, never the long á.

The medial g is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] of Old Norse — softer than the English stop — followed by dental nasal [n] and short close [i]. The name ends in the ja-stem ending -i: there is no nominative -r as in Þórr or Baldr.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAHG-ni' — a short open 'ah', the g softened to a voiced fricative between the vowels; Modern Icelandic hardens the same g to [k]: 'MAHK-ni'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Magni, 'the strong one', son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa; from the common noun magn/megn, 'strength, might'.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Magni — unchanged in spelling for a thousand years and still a living given name.

kin.label: Proto-Germanic
kin.form: *maginą, 'strength, power' — the same root as Old English mægen ('main, might') and the verb magan 'be able' that gives English may and might.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i) — the ᚴ k-rune writes g, and there is no final nominative -r to carve.

pronunciation.note: Magni is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn, no eth for the restoration to recover. The strongest boy in the Edda has one of its plainest names; only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input.

domains.title: Strength, Son of Thor
domains.subtitle: The Three-Night-Old Who Lifted Hrungnir's Leg — and the Heir of Mjǫllnir
domains.lead: Magni is Þórr's son by the giantess Járnsaxa: the prodigy of the Edda, three nights old when he freed his father from under the fallen Hrungnir's leg — the feat all the Æsir together could not manage. And Vafþrúðnismál looks past the end of the world to give him the hammer itself: after Ragnarǫk, Magni and his brother Móði inherit Mjǫllnir.

cards.name: Hrungnir's Leg
cards.desc: The stone giant fell with his leg across Þórr's neck, and all the Æsir could not move it. Magni, three nights old, flung it off.

cards.name: Gullfaxi
cards.desc: Gold-mane, Hrungnir's horse and the prize of the duel — Þórr gave him to the boy, and Óðinn reproved the gift.

cards.name: Mjǫllnir
cards.desc: The hammer the brothers inherit: 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjǫllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done' (Vafþrúðnismál 51).

cards.name: Járnsaxa
cards.desc: 'Iron-knife', the giantess mother — the Edda names her once, as the reason Óðinn grudged the boy his horse.

symbols.name: Hrungnir's stone leg
symbols.meaning: The weight of the giant world on the gods — and the proof that strength answers to youth, not seniority

symbols.name: Gullfaxi, the gold-maned
symbols.meaning: The horse given to the giantess's son: a father's pride against a grandfather's protocol

symbols.name: Mjǫllnir inherited
symbols.meaning: The hammer carried past Ragnarǫk — the one treasure of the old world guaranteed to the new

symbols.name: The whetstone shard
symbols.meaning: Hrungnir's broken weapon lodged in Þórr's head — the scar the duel left when the leg was lifted

mythology.lead: Magni's dossier is two scenes and a promise: a duel's aftermath, a gift reproved, and a prophecy at the end of the world. The sources tell them in a few lines each, and those lines have carried him for eight hundred years.

myths.title: The Duel at Grjótúnagarðar
myths.text: Hrungnir, the stone-hearted giant, rode his gold-maned stallion Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr on the heels of Óðinn's wager over whose horse was fastest; feasted, he drank Þórr's ale and boasted he would carry off Valhǫll and kill every god but Freyja and Sif. Þórr was summoned, and the duel was set at Grjótúnagarðar, the stone courts. The giants, fearing for Hrungnir, built him a companion of clay nine leagues tall — Mǫkkurkálfi, Mist-calf, with a mare's heart that failed him — and Hrungnir came with a heart, a shield, and a weapon all of stone, his whetstone raised. Þjálfi ran ahead and cried that Þórr would come up from below, so the giant stood on his shield to guard his feet; the thunderer came in fury and hurled Mjǫllnir through the whetstone, shattering it — one shard lodged in Þórr's own head — and Hrungnir crashed forward with his leg across Þórr's neck.

myths.title: Three Nights Old
myths.text: Þjálfi dispatched the clay giant, then went to lift Hrungnir's leg off Þórr and could not; all the Æsir came, and none of them could move it either. Then Magni arrived — the son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa, and he was three nights old — and he flung the leg off his father and said it was a shame he had not come sooner: he thought he could have struck the giant dead with his bare fist. Þórr, delighted, gave him the horse Gullfaxi that Hrungnir had ridden. Óðinn objected: Þórr did wrong, he said, to give so fine a horse to the son of a giantess and not to his own father. It is the whole of Magni's boyhood in one scene — and the only childhood the Edda gives any of the gods.

myths.title: The Hammer After
myths.text: In the wisdom-contest, when Óðinn has wrung the fates of the gods from the giant Vafþrúðnir, one answer carries the brothers past the end of the world: 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done.' Vingnir is Þórr's own name. The prophecy does not flinch from what it costs — the father falls — and it does not waste words on grief: it states the inheritance, the weapon passing whole into the hands of the sons.

myths.title: The Sons at Íðavöllr
myths.text: At Ragnarǫk Þórr meets Jǫrmungandr, the Midgard serpent, and strikes it dead — and walks nine paces before he falls to the venom it spat at him. But the world does not end there. Snorri's vision of the green earth after the fire gathers the survivors at Íðavöllr, where Ásgarðr stood: Baldr and Höðr return from Hel, reconciled, and 'Þórr's sons Móði and Magni shall come there, and they shall have Mjöllnir.' The hammer survives the god. The Edda's strangest consolation is also its plainest: the fathers die in the fire, and the sons carry their tools out of it.

myths.title: The Father's Boast
myths.text: The Poetic Edda's other notice of Magni is a single genealogical line, and a revealing one. In Hárbarðsljóð, trading insults with the disguised ferryman, Þórr finally names himself at full strength: 'I am Óðinn's son, Meili's brother, and Magni's father' — Magna faðir. Of all the titles the thunderer could have chosen to close a flyting — breaker of giants, lord of Thrúðheimr, wielder of the hammer — the name he reaches for is his son's.

magni.syncretism: Magni's scene belongs to one of the oldest hero-patterns in the Indo-European world: the prodigious infant. Greek tradition sets it at the beginning of Heraklês' life — the baby strangling the serpents in his cradle, sung by Pindar in the first Nemean ode and told by Apollodorus (Library 2.4.8) — and Irish tradition builds the boyhood deeds of Cú Chulainn on the same armature, the macgnímrada of the Táin, where a child performs the feats of grown champions. The North compressed the whole pattern into a single sentence: three nights old, and already the strongest person in the story. The comparison is one of motif, not borrowing — Simek and Lindow treat Magni as a native figure of the Þórr-complex, and no line of transmission is needed. His name, meanwhile, is ordinary Germanic vocabulary: *maginą, 'strength', an element that built personal names all over the North — so that the strongest boy in the Edda wears the plainest possible label: 'the strong one'.
magni.culturalLegacy: Magni's afterlife ran quiet for centuries: the Icelandic given name Magni never died out, and Victorian mythographies kept the Hrungnir duel in circulation as one of Þórr's set-pieces — the Kearys' Heroes of Asgard (1857) retold it for generations of children. The twenty-first century put the brothers back on stage. Marvel Comics introduced Magni Thorson, a future son of Thor, in the 'Reigning' storyline of Thor in the early 2000s; and Santa Monica Studio's God of War (2018) cast Magni and Modi as their father's enforcers, carrying the pair to an audience far larger than the Edda's. Modern Heathenry keeps him among the sons of the Æsir honored for the survival of the world after Ragnarǫk — the generation for whom the hammer is kept.
magni.extendedMeditation: Magni is the Edda's answer to the question every parent eventually asks: will anyone be strong enough when I cannot stand up? The myth answers it twice. Once at Grjótúnagarðar, where the whole company of the gods heaves at a dead giant's leg and fails, and a three-night-old boy walks up and does it — strength, the story insists, is not a function of age or rank, and help can arrive from the person everyone overlooked. And once at the end of the world, where the father kills the serpent, walks nine paces, and falls — and the hammer is not buried with him. Móði and Magni carry Mjǫllnir into the green world. The Edda does not promise that the strong live forever. It promises that strength, like the hammer, is inheritable.
magni.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Magni — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i, the ᚴ rune writing g; the name ends in the ja-stem -i, so there is no nominative -r as there is in Baldr's ᛒᛅᛚᛏᛦ). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: magni.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál 51 ('Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir'), Hárbarðsljóð 53 (Þórr as 'Magni's father'), Vǫluspá 56 (Þórr's death)
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17 (the Hrungnir duel; Magni, three nights old, lifts the leg; Gullfaxi) and Gylfaginning 51, 53 (Þórr's fall; the sons inherit Mjöllnir at Íðavöllr)
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. magn, magni, Magni
Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. Magni
Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology; Orchard, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend; Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide — s.v. Magni, Móði, Hrungnir

magni.archaeology: Magni is a purely textual figure: no runestone invokes him as a god, no votive deposit or place-name can be securely tied to his cult, and no picture stone has been convincingly read as the lifting of Hrungnir's leg. The material record keeps only his name's raw material: Magni occurs as an ordinary human personal name in Viking-Age runic inscriptions (collected in Peterson's Nordiskt runnamnslexikon), built on the same magn 'strength' element that names the god. The textual witnesses hang by the usual thin threads: Vafþrúðnismál, Hárbarðsljóð, and Vǫluspá in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); Skáldskaparmál in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister manuscripts; and the giantess þulur of the Skáldskaparmál, which list his mother Járnsaxa among the troll-women.

phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) dental stop [dʲ], the tongue raised toward the hard palate — the soft 'dy' onset Irish keeps to this day.
Short front [e] followed by a slender r [ɾʲ], the stressed syllable — brief and bright, never the English 'eer'.
Lenited [ð], the voiced dental fricative of English 'this', running into a second slender r [ɾʲ]; the manuscript writes plain d, the sound has softened.
The close front ending [u] with a palatal off-glide — the Old Irish nominative Derdriu ends on a light rising note.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DYER-dryu' — stress the first syllable; slender d, short 'e', the second d melted into the soft 'th' of 'this'. Modern Irish says 'DYER-dra', and English has long settled on 'DEER-dree'.

kin.label: Old Irish
kin.form: Derdriu, the manuscript form of the Book of Leinster; the name is also attested as an ordinary woman's name in early Irish records

kin.label: Modern Irish
kin.form: Deirdre, the normalized living form and the temple's spelling

kin.label: Scottish Gaelic
kin.form: Deirdre / Dèirdre, kept in the Gaelic tradition of Alba that localized her exile in Argyll

kin.label: Anglicized
kin.form: Deirdre, unchanged — the name crossed into English without losing a letter

pronunciation.note: Deirdre is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the standing of Ireland's most tragic heroine in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Tragedy, Beauty
domains.subtitle: The Woman the Prophecy Named, Ireland's Most Sorrowful Heroine
domains.lead: Deirdre is the tragic heart of the Ulster Cycle: the girl whose beauty a druid prophesied at birth would bring ruin on Ulster, raised in secret by King Conchobar mac Nessa to be his own bride, who chose instead the young Naoise son of Uisnech and fled with him and his brothers to Alba. Lured home by a king's treachery, she saw her lovers slain at Emain Macha, lived a year without smiling, and dashed out her own life rather than pass to the man who had betrayed her — the death that made her, in the medieval phrase, the heroine of one of the Three Sorrowful Tales of Ireland.

cards.name: The Raven on the Snow
cards.desc: She saw a raven drinking blood in the snow and wished for a man with hair black as the raven, cheeks red as the blood, skin white as the snow — and Lebarcham named Naoise.

cards.name: The Sons of Uisnech
cards.desc: Naoise, Ardan, and Ainnle — the three brothers whose singing could lull the world, whose exile and death the whole tale turns upon.

cards.name: Emain Macha
cards.desc: Conchobar's royal seat, the court that raised her, the fort where the sons of Uisnech were slain — and the place she would not survive.

cards.name: The Two Trees
cards.desc: In the later telling, two yews grew from the graves of Deirdre and Naoise and wove their tops together over Emain Macha — love outlasting the king.

symbols.name: The raven, the blood, the snow
symbols.meaning: The three colours of her desire, spoken before she had seen a man — the wish the whole tragedy answers

symbols.name: The three sons of Uisnech
symbols.meaning: Naoise, Ardan, and Ainnle — one fate shared by three brothers; loyalty that follows her into exile and death

symbols.name: Emain Macha
symbols.meaning: The royal fort of Ulster — safety that was a cage, and the gate to which exile could not safely return

symbols.name: The crossing to Alba
symbols.meaning: The sea between Ireland and Scotland — the only escape the tale allows, and never a lasting one

symbols.name: The two entwined trees
symbols.meaning: Yews from the lovers' graves woven together — the later tradition's one gesture toward consolation

mythology.lead: Deirdre's story is the most perfectly shaped tragedy in medieval Irish literature: a prophecy, a wish, an elopement, an exile, a betrayal, and a death, told in Longes mac nUislenn — the Exile of the Sons of Uisnech — with an economy no retelling has improved. It is a fore-tale of the Táin, and it leaves Ulster's honour in ruins before the great cattle-raid ever begins.

myths.title: The Prophecy at Her Birth
myths.text:
She was born to trouble. At the feast of Fedlimid mac Daill, Conchobar's storyteller, Fedlimid's wife cried out from the womb she carried, and the druid Cathbad laid his hand on her belly and spoke the child's fate: a girl of yellow hair and grey eyes and foxglove lips, whose beauty would be ruin — kings would fight for her, the sons of Uisnech would die for her, and Ulster would lose its greatest heroes because of her. The warriors of Ulster cried out to kill the infant at once.

Conchobar refused. He would take the child, he said, and raise her apart, and she would be his own wife — no one else's ruin. So Deirdre was reared in a secluded house with her foster-parents and her nurse Lebarcham, seeing no man but those three and the king who meant to claim her. The prophecy is the tale's first sentence; everything after is its unfolding.

myths.title: The Raven on the Snow
myths.text:
One winter day her foster-father flayed a calf in the snow for her dinner, and a raven came down to drink the blood. Deirdre looked at the three colours and said to Lebarcham: she could love a man with those three colours — hair black as the raven, cheeks red as the blood, skin white as the snow. Lebarcham told her such a man was near: Naoise son of Uisnech, of Conchobar's own household.

Deirdre sent for him, and when Naoise came she put her two hands on his ears — 'two ears of shame and derision,' she said, if he would not take her away — and bound him by the honour of an Ulster warrior. That night Naoise took her, and with his brothers Ardan and Ainnle and a hundred and fifty warriors they fled the king's house. The wish spoken over the calf's blood is the tale's hinge: the one moment Deirdre chooses, and all the rest follows from the choosing.

myths.title: The Exile in Alba
myths.text:
Conchobar pursued them through Ireland until they crossed the sea to Alba, and there they made a life the tale calls happy: the sons of Uisnech hunted, Deirdre kept house, and their singing was famous. But the same pattern waited across the water — the king of Alba heard of her beauty and desired her, and the brothers had to fight free and flee again, from glen to glen and island to island, until no place in Alba was safe for a woman too beautiful and the men who would not give her up.

It was then that Conchobar's messengers came with peace on their lips. The king swore he longed for them; he sent sureties — in the old version, Fergus mac Róich, Conchobar's greatest champion, stood pledge for their safety. Deirdre alone did not believe it. She had dreamed, she said, of three birds from Emain carrying honey in their beaks who left with blood — the honey the fair words, the blood the truth of them. But the sons of Uisnech trusted the surety of Fergus, and they sailed home.

myths.tag: Longes mac nUislenn / Oided mac nUislenn
myths.title: The Betrayal at Emain Macha
myths.text:
The trap was laid in the old way, through honour itself. As Fergus escorted the exiles south he was detained by an engineered feast — a geis-bound invitation he could not refuse — and sent the sons of Uisnech on to Emain under the protection of his sons, while Deirdre sang warnings at every stop. At Emain they were lodged in the house of the Red Branch, and when Conchobar sent to know whether Deirdre had kept her looks, and heard she had, he sent his warrior Maine against the house. The sons of Uisnech fought; the sons of Fergus died defending them; and at last Naoise and Ardan and Ainnle were cut down together, one sword-stroke taking the three, as Deirdre had foreseen in the blood-red dream.

Then Deirdre sang the laments the tradition kept as the summit of Irish elegy — for Naoise, 'fair and great and gentle', for the brothers, for the dún they would see no more. The betrayal broke Ulster: Fergus and three thousand of the Ulaid went into exile to Connacht, to Ailill and Medb — and that is why, when the Táin begins, Ulster's greatest champion stands in the enemy's host. Deirdre's tragedy is the Táin's hidden prologue.

myths.title: The Year Without a Smile, and the Death
myths.text:
Conchobar took Deirdre, and for a year she lived in his house and did not smile, did not raise her head from her knee, did not eat her fill or sleep her fill. When the king asked what she hated most in the world, she answered: 'You, and Éogan mac Durthacht' — the man who had struck down Naoise. So Conchobar gave her to Éogan, to be passed like a debt between the two men she loathed.

The next day she was driven beside Éogan's chariot, and as they went she saw the standing stone before her and put her head out of the chariot and dashed it against the rock, and so died. The later telling, Oided mac nUislenn, gives the tradition its consolation: she was buried beside Naoise, a yew grew from each grave, and the two trees wove their tops together over Emain Macha. The old version grants no such mercy — it ends with a woman who had been a prize since the hour of her birth taking back, in the only way left, the disposal of herself.

deirdre.syncretism: The Welsh corpus knows no Deirdre, and the silence is honest: the Mabinogi and its wider tradition preserve no figure derived from her name. The instructive comparison within Celtic literature is structural — Blodeuwedd in the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, the woman made from flowers for a husband she does not choose, who takes her own lover and pays for it: the medieval Celtic literatures staged, more than once, the tragedy of a woman treated as a thing made or kept for a man. Scholars have also compared the wider motif-cluster — the beauty prophesied at birth to ruin a kingdom — with the classical pattern of Helen, a comparison of motifs, never of descent. Within Ireland, her closest company is the cycle's own doomed: the tradition itself grouped her tale with the Children of Lir and the sons of Tuireann as the Three Sorrowful Tales of Ireland, and her one year of silence beside Conchobar is the cycle's starkest answer to a king's power.
deirdre.culturalLegacy: No Irish heroine has had a longer afterlife. The Gaelic tradition of Scotland kept her in Alba — the late recension of her death-tale survives in the Glenmasan manuscript, and Argyll named her exile's glens and lochs after her. The Irish literary revival made her its central woman: AE staged Deirdre in 1902, Yeats his Deirdre in 1907, Lady Gregory wove the tale through Cuchulain of Muirthemne, and J. M. Synge left at his death the unfinished Deirdre of the Sorrows (1910), the play that fixed her English name — the sorrows — forever. In the revolutionary generation she became an emblem of Ireland itself, the beautiful land betrayed and bereaved; and the name never left the language, Deirdre remaining a living Irish given name into the present century.
deirdre.extendedMeditation:
Deirdre is the rare tragic heroine whose tragedy is not what she suffers but what she is denied: a single choice. The tale gives her exactly one free act — the wish by the calf's blood, the hands on Naoise's ears — and then spends its length closing every door it opened. The druid's prophecy is not a curse on her; it is a verdict on everyone around her, and the tale is careful to prove the druid right by the men's deeds, not hers. Conchobar's 'mercy' at her birth is only a longer leash; Fergus's surety is only a prettier trap. What the sons of Uisnech die of is not her beauty but a king's appetite wearing the mask of pardon.

Her answer, when every door is shut, is the hardest the Irish corpus knows: a year of silence, and then the standing stone. The medieval tale does not sentimentalize it. She will not be consoled, will not smile, will not be passed on; the later tradition added the entwined yews because the audience needed the mercy, but the old text ends at the rock. Ireland grouped her story among its Three Sorrowful Tales not because a woman died, but because a whole kingdom's honour died with her — and the woman, in the end, was the only one who kept hers.
deirdre.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in the Book of Leinster in the Old Irish form Derdriu, written in the Insular Latin script — plain Latin letters, with no diacritic for the restoration to recover; the temple form Deirdre is the normalized Modern Irish spelling. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: deirdre.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

deirdre.archaeology: Deirdre is a textual heroine: no ogham stone names her and no votive inscription invokes her, as befits a figure of heroic legend rather than cult. Her mythic address, however, is one of the most excavated sites in Ireland: Emain Macha, Conchobar's royal seat, survives as Navan Fort in County Armagh, where excavation revealed a great circular timber structure of the first century BC — raised, filled with stones, burned, and mounded over in what reads as a single enormous ritual act, dated by dendrochronology to 95/94 BC. Her manuscript witnesses are exact: Longes mac nUislenn survives earliest in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster (Trinity College Dublin, MS H 2.18), the basis of Hull's edition, while the expanded death-tale Oided mac nUislenn is preserved in the fifteenth-century Glenmasan manuscript (National Library of Scotland, Advocates' MS 72.1.37), the text that carried her story into the Gaelic tradition of Scotland. The name itself was a real one: eDIL records Derdriu as an ordinary woman's name in early Irish sources, so the heroine bore a name of her own world, not an invented one.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m] followed by short open [a], the light unstressed first syllable.
Alveolar nasal [n] and a second short open [a]; Welsh stress has not yet fallen.
The stressed penult: a labial-velar glide [w] into the Welsh high-central vowel [ɨ], the sound English has no letter for — between the 'i' of 'bit' and the 'u' of 'put'.
Voiced alveolar stop [d], short open [a], and final alveolar nasal [n], closing the name unstressed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'man-ah-WIH-dan' — stress the third syllable (the Welsh penult); the w is a quick glide and the y is the Welsh central vowel [ɨ], a sound with no English equivalent, closest to a tight, short 'ih'.
