The lexicon's gloss is 'Manannán (Welsh form)', and that is the defensible line: Ifor Williams derived the name from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, and the Old Irish Manannán is its cognate. The brief that sometimes floats around — *man-, 'mind' — is not the derivation the handbooks print, and this temple does not use it.

domains.title: The Wise Survivor of Dyfed
domains.subtitle: Sea, Craftsmanship — the Son of Llŷr who outwitted an enchantment
domains.lead: Manawydan fab Llŷr is the Mabinogi's counselor and craftsman: a son of the sea-named Llŷr and brother of Brân the Blessed, one of the seven who came home from Ireland with the wondrous head — and the man who, when Dyfed was stripped bare by enchantment, kept his patience, took up the saddler's, the shield-maker's, and the shoemaker's trades, and unmade the spell without a sword-stroke, by hanging a mouse and refusing three ransoms.

cards.name: Son of Llŷr
cards.desc: Brother of Brân and Branwen, of the house whose very name is the sea — the Welsh face of the figure Ireland calls Manannán mac Lir.

cards.name: The Golden Shoemaker
cards.desc: In exile at Hereford he made shoes so fine the triads remember him among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain.

cards.name: Gorsedd Arberth
cards.desc: The mound above Arberth where the thunder came and the mist fell — and where Manawydan later built a gallows for a mouse.

cards.name: The Tried Mouse
cards.desc: The fattest of the wheat-thieves, caught and judged as a felon — the lever that finally pried the whole enchantment open.

symbols.name: The golden bowl
symbols.meaning: The enchanted vessel on the marble slab — the snare that took Pryderi and Rhiannon by their own reaching

symbols.name: The white boar
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld lure that leads men out of the world they know, shining and wrong

symbols.name: The mouse on the gallows
symbols.meaning: Patience armed with procedure — the smallest catch that bought back a kingdom

symbols.name: The shoemaker's last
symbols.meaning: Craft as survival: the trades a dispossessed prince practiced better than the guildsmen

symbols.name: Gorsedd Arberth
symbols.meaning: The mound of wonders, where sitting is never safe and where the case was finally tried

mythology.lead: Manawydan's dossier is the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi: Branwen ferch Llŷr, where he is one of the seven who bring the head home, and Manawydan fab Llŷr, the branch that bears his name — the quietest and most perfectly built of the Four, a tale in which an entire kingdom is stolen by silence and won back by patience.

myths.title: The Seven Who Brought the Head Home
myths.text:
Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the whole catastrophe. When the insult of the mutilated horses has festered into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host that crosses with him comes home as seven men: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life.

At Harlech they feast seven years with the head, the three songs of the birds of Rhiannon singing to them, and time does not move. At Gwales in Penfro they find a royal hall with two doors open and one shut — toward Cornwall — and there they pass eighty years in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head, forgetting every sorrow, until Heilyn fab Gwyn says 'shame on my beard if I do not open the door' — and opens it, and all their losses come back at once like a tide. Then they do as the head had commanded: they carry it to London and bury it in the White Mount, facing France, and the triads count that burial among the Three Fortunate Concealments of the Island of Britain. Manawydan, who had counseled the wedding, survives its end — the pattern of his whole life in one branch.

myths.title: The Counsel and the Marriage
myths.text: While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London. Pryderi, lord of Dyfed and son of Pwyll and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], would have fought him; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war. It is the most characteristic speech in the whole Mabinogi — a man with the best claim to vengeance declining it out of arithmetic and mercy. Pryderi yields, and gives Manawydan the fairest compensation the tale can imagine: his mother's hand and the seven cantrefs of Dyfed. Manawydan and Rhiannon wed, and the four — Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi, and Pryderi's wife Cigfa — live at Arberth in unbroken fellowship.

myths.title: The Thunder and the Mist
myths.text: They go up Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where, in the First Branch, wonders came to Pwyll — and wonder comes. As they sit, a peal of thunder falls, and with it a mist so thick they cannot see one another. When it lifts, Dyfed is gone: no dwelling, no animal, no smoke, no man, no woman — only the four of them and the empty land, house and court and courtiers vanished together. For a year they live by hunting and the kindness of the emptied land; for a second year they bear it; in the third they grow weary of it, and the tale turns from endurance to answer.

myths.title: The White Boar and the Golden Bowl
myths.text: Hunting, Pryderi and Manawydan rouse a boar shining white, which leads their dogs to a fortress neither has ever seen — and no one ever sees twice. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in after the dogs and finds a fountain with a marble slab, and on the slab a golden bowl fastened by chains, wrought with a craftsmanship he cannot fathom. He reaches for it: his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon, hearing her son lost, reproaches Manawydan for returning without him, goes in, lays hold of the bowl, and is taken the same way — and with thunder and a fall of mist the fortress vanishes with them both. Manawydan is left with Cigfa, and the branch's second act belongs to them alone.

myths.title: The Three Crafts of Hereford
myths.text: Manawydan will not beg his bread in an emptied kingdom: 'Let us go into Lloegr,' he tells Cigfa, 'and take up a craft.' At Hereford he becomes a saddler, and his saddles are so fine that Hereford's saddlers, losing every customer, conspire to kill the strangers; Pryderi's heir would fight, Manawydan counts the odds, and they move on. He becomes a shield-maker — the same beauty, the same conspiracy, the same dignified retreat. He becomes a shoemaker, gilding the shoes, and the cordwainers drive them out like the rest. Three trades, each mastered at first attempt, each surrendered rather than repaid in blood: the triads never forgot it, ranking Manawydan among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain.

myths.title: The Trial of the Mouse
myths.text:
Back in empty Dyfed, Manawydan sows three crofts of wheat, and they come up the finest in the land. The first croft, ripe for reaping, is found in the morning stripped to the bare straw; the second goes the same way. On the third night Manawydan keeps watch, and sees a host of mice descend on the ears, each mouse stripping an ear and carrying it off. He runs them down and catches one — the fattest, and slow, and heavy with young. He sets a miniature gallows on the gorsedd and condemns her as a thief.

Then the ransomers come: a scholar, then a priest, then a bishop, each more richly robed than the last, each offering money for the felon's life, and to each Manawydan answers that he will not sell a convicted thief — until the bishop, pressed to name his terms, hears them whole: Pryderi and Rhiannon freed, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, no vengeance taken on the mice, and no spell ever laid on the seven cantrefs again. The bishop is Llwyd fab Cil Coed, enchanter and friend of Gwawl fab Clud — Rhiannon's jilted suitor from the First Branch — and the whole desolation was his long revenge; the mice were his own household and warband under shape, and the fat one his wife. Pryderi comes back with the gate-hammers he had been made to carry, Rhiannon with the collars of asses about her neck, the mist lifts from Dyfed, and Manawydan keeps his word to the letter: not one mouse is harmed. It is the Mabinogi's most complete victory, and no sword is drawn in it.

manawydan.syncretism: Manawydan's one great comparison is also the deepest fact about him: he is the Welsh form of the figure Ireland knows as [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], the sea god and guardian of the Otherworld. The names are cognates — Ifor Williams derived both from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, so that 'Manawydan' and 'Manannán' each mean, in effect, the Manxman — and the fathers match exactly, Welsh Llŷr against Irish Lir, each a personification of the sea. What the Welsh tradition did with the inheritance is the interesting part: where Manannán strides through Irish myth as a god of mist, ships, and wonder-working treasure, the Mabinogi keeps only the sea-kinship and the uncanny craft, and makes its Manawydan mortal, patient, and wise — a euhemerized sea god filed down to a counselor. Whether the Welsh figure is descended from the Irish, or both from a lost common sea god, is debated (Mac Cana; Koch); the handbooks register the kinship and leave the direction open. In Manx folklore the same figure survived as Mannan beg mac y Leir, first man of the island, and gave the Isle of Man its name. No Gaulish counterpart has ever been convincingly proposed; the comparison is an insular affair, Irish Sea water on both sides of it.
manawydan.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Manawydan into English, and the Third Branch has held a special place ever since: critics from Ifor Williams onward have called it the most perfectly constructed of the Four Branches, and the trial of the mouse — the courtly ransomers, the miniature gallows, the terms exacted one by one — is the anthology piece of Welsh prose comedy and wisdom in one. Scholarship gave the name its modern standing: Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text and the Manaw etymology, and Mac Cana's The Mabinogi made the branch's architecture a set text of Celtic studies. Modern Druid and pagan practice honors Manawydan as a patron of craft, patience, and the sea-kinship; in Wales the name survives as a rare literary given name, carried less by folk memory than by the sheer durability of the Third Branch, which has never gone out of print since Guest.
manawydan.extendedMeditation: Manawydan is the Mabinogi's argument that wisdom is a kind of patience. Every test the tale sets him, he passes by declining the heroic option: when Caswallawn usurps the crown, he counts the cost of war and stays his hand; when Dyfed is emptied, he hunts, endures, and waits; when his companions are taken, he does not storm the fortress — he learns three trades and practices them beautifully in exile. Even his victory is procedural: a watch kept, a mouse caught, a gallows built, three ransoms refused, and terms — release, restoration, amnesty, guarantee — exacted one by one before the noose is loosened. He is the only hero in the Four Branches who wins everything he wants and kills nothing to get it. The sea-named son of Llŷr spends his great story on land, but the sea is in the method: he outlasts what he cannot fight, and the tide turns. The question the branch leaves is uncomfortable and exact — how much of what we call courage is only impatience wearing armor?
manawydan.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Manawydan — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi, with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: manawydan.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/manawydan/ in the meantime.

manawydan.archaeology: Manawydan is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of the Third Branch is real and visitable: Dyfed is the historic kingdom of southwest Wales; Arberth is Narberth in Pembrokeshire, and the gorsedd is traditionally located on the hill above it; the seven cantrefs of Dyfed were still an administrative reality when the tales were written. The nearest linguistic trace of the sea-kinship is onomastic rather than archaeological: Manaw survives in the Welsh name of the Isle of Man and in Manaw Gododdin, the district of the old North remembered in place-names such as Clackmannan and Slamannan.

pronunciation.approximation: MAATH — a long, open 'ah', held like the a of 'father', closing on the soft voiceless th of English 'thin'. One syllable; the whole weight of the name sits on the length of the vowel and the hush at the end.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Math (Math uab Mathonwy) is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The standard etymology derives the name from Proto-Celtic *matu- 'bear' — compare Old Irish math 'bear' (attested in the compound mathgamain), the Irish name Mathgen borne by the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish Matugenos 'bear-born'. The father's name, Mathonwy, is built on the same root, and the handbooks treat the bear-derivation as the best-supported reading.

domains.title: Magic, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Math
domains.lead: In the celtic tradition, Math governed magic, kingship. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.name: The Wand of Office
cards.desc: Math's hutlath — the magic wand that tested Arianrhod, turned his nephews into beasts for three years, and helped fashion a woman out of flowers.

cards.name: The Footholder's Geas
cards.desc: The strange condition of his kingship: Math could not live except with his feet in the lap of a virgin, unless the turmoil of war released him.

cards.name: The Threefold Sentence
cards.desc: His justice wore animal skins: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy spent a year each as deer, boars, and wolves — and their beast-children were baptized at his court.

cards.name: The Flower Bride
cards.desc: With Gwydion he took oak, broom, and meadowsweet and made Blodeuwedd — the wife no earthly race could supply for the nephew fated to have none.

symbols.name: The magic wand (hutlath)
symbols.meaning: The rod of transformation and testing — proof, punishment, and creation carried in one length of wood

symbols.name: The virgin's lap
symbols.meaning: The footholder's office — the geas that bound the king's life to an untouched maiden, save in time of war

symbols.name: Goewin ferch Pebin
symbols.meaning: The footholder of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, wronged in the king's own house and made his queen in redress

symbols.name: The swine of Annwfn
symbols.meaning: The otherworld herd whose engineered theft gave Gwydion his war — the first pigs in Wales, and the pretext that broke the geas

symbols.name: Hyddwn, Hychddwn, and Bleiddwn

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet

mythology.lead: Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi — the branch that bears his name: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His rule hangs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live except with his feet in a virgin's lap, unless war calls him out — and around that geas the whole plot turns: the theft of the swine, the wrong to Goewin, the justice of the three animal years, and the making of a bride from flowers.

myths.title: The Geas of the Footholder
myths.text:
Math son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and the tale's first fact about him is the condition of his life: except when the turmoil of war prevented it, he could not live unless his feet lay in the lap of a virgin. The office of footholder went to Goewin daughter of Pebin of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, the fairest maiden of her generation; and while Math kept the lap, his sister's sons Gwydion and Gilfaethwy ruled the realm in his stead.

The arrangement is neither joke nor luxury: it is the Fourth Branch's picture of sacral kingship, a rule whose life is bound by taboo. When Gilfaethwy sickened with desire for Goewin, Gwydion read the geas like a statute. The king may leave the lap for one thing only — war. Therefore there would be a war.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
Pryderi of Dyfed held the hobeu, the swine sent him from Annwfn by its king Arawn — the first pigs ever brought to Wales. Gwydion went south in the guise of a poet, conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, traded the day's glamour for the herd, and was gone before the illusion faded. Pryderi mustered and came north, and Math led Gwynedd out to meet him — out of the lap, exactly as the condition required.

At the parley Pryderi demanded single combat, for it was because of him that the hosts had come; at the maenor of Penardd Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed gave hostages and went home under tribute. But while Math marched, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin in the king's own chamber. The war had only ever been the key, and the lap the lock.

myths.title: The Queen and the Three Skins
myths.text:
Goewin would not hide what had been done to her, and Math's first act was redress: he took her as his wife and made her queen, so that the disgrace should not fall on her. Then came judgment. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third.

Each year's offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — the king took in beast-shape, restored to human form, baptized, and raised. After the third year he struck the brothers back into men: they had had punishment enough, he said, and been greatly shamed, and he received them back into honour. It is the most exact justice in the Mabinogi — transformation as sentence, a year for each skin of the debt, and restoration without residue.

myths.title: The Stepping over the Wand
myths.text:
A new footholder was needed, and Gwydion named his own sister, Arianrhod daughter of Dôn. Math put the question plainly — was she a virgin? — and set the test: step over my wand. As she stepped, she dropped a sturdy yellow-haired boy. Math had him baptized at once and named him Dylan, and the boy made straight for the sea and took its nature, Dylan son of Wave.

And as Arianrhod turned to go, she dropped 'something small', which Gwydion swept up and hid in a chest at the foot of his bed — the boy who would be Lleu Llaw Gyffes. The wand that punishes is also the wand that proves: in one gesture the age of footholders ended and the age of the Children of Dôn began.

myths.title: The Bride Made of Flowers
myths.text:
Arianrhod, shamed before the court, laid her tynghedau on the boy: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion's craft undid the first two; for the third there was no earthly answer, and it was Math who joined him in making one. The two enchanters took their wands and, from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet, fashioned the fairest and most beautiful maiden anyone had seen, baptized her, and named her Blodeuwedd — and gave her to Lleu.

The tale records no death for Math. The branch ends with Lleu restored and avenged, ruling Gwynedd after, and the old king simply withdraws from the record — the stillness at the centre to the last.

math.syncretism: Math is the Welsh reflex of a pan-Celtic institution: the sacral king whose rule is bound by taboo. Irish tradition gives the condition its clearest grammar — the gessi of kings, the network of prohibitions whose slow breaking dooms Conaire Mór in Togail Bruidne Da Derga — and Math's footholder geas is the same machinery in Welsh dress, a kingship valid only while its condition holds. Mac Cana reads the Children of Dôn as the Welsh counterpart of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the name itself crosses the water on its own root: Cath Maige Tuired names Mathgen as the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish epigraphy attests Matugenos — both 'bear-born', from the *matu- that names the king and his father. Within the Mabinogi the root echoes across the branches: [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the Irish king of the Second Branch, carries the same Math- element. His closest kin are the members of his own house — his sister [[don|Dôn]]'s children, above all [[gwydion|Gwydion]], whose plots the geas licences and whose punishments the king's wand performs — and the co-made bride [[blodeuwedd|Blodeuwedd]], his one act of creation.
math.culturalLegacy: Math's afterlife is quieter than his nephews', but the Fourth Branch carried him far. In the twentieth century the branch was remade twice over: Evangeline Walton's The Virgin and the Swine (1936) retells his story as a tragedy of old religion and new, with the geas and the three animal years as its moral engine, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain made Math son of Mathonwy the aged High King of Prydain for a generation of young readers — the geas laid aside, the grave authority kept. Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) drew its haunting from the Blodeuwedd strand that Math's wand set in motion, the branch repeating itself down the generations of a Welsh valley. In scholarship he stands at the centre of the Mabinogi industry: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi fixed the text, Sioned Davies's Oxford translation carries it to the world's readers, and Mac Cana's and Koch's handbooks treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose, with the footholder geas among the most-discussed cruxes in Celtic studies.
math.extendedMeditation: Math is the proof that a story's most powerful figure can be its stillest. He does not trick, march, or seduce; he sits, and the sitting is the kingship — feet in a maiden's lap, the realm held by nephews, the whole arrangement waiting for someone to notice that war is the one door out of the geas. What makes him great is what he does after the door is used against him: redress before revenge, a wronged girl made queen, a sentence fitted exactly to the crime and limited exactly to it, and then — the rarest thing in any mythology of punishment — restoration without residue. His wand does everything the tale needs: it tests, it transforms, it creates. But its deepest work is juridical. Math is the king whose magic is law and whose law has a measure — three years, three skins, and the account closed — and whose stillness is not weakness but the condition of rule itself.
math.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Math (Math uab Mathonwy), in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain math.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

math.archaeology: Math is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), the two codices in which the Fourth Branch survives. The epigraphic witness belongs to the root rather than the man: Gaulish personal names such as Matugenos, 'bear-born', attest the *matu- element in the onomastics of the continental Celts. The tale's own geography is real Gwynedd terrain — Dôl Pebin in Arfon, where Goewin's father held his land — and the branch's southern war-road runs to the maenor of Penardd, where Pryderi fell.

phonemes.desc: Unstressed open [ma], the light first syllable — the 'ma' of 'matter' held brief.
Voiceless dental fricative [θ], the 'th' of English 'thin' — Welsh writes it with the digraph th, sharply distinct from dd, which is the voiced 'th' of 'this'.
Short stressed [ɔ], the 'o' of 'off', carrying the word's penultimate stress, as Welsh words do.
Welsh w is a full vowel, here short [ʊ] like the 'u' of 'put'; ch is the voiceless velar fricative [x], the rough ch of Scottish 'loch'.

pronunciation.approximation: ma-THOL-ukh — stress the middle syllable; 'th' as in 'thin'; the w is a short 'oo'-like vowel; the final ch is the rough, breathy ch of Scottish 'loch', as in modern Welsh.

domains.title: The King Across the Sea
domains.subtitle: The Thirteen Ships, the Maimed Horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth
domains.lead: Matholwch is the king of Ireland in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr: the bridegroom who came with thirteen ships to Harlech to ask for Branwen's hand, the wronged man appeased with gold and a cauldron that raises the dead, and the husband who could not shield his queen when the insult of the maimed horses came home to his court — the man whose marriage laid two islands waste.

cards.name: The Thirteen Ships
cards.desc: The fleet that brought him to Harlech to ask for Branwen — Ireland arriving as a suitor, and sailing home as a husband.

cards.name: The Maimed Horses
cards.desc: Efnisien's insult — lips, ears, tails, and eyelids cut to the bone — the wound no compensation could make Ireland forget.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
cards.desc: Given to Matholwch in recompense: the slain cast in at evening rise fighting-fit by morning — all but their speech.

cards.name: The Starling
cards.desc: Branwen's tamed messenger, taught to speak, carrying her letter across the sea to Brân when no ship could sail.

symbols.name: The thirteen ships
symbols.meaning: Sea-borne kingship — the power that comes across the water to ask, and can always sail away

symbols.name: The maimed horses
symbols.meaning: An insult done to property but felt in honor — the wound that recompense could not close

symbols.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
symbols.meaning: Resurrection without speech: the body restored, the voice withheld

symbols.name: The starling
symbols.meaning: The smallest thing in the tale that crosses the sea — a tamed bird against a kingdom's embargo

symbols.name: The house of a hundred pillars
symbols.meaning: Peace built as a trap: a pillar for every beam, a bag on every pillar, an armed man in every bag

mythology.lead: Matholwch has essentially one story — but it is the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, the tale medieval Welsh literature remembers as its national tragedy: a marriage between the two islands that ends with the hosts of both destroyed.

myths.title: The Thirteen Ships at Harlech
myths.text: Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed, crowned king of Britain — was seated on the rock of Harlech above the sea, with his brother Manawydan and his half-brothers Nisien and Efnisien, when they saw thirteen ships coming from the south of Ireland, fair and swift, their shields above their gunwales. It was Matholwch, king of Ireland, come to ask for Branwen, Brân's sister, fairest maiden in the world, so that Ireland and the Island of the Mighty might be joined by marriage and grow stronger together. Brân consented, and the wedding was held at Aberffraw — and because no house had ever been built that could contain Brân, they slept in tents.

myths.title: The Maiming of the Horses
myths.text:
Efnisien, the half-brother whose gift was quarreling, had not been consulted, and he took the omission as an insult to his honor. Coming on Matholwch's horses stabled apart, he asked whose they were, and hearing, he fell on them in a rage: he cut their lips back to the teeth, their ears back to their heads, their tails to the skin, and their eyelids back to the bone. Matholwch's men could make no sense of it — a king given a bride and mutilated horses in the same week. They armed for home in silence, which Brân read rightly as the beginning of a war.

Brân sent an embassy led by Manawydan to ask what recompense would content him. Matholwch was offered the full replacement of the horses, a silver staff as tall as himself, a golden platter as broad as his face — and, beyond all price, the Cauldron of Rebirth. The tale is exact about the transaction: the honor-price was paid, the peace was sworn, and neither was ever real again.

myths.title: The Cauldron of Rebirth
myths.text:
Matholwch asked where such a cauldron had come from, and Brân told him: it had come to him out of Ireland itself. A man named Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife Cymidei Cymeinfoll — a woman who gave birth to a fully armed warrior every six weeks — had fled the Irish king's plot to burn them alive in a white-hot iron house, and had brought the cauldron with them to Wales. Its property was this: cast a slain warrior into it at evening, and by morning he rises as fighting-fit as before, except that he never again has the power of speech.

So the cauldron returned to Ireland as a wedding-gift of reconciliation — a thing that cancels death but keeps its silence, given to heal an insult that would not stay healed. The irony is the tale's own: the Irish fought their last battle with it, feeding their slain back into the war, until it was destroyed from within.

myths.title: The Starling and the Crossing of the Sea
myths.text:
Matholwch sailed home with his bride, and Ireland welcomed her; gifts were given, and in due time she bore a son, Gwern. But the insult of the horses would not lie down. Matholwch's nobles nursed the grudge until they drove their king to atone for it: Branwen was put out of the chamber and into the kitchen, and the butcher came every day and struck her a blow on the ear. All passage to Wales was stopped, so that no word could reach her brother.

Branwen reared a starling at the edge of the kneading-trough, taught it speech, tied her letter beneath its wing, and sent it across the sea. The bird found Brân at Caer Seint in Arfon and settled on his shoulder. What followed is the great set-piece of the branch: the crowned king of Britain crossed the sea at the head of his host — wading, for no ship could hold him — and when the Irish destroyed the bridges and his men asked his counsel, he answered with the sentence Welsh has never let go: 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and lay down across the river so the host could pass over him.

myths.title: The Hundred Pillars and the End of the Cauldron
myths.text:
The Irish sued for peace on their knees: they would give the kingship of Ireland to Gwern, Matholwch's son by Branwen, and build Brân a house — the first ever made that could hold him. The house was raised with a hundred pillars, and on every pillar a bag, and in every bag an armed man. Efnisien came in first to inspect the peace, asked what was in the bags — 'Flour,' they said — and crushed each head between his fingers, one by one, until he felt the bone give.

At the feast the boy Gwern was passed lovingly from lap to lap until he came to Efnisien's, and Efnisien rose and cast him into the fire. Branwen would have leapt after her son; Brân held her with one hand and took up his shield with the other. Then came the battle the whole tale had been marching toward. The Irish threw their slain into the Cauldron of Rebirth and sent them back each morning, mute and fighting — until Efnisien, in the act that pays for all the rest, lay down among the Irish dead as if slain, was cast into the cauldron with the corpses, and stretched himself out inside it until the cauldron burst in pieces and his own heart burst with it. Of the Irish there escaped only five pregnant women, from whom the five provinces of Ireland were repeopled; of the Welsh host, seven men — Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu, Taliesin, Ynawg, Grudyeu, and Heilyn — and Brân, dying of a poisoned spear in the foot, who bade them cut off his head and carry it home. Branwen died of a broken heart on the bank of the Alaw, crying that two good islands had been laid waste because of her. Of Matholwch himself the tale says nothing more: he is not given a death-scene, only swallowed in the general ruin of his kingdom.

matholwch.syncretism: Matholwch is a Welsh invention wearing an Irish crown, and the tradition knows it: no Irish-language tale names him, and his kingship of Ireland exists only inside Branwen ferch Llŷr. The honest comparisons are structural, and Proinsias Mac Cana's monograph Branwen Daughter of Llŷr mapped them: Brân's sea-crossing against the Voyage of Bran mac Febail (Immram Brain), the children of Llŷr against the Irish family of Lir, and above all the Cauldron of Rebirth against the cauldron-lore of Ireland — the Dagda's cauldron from Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standard parallel for the Celtic vessel of inexhaustible power. The Welsh and Irish cauldrons divide the two ends of the motif between them: Ireland's feeds the living, Wales's revives the dead — and takes their speech as payment. Arthurian scholarship, from Loomis onward, has long set the cauldron and the carried head beside the Grail procession of Peredur; the comparison is illuminating and unprovable, and this temple registers it as such.
matholwch.culturalLegacy: Matholwch entered the world's reading with Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49), which carried the Second Branch into English and made the maimed horses and the Cauldron of Rebirth part of the general inheritance of fantasy literature. Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text for scholarship, and Sioned Davies's translation (2007) is the modern English standard. The branch's sentences have never left Welsh letters — 'a fo ben, bid bont' is quoted wherever leadership is discussed — and Evangeline Walton's The Children of Llyr (1971) retells the whole catastrophe as a novel. The cauldron motif, transmitting through the Welsh tradition, stands behind every modern cauldron that raises armies of the dead; Lloyd Alexander's Prydain chronicles drew freely on the Mabinogion's world. On Anglesey, the Bronze Age cairn beside the river Alaw still answers to the name Bedd Branwen, Branwen's grave — the tale's one fixed point in the landscape of two islands.
matholwch.extendedMeditation:
Matholwch is the king who accepted the compensation and could not accept it. Nothing in the tale is more carefully drawn than the failure of the settlement: the horses replaced, the silver staff, the golden platter, the cauldron itself — a full honor-price, formally paid, formally received. And still the insult kept working, not in him alone but in his nobles, until it expelled the queen to the kitchen and the butcher's daily blow. The Second Branch is the Mabinogion's treatise on the difference between settling a wrong and healing one.

His cauldron is the perfect emblem of the settlement's logic: it undoes the death and keeps the silence. The men who climb out of it fight as well as ever and cannot speak — cannot say what the war cost, cannot forgive, cannot testify. Matholwch ends as he began, a king whose kingdom is decided by what others do around him: Efnisien maims his horses, his nobles disgrace his wife, his guests massacre his peace, his bridegroom's gift arms his own destruction. The tale does not even grant him a death. It grants him something more instructive — a marriage made in good faith between two islands, and the proof that good faith is not enough when honor has been taught to count higher.
matholwch.originalScriptNote: The normalized Middle Welsh form is Matholwch — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet, and its distinctive sounds are carried by digraphs (th, ch, ll) and the vowel-letter w, none of which the ASCII set lacks. The earlier monumental scripts of the two islands — the ogham stones of Ireland and Wales — predate the manuscript tradition, but no attestation of this name has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: matholwch.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

matholwch.archaeology: Matholwch is a textual figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or place-name in Ireland names him, and his kingship exists entirely within the Welsh tale. His manuscript witnesses are exact — the Second Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 4, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425), the two great codices on which Williams's edition rests. The tale's one fixed point in the landscape is Welsh: Bedd Branwen, the cairn beside the river Alaw on Anglesey where the branch says Branwen was buried, is a genuine Bronze Age burial monument — cremation urns were recovered when the cairn was opened in the early nineteenth century, and later excavations confirmed its prehistoric date. The name attached to it is medieval folklore, not prehistory — but it proves the story was already rooted in Welsh ground centuries ago. The nearest epigraphic kin of his name-element are the Gaulish personal names in Matu- (Matugenos and kin): comparative evidence only, never identification.

phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) m [mʲ] — the m of 'muse', not 'mud'; Old Irish keeps the slender quality before the front vowel.
Short front [e], the stressed vowel of the name's single syllable — the 'e' of 'bed', held brief.
Lenited d, the voiced dental fricative [ð] — the soft 'th' of English 'this'; Old Irish orthography writes lenition in this position without marking it.
Final lenited b, [v] — the ancestor of the -bh of Modern Irish Meadhbh and of the English form 'Maeve'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MYETHV' — one short syllable: slender m, brief e, the d melted into the soft 'th' of 'this', finishing on 'v'. The modern Irish Meadhbh, anglicized Maeve, has collapsed the middle consonant and sounds simply 'mayv'.

kin.form: Meadhbh, the unbroken living form — Anglicized as Maeve

kin.form: Welsh meddw, 'drunk, intoxicated' — the same adjective, worn smooth

kin.form: PIE *médhu, 'sweet drink' — English mead, Greek méthu ('wine'), and Sanskrit mádu, all one word

pronunciation.note: Medb is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: normalized Old Irish writes the name in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The temple form differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital; the queen's standing in the tradition is beside the point. The etymology, by contrast, is one of the most secure in the Celtic corpus: Old Irish medb, 'intoxicating, she who intoxicates', cognate with the noun medb, 'mead', continuing Proto-Indo-European *médhu, 'sweet drink'. The name is the sovereignty drink made personal.

domains.title: The Queen Who Chooses
domains.subtitle: The Pillow-Talk, the Bride-Gift Speech, and the Cattle Raid of Cooley
domains.lead: Medb of Crúachan is the ruling queen of Connacht and the driving will of the Táin Bó Cúailnge: the woman who audited fortunes with her husband in the night and invaded Ulster in the morning, who set the terms of her own marriages — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — and whom scholarship reads as Ireland's clearest survival of the sovereignty goddess, the land's own power to make and unmake kings.

cards.name: The Pillow-Talk
cards.desc: The night audit at Crúachan: Medb and Ailill count their wealth and find themselves equal in everything — save one bull.

cards.name: The Two Bulls
cards.desc: Finnbennach the White-Horned, who scorned a woman's keeping, and the Donn of Cúailnge — the balance of power on four legs.

cards.name: The Bride-Gift Terms
cards.desc: A husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — the bride-gift no woman before her had asked of a man of Ireland.

cards.name: Crúachan and Oweynagat
cards.desc: Her royal rath at Rathcroghan, and beneath it the Cave of the Cats — the gate of the Otherworld in the medieval tales.

symbols.name: The marriage-bed of Crúachan
symbols.meaning: The pillow-talk itself: sovereignty as an audit — equality counted coin for coin in the dark

symbols.name: The two bulls
symbols.meaning: Finnbennach and the Donn of Cúailnge: wealth, prestige, and the one point on which two rulers cannot be equal

symbols.name: The bride-gift terms
symbols.meaning: No meanness, no jealousy, no fear: the queen's own charter, demanded where a dowry was expected

symbols.name: The march of the four provinces
symbols.meaning: The raid she willed into being: armies moved by a single insistence that the account be balanced

symbols.name: Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld gate beneath her rath — the source in the tales of the things that come up on Samain night

mythology.lead: Medb's dossier is the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the longest and greatest tale of the Ulster Cycle — and unlike every other great name in Irish myth, she is not a goddess remembered as a woman but a queen the tradition may once have worshipped as a goddess. The tale itself never says which.

myths.title: The Pillow-Talk
myths.text:
One night at Crúachan, when the royal bed had been made for Medb and Ailill, they fell into a 'bolster-conversation' — comrac chind cherchailli — and Ailill boasted that the woman married to a wealthy man is well off. Medb answered that she was well off before him: daughter of Eochu Feidlech, high king of Ireland, and the wealthier of the two. To settle it they had every treasure counted — cups, rings, cattle, sheep, horses — and the tally came out exactly even, save one item: the great bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd, had scorned to be counted a woman's chattel and walked over into Ailill's, where he stood as the White-Horned of Connacht.

That one beast broke the equality Medb would not live without. Her steward Mac Roth found the match: the Donn of Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb sent for a year's loan of him at princely terms — fifty heifers a year, a stretch of the plain of Aí, her own chariot, and the friendship of her thighs — and Dáire agreed. But the messengers drank and boasted that had the loan been refused they would have taken the bull by force, and Dáire swore that only by force would he ever be taken. The embassy came home empty, and Medb resolved on war.

myths.title: The Bride-Gift Speech
myths.text:
The Táin lets Medb state her own terms, and the speech is the charter of her queenship. Daughter of the high king, wooed by the kings of Ireland, she refused them all, she says, 'for I asked a strange bride-gift such as no woman before me had asked of a man of the men of Ireland — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear.' If he were mean, their wealth could not sit together, for she is generous in gifts; if jealous, she could not live beside him, 'for I was never without one man in the shadow of another'; if fearful, he would shame her in the front of every fight.

Such a man she found in Ailill mac Máta: no meanness, no jealousy, no fear. She brought him the bride-gift — the clothing of twelve men, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals, the width of his face in red gold, the weight of his left forearm in bronze — and it is into her province, not his, that he came. The Táin is blunt about the arithmetic: he is king of Connacht because he is married to Medb of Crúachan.

myths.title: The Debility and the Boy at the Ford
myths.text:
Medb timed the raid for the cess noínden, the pangs of the Ulstermen — the debility laid on the warriors of Ulster by [[macha|Macha]], whom they had forced to race the king's horses when she was great with child. With Ulster's fighting-men abed, Medb marched the hosting of four provinces north — Connacht's own, the Leinster Galeóin, and the exiles of Ulster under Fergus mac Róich, who knew every road and ford of the way and, the tale says plainly, shared the queen's bed with Ailill's leave, for the road could not be found without him.

One boy stood against the whole hosting: [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], untouched by the debility, who held the fords in single combat and took the heads of the best of Connacht one by one. Medb spent everything on him — terms, ambushes, satirists, her daughter Findabair promised to a dozen champions at once — and the hardest price fell on Ferdia, Cú Chulainn's own foster-brother, whom she plied with drink and the promise of Findabair until he took the ford. Four days they fought; the gae bolga ended it; and the march went on over the body of the one man Medb could not buy twice.

myths.title: The Battle of the Bulls
myths.text:
The hosts met at Gáirech and Irgáirech when the pangs lifted and Ulster rose; Medb's army broke, but the prize was already driven south — she had the Donn of Cúailnge, and she covered the retreat herself, in the tale's most unsparing passage, when her gush of blood came on her and she asked Cú Chulainn's protection for her army's rear. He granted it: 'no coward's weapon is the weapon of a woman.' Fergus mac Róich, looking back over the ruin of the hosting, gave the raid its verdict: 'This is what usually happens to a herd of horses led by a mare — their substance is taken and carried off and destroyed as they follow a woman who has misled them.'

The bulls settled the account themselves. Finnbennach saw the Donn and bellowed; they fought through the night across Ireland, and in the morning the men of Connacht found the Brown Bull standing over the White-Horned trampled to pieces. The Donn carried Finnbennach's carcass on his horns through Connacht — scattering the loin at Áth Luain, the liver at Trim — then turned north for Cúailnge and died there of his wounds and his victory. Medb had her bull, and her equality, and the Táin's dry arithmetic: the two most valuable beasts in Ireland, both dead, and nothing left to count.

myths.title: The Cheese of Inis Cloithrinn
myths.text:
Medb outlived the raid, outlived Ailill — slain at Conall Cernach's hand — and kept her sovereignty into age, spending her last years at Inis Cloithrinn, her island on Lough Ree, where she bathed in the pool every morning at sunrise. She had killed her sister Clothru, and Clothru's son Furbaide had been cut from his mother's womb — whence his name, Ferbend, 'of the cutting' — and he grew up with the debt of it.

Furbaide found the queen's bathing place and measured it the patient way: morning after morning he stood on the shore opposite and practiced his cast against the distance, until the stone flew true by habit. Then one sunrise, as Medb came to her bath, his sling let fly — a ball of hard cheese, the tale insists, the humblest weapon in Ireland — and the queen of Connacht, who had moved four provinces against Ulster and asked no man's leave for anything in her life, died by her nephew's hand at the water's edge. Her grave, the local tradition says, is the great cairn on Knocknarea in Sligo, where she stands buried upright, facing Ulster.

medb.syncretism: The Welsh corpus preserves no Medb — but it preserves her word: Welsh meddw, 'drunk', is the same adjective, and the Mabinogi gives the Brythonic side of the theme she embodies: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] arriving as a mounted marvel no rider can catch, and the footholder Goewin whose office is bound to Math's life, are the Welsh faces of the kingship-and-goddess complex that Mac Cana traced through Irish literature. Medb's deepest kin are lexical and ritual at once. Her name is the same word as the drink by which kings were made: the Irish inauguration knew the banais ríghe, the 'wedding-feast of kingship', in which the goddess of the territory offered the king the cup — or the bed — and scholars since Mac Cana's foundational study of king and goddess have read Medb of Crúachan as that figure euhemerized into a queen. The tradition kept a second Medb to prove the point: Medb Lethderg of Tara, of whom the Book of Leinster records that she slept with nine kings of Ireland and that no king ruled at Tara who had not slept with her. Her closest kin inside the lexicon are the pantheon's other keepers of the land's consent: [[macha|Macha]], whose curse opened Ulster to her army, and [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]], who rides the same war-paths from the Otherworld side.
medb.culturalLegacy: The Táin's modern reception made Medb the most argued-over woman in Irish literature. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) carried the epic into English; Thomas Kinsella's translation (1969), with Louis le Brocquy's ink drawings, fixed the Táin as the Irish national epic for the modern reader — and Medb at its centre as its engine, not its ornament. Scholarship split over her nature: Mac Cana read her as the sovereignty goddess of Connacht demoted to a queen, the standing type-case of the king-and-goddess theme; more skeptical voices, notably J. P. Mallory's, have tested the Táin against the Iron Age record and found a tale shaped by its medieval tellers rather than a window on the pagan past. Popular culture settled the argument in its own way: the Anglicized Maeve has become one of the most fashionable Irish girls' names in the English-speaking world, and 'Queen Maeve' — the woman who wrote her own terms, chose her own husbands, and out-argued every man in the tale — stands as a feminist icon far beyond the universities. The cairn on Knocknarea that folklore calls her grave draws climbers every summer; the visitor centre at Rathcroghan interprets her rath; and in Irish itself Meadhbh never left: the living name has meant the same ungovernable queen for twelve hundred years of the written language.
medb.extendedMeditation:
Medb is the only great figure in the Celtic corpus who insists, in her own voice, on being counted equal — and then proves the point by going to war over the one item on which she was not. Read her as a goddess and she is sovereignty itself, the land auditing its king; read her as a woman and she is something rarer in medieval literature: a ruler whose motives are entirely legible and entirely her own. The pillow-talk is not vanity. It is the whole doctrine of her queenship in one scene — that the account must balance, that consent is owed to her and not by her, that a husband is a choice with terms attached.

The tradition punishes her and cannot dismiss her. The raid ends in ruin, the bulls destroy each other, the covering of the retreat is hers to do in the tale's most humiliating passage — and afterward she goes home and keeps the throne, keeps her terms, keeps choosing, until a nephew's measured patience and a piece of cheese end her at her morning bath. Medb asks the question the audit poses: what would you move an army to keep equal — and what, when the counting is done, was ever actually at stake?
medb.originalScriptNote: Old Irish writes the name Medb (genitive Medba) in the Insular Latin script of the great codices — Lebor na hUidre and the Book of Leinster preserve the Táin; normalized Old Irish spells it with plain Latin letters and no diacritic. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, carries the name-type exactly once, and in the most suggestive place in Ireland: on a stone in the Oweynagat cave at Rathcroghan, Medb's own royal complex, reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI — '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb'. Because the normalized form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: medb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

medb.archaeology: Medb's mythic address is the best-documented royal landscape in Ireland: Crúachan Aí, the Rathcroghan complex in County Roscommon, a five-kilometre spread of more than two hundred and forty recorded monuments — ring-barrows, mounds, and enclosures — dominated by the great flat-topped Rathcroghan Mound itself. Beneath the complex opens Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats, the souterrain-fed natural cave the medieval tales call a gate of the Otherworld; within it stand two ogham stones, one reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI, '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb' — the name-type's only epigraphic attestation, at the site the tradition assigns to the queen herself. Her death-place, Inis Cloithrinn (Inchcleraun), survives as the largest island of Lough Ree on the Shannon, crowned by the early monastic ruins of Templemurray; her reputed grave is the great unexcavated Neolithic cairn (c. 3200 BCE) on the summit of Knocknarea above Sligo — Miosgán Meadhbha, 'Medb's heap', which local tradition insists she fills standing upright, spear in hand, facing Ulster. The textual witnesses are exact: the oldest substantially complete Táin (Recension I) is in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow, written at Clonmacnoise around 1106, and the fullest recension in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; O'Rahilly's editions are the modern bases. J. P. Mallory's In Search of the Irish Dreamtime (2016) is the standard archaeological cross-examination of the whole epic.

phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) bilabial nasal [mʲ], the m pronounced with the tongue arched toward the hard palate — Old Irish distinguished slender from broad consonants throughout.
Long close front vowel [iː], the long í that modern editors mark with a síneadh fada when they print Mídir.
Lenited dental [ð], the soft voiced 'th' of English 'this'; Old Irish orthography writes the lenited consonant with a plain d.
Short unstressed [ɪ] closing in a slender (palatalized) tap [ɾʲ], the light final r of the o-stem name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MEE-thir' — a long 'ee', the soft 'th' of 'this' for the d, and a whispered palatal r at the end. The modern Irish Mídír keeps essentially this sound.

domains.title: Underworld, Fairy King
domains.subtitle: The proud lord of the síd of Brí Léith
domains.lead: Midir — Old Irish Mídir, styled the Proud — is the lord of the síd of Brí Léith, the Otherworld mound by Ardagh in Longford, and the central figure of Tochmarc Étaíne, the Wooing of Étaín. His dossier is the strangest kind of kingship in the Irish corpus: not the spear or the plunder, but the board game, the wager, and the patience that spans a thousand and twelve years and two births of the same woman. He fostered [[aengus|Óengus]], the son of the young; he won Étaín Echraide by her father's impossible labors; he lost her to jealousy, found her again in another lifetime, and took her from the high king of Ireland at a game of fidchell played in the middle of Tara. Where other gods take what they want, Midir stakes, loses, waits, and wins.

cards.name: The Fidchell Board
cards.desc: The game of kings at which Midir sat across from Eochaid Airem in Tara, losing stake after stake until the board was set for the one prize he had come for.

cards.name: The Two Swans
cards.desc: The payment taken in flight: Midir and Étaín rising through Tara's smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, while the king's guard watched from the walls.

cards.name: Brí Léith
cards.desc: His síd by Ardagh in Longford — the mound Eochaid's host dug open in the war of the spades, and the hill the Dindsenchas names as his.

cards.name: The Scarlet Quicken-Rod
cards.desc: Fuamnach's jealous stroke in his own hall, which made Étaín a pool of water, a worm, and a purple fly — the malice his kingship could not keep out.

symbols.name: The fidchell board
symbols.meaning: The game of kings played at Tara — patience staked as strategy, and a wager that was really a judgment

symbols.name: The silver chain

symbols.name: The sloe-thorn

symbols.name: Brí Léith

mythology.lead: Midir's mythology is a single long courtship told in two lifetimes — the fullest Otherworld dossier in the Irish corpus, preserved entire in Tochmarc Étaíne. It begins with a sloe-thorn and a bride-price, passes through jealousy and transformation and a rebirth eleven hundred years later, and ends at a fidchell board in Tara and a war of spades against the hollow hills. Around that spine the tradition adds the fosterage: the lord of Brí Léith reared [[aengus|Óengus]], the Dagda's son, and the tie between the two mounds frames both gods' tales.

myths.title: The Sloe and the Bride-Price
myths.text:
Midir of Brí Léith was the foster-father of Óengus, and he came to Brú na Bóinne to visit his fosterling. While the boys of the Brug were at their hurling, a sloe-thorn sprang from the play and put out Midir's eye; he stayed a year in the mound while Dían Cécht, the physician of the Túatha Dé Danann, made him whole. For his reward and his heart's desire he named Étaín Echraide, daughter of Ailill, the fairest woman in Ireland — and it was Óengus who went to win her.

Her father Ailill mac Máta, king of the Ulaid, set a bride-price no mortal could pay: twelve plains cleared of their stones and wood, and twelve rivers led out of the land to the sea. Óengus performed the labors with the Dagda's strength behind him, and Midir brought Étaín home to Brí Léith as his wife. The tale's arithmetic is exact: the god's first possession of Étaín was bought by service, the price of a wounded eye — and it was the one part of the story that ended peaceably.

myths.title: The Fly in the Crystal Bower
myths.text:
Midir already had a wife: Fuamnach, foster-daughter of Bresal the druid, and versed in her foster-father's arts. When Étaín came home to Brí Léith, Fuamnach's jealousy found its instrument — a rod of scarlet quicken-tree — and one stroke made her rival a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly of wondrous size and sweetness. For seven years the fly that was Étaín went with Midir wherever he went, and he knew her in her shape; but Fuamnach's malice outlasted his keeping.

The fly came at last to Brú na Bóinne, where Óengus knew her and built her a grianán, a crystal sun-bower filled with healing herbs — until Fuamnach raised a magic wind that swept her across Ireland for seven years more, to fall into the cup of the wife of Étar, an Ulster warrior, at the Bay of Cíú. She was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth: Étaín, daughter of Étar. Midir's house is the still center of the storm — the husband whose hall became the battlefield of two women's powers, and who waited out the centuries the tale demanded of him.

myths.title: The Long Game at Tara
myths.text:
In her second life Étaín married Eochaid Airem, high king of Ireland at Tara, and Midir came for her as the tale had promised. First he came in the shape of Ailill Anglonnach, the king's brother, who was wasting with love of her — three nights he lay beside her in that likeness and did not touch her, and so saved both her honor and Ailill's life. Then he revealed himself and asked her to come away with him; she answered that she would not go without her husband's leave. So Midir took the leave the hard way.

He came to Tara and challenged Eochaid to fidchell. Game after game Midir lost, and paid the stakes without stint — horses and treasures in such plenty that the king's greed was schooled by the god's purse. Then the board was set once more, and the stake named was an embrace and a kiss from Étaín; Midir won. Eochaid deferred the payment for a month, and when the month was out Tara stood ringed with warriors and the house barred. Midir appeared all the same in the midst of the hall, sang to Étaín the invitation to the wondrous land, took her in his arms, and the two rose through the smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, while the host of Ireland watched from the ramparts and could do nothing.

myths.title: The Fifty Women in One Likeness
myths.text:
Eochaid's answer was the spade: he set the men of Ireland to digging up the síd-mounds one by one, a war of delving against the hollow hills, until the host stood over Brí Léith itself. Then Midir came to the parley, and the bargain struck was surrender of a kind: on the morrow fifty women came out of the mound, every one of them in Étaín's exact likeness, and the king was told to choose his wife.

He chose — and chose his own daughter, born to Étaín in the síd and hidden in the likeness of her mother. By that unwitting union a daughter was conceived who was exposed and spared, reared as Mess Búachalla, the cowherd's fosterling, and through her the line ran down to Conaire Mór, the doomed king of the Bruiden Da Derga. When Midir revealed the deception he gave back the true Étaín as well; the tale lets the god keep the last word and the king keep his shame. It is the Otherworld's coldest jest: the wager was never about the game, and the digging was never going to win.

myths.title: The Foster-Father of the Young God
myths.text:
Behind the wooing stands the fosterage. When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, his son Óengus was away with Midir of Brí Léith, being fostered, and received nothing — the absence that led to the famous quibble of the day and the night, and to Brú na Bóinne passing to the son. The tradition thus ties the two mounds together from the beginning: the young god reared at Brí Léith, the proud god's eye healed at the Brug.

The foster-bond runs both ways through the dossier. It was for Midir that Óengus won Étaín Echraide and performed her father's labors; it was in Óengus's bower that Étaín the purple fly found her one refuge. Irish fosterage was no light tie — it stood beside blood, and the tales honor it. Midir's proudest title is not lord of Brí Léith but the one the stories keep proving: the man who raised the son of the young.

midir.syncretism: Midir has no cross-border witness of his own, and the honest comparison is typological rather than genetic. No Gaulish altar names him and no scholar has proposed one; where the Dagda can be set beside Sucellos on the strength of club and cauldron, Midir's dossier — the wager, the hunted bride, the mound that is a court — belongs to the Otherworld-king figure-type that Mac Cana and Sjoestedt trace through the Celtic materials without anchoring it to any single epigraphic god. Within Ireland his structural kin are the síd-lords of the neighboring tales: Bodb Derg of the Munster síde, who answers the Dagda's search in the Aislinge, and [[manannan|Manannán]], the sea-going master of the Otherworld's glamour. The Welsh corpus offers only a functional parallel — [[arawn|Arawn]], the lord of Annwn who likewise binds a mortal king by a bargain with a hidden edge — and the parallel is a pattern, not a pedigree. The comparisons instruct; none of them identifies him.
midir.culturalLegacy: Midir's afterlife is the afterlife of Tochmarc Étaíne itself, the tale that never let him go. P. W. Joyce carried 'The Wooing of Etain' into modern English in Old Celtic Romances (1879), and Lady Gregory made the fidchell game and the swans part of the Celtic revival's furniture in Gods and Fighting Men (1904). James Stephens gave the story its strangest modern retelling in In the Land of Youth (1924), where Midir's arrival at Tara is staged as high comedy turning to awe. Bergin and Best's edition in Ériu (1938) fixed the text for scholarship, and Jeffrey Gantz's Penguin translation (1981) put the whole dossier on the general reader's shelf, where it has stayed: the fidchell game is now the standard citation whenever Irish literature wants to prove that its gods play a longer game than its kings. The name itself took no second path — no Angus, no Brigit: Midir never became a given name, a place, or a pub, and remains what the manuscripts made him, a proper noun with a single bearer.
midir.extendedMeditation:
Midir is the god of the long game, and the tradition tells you so in his name before it tells you in his story: the handbooks gloss it, cautiously, as judge — and a judge is exactly what a wager needs. Watch how he plays Eochaid. He loses, and loses, and pays without stint, because the losses are the lesson: the king is being taught that the man across the board can afford anything, that the stakes are a language, and that the only sentence being written is the last one. When the final stake is named — an embrace, a kiss — the game has already been won for a month. The fidchell board is a court, and the house always already holds the verdict.

That patience is the Otherworld's whole tempo. A mortal wooing is measured in seasons; Midir's spans a thousand and twelve years, two births of the same woman, and a war of spades against his own roof — and he never hurries, because time is the one currency his kind does not spend. His foster-son [[aengus|Óengus]] parses time into a loophole and holds a mound on a day without a term; the foster-father plays time into a stake and holds a woman across two lifetimes. Between them the síd of Ireland teaches the same doctrine: the hollow hills do not take what they want. They wait until the wanting itself concedes.
midir.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Insular Latin script as Midir — the spelling Bergin and Best print from Lebor na hUidre; many modern editors add the fada and write Mídir to mark the long vowel, an editorial convention rather than the manuscript norm. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: midir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

midir.archaeology: Midir is a textual god — no ogham stone names him and no votive inscription invokes him — but both halves of his mythic geography are real and visitable. Brí Léith is a hill by Ardagh in County Longford, the mound the Dindsenchas names as his síd, and the surrounding Longford bogland preserves one of the showpiece monuments of the Irish Iron Age: the Corlea Trackway, a massive oak togher across the bog a few miles south of Ardagh, excavated under Barry Raftery and fixed by dendrochronology to 148–147 BCE — a road of the very centuries in which the síd-lord's landscape was being imagined. The tale's other stage is Tara in County Meath, where the earthworks of Ráith na Rí, the Forrad, and the long banquet-hall trench called Tech Midchúarta still ridge the hill on which Eochaid Airem kept his court and lost his wager. The manuscript witnesses are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved, incompletely, in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre (RIA MS 23 E 25) and completed in the fifteenth-century Yellow Book of Lecan, the twin bases of Bergin and Best's edition; the companion Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], exactly the English m; the name opens on the same sound as the place-name Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) from which it descends.
The Welsh clear y, an unstressed-quality central vowel [ə] — the 'uh' of English 'about' — because it stands in the stressed penult.
Voiced dental fricative [ð], the soft 'th' of English 'this'; Welsh writes the sound with the digraph dd, and it never hardens to a stop.
Final unstressed syllable with the Welsh final-y sound [ɨ], a high central vowel between the i of 'bit' and the Welsh u, closing on [n].

pronunciation.approximation: 'MUR-thin' — stress the first syllable (the Welsh penult); the dd is the soft 'th' of 'this', and the whole name takes two short beats, never 'MER-lin'.

kin.label: Name origin
