sigyn.archaeology: Sigyn has one candidate image and it is famous: the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria, carved in the first half of the tenth century, whose programme of Ragnarök scenes includes a bound male figure with a smaller figure kneeling beside him holding a bowl — standardly interpreted as Loki bound and Sigyn with the basin (Bailey; Lindow), the one Viking-Age monument that may show her at her post. Otherwise she is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no other image can be securely identified. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the Loki cycle — the Codex Regius for Völuspá 35 and the Lokasenna prose epilogue, and the Codex Regius, Codex Wormianus, and Uppsala codices of Snorri's Edda for Gylfaginning 34 and 50 — with Þjóðólfr's Haustlöng (c. 900), quoted in Skáldskaparmál, proving the kenning 'the burden of Sigyn's arms' was already current a century before Iceland's conversion.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], plain and unaspirated, as in English 'spark'; Old Norse initial s never weakens.
Short close front unrounded [i], clipped brief — the short i of Old Norse, never the long í.
Nasal [n] plus the epenthetic stop [d] that Old Norse grew between n and r, then trilled or tapped [r] — the cluster the runes write with t.
Final short [i], fully sounded — Old Norse masculine -i names end in a true vowel, not a schwa.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SIN-dri' — two short beats, the weight on the first, the d clicked crisply between the n and the r as in 'laundry' said fast, both vowels clipped.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Sindri, brother of Brokkr and maker of Gullinbursti, Draupnir, and Mjǫllnir; beside the verb sindra, 'to sparkle, throw off sparks', and sindr, 'forge-slag, sparks'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᛁᚾᛏᚱᛁ (s-i-n-t-r-i), the Viking-Age runic rendering; the short-twig row writes the n-d-r cluster with its undifferentiated stop rune.

kin.label: Manuscript variant
kin.form: Eitri — part of the manuscript tradition of Skáldskaparmál names Brokkr's brother thus, and the handbooks treat Sindri and Eitri as one smith.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Sindri, an unbroken living male given name in Iceland, still carrying the forge's spark.

pronunciation.note: Sindri is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The smith whose name means 'sparkling' leaves his mark in meaning, not in orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Dwarf Smith
domains.subtitle: The Forge of the Three Treasures
domains.lead: Sindri is the dwarf at the anvil while his brother [[brokkr|Brokkr]] works the bellows: the smith who took Loki's wager and cast, in three heats, the golden-bristled boar Gullinbursti for Freyr, the ring Draupnir for Óðinn, and the hammer Mjǫllnir for Þórr — the greatest single afternoon's work in the northern corpus, done to win a bet staked on a trickster's head. His name is his trade: sindra, 'to sparkle', the forge-word for metal throwing off sparks. And Völuspá gives him a second life beyond Snorri's forge-scene: north on Niðavellir stands a hall of gold belonging to the kindred of Sindri, a dwarf chieftain of the verse tradition whose family owns the golden house.

cards.name: The Bellows That Must Not Stop
cards.desc: Brokkr's station and the wager's condition: the bellows must blow without pause through each casting, and the one moment they faltered — a fly's sting between the eyes — shortened the hammer's handle forever.

cards.name: Gullinbursti
cards.desc: The boar with bristles of gold, cast from a pigskin in the first heat and given to Freyr — Gold-Bristle, who runs through sky and sea faster than any horse and lights the darkest night with his shining mane.

cards.name: Draupnir
cards.desc: The gold arm-ring cast in the second heat and given to Óðinn — the Dripper, from which eight rings of equal weight drop every ninth night; Óðinn laid it on Baldr's pyre, and Baldr sent it back from Hel.

cards.name: Mjǫllnir the Short-Handled
cards.desc: The hammer cast in the third heat and given to Þórr — it never misses, never breaks, and always returns to the hand, yet its handle is a finger too short: the one flaw in the corpus's greatest treasure, made by an interrupted bellows-stroke.

symbols.name: The bellows
symbols.meaning: The wager's condition and the forge's heartbeat — the one tool whose failure, for a single instant, marks the hammer forever

symbols.name: The fly that stung
symbols.meaning: Loki's sabotage in miniature — the god who cannot win the contest fairly trying to spoil the work, and succeeding only at the handle

symbols.name: Draupnir
symbols.meaning: The ring that drips eight rings every ninth night — wealth that renews itself, the forge's answer to Andvari's cursed gold

symbols.name: Mjǫllnir's short handle
symbols.meaning: The flaw in perfection — the Æsir's best defense carries the permanent mark of the moment the work was broken

symbols.name: The golden hall at Niðavellir
symbols.meaning: Völuspá's witness — the house of gold of Sindri's kindred in the dwarf-fields, a chieftain's seat beyond Snorri's forge-scene

mythology.lead: Sindri's dossier is one long scene in Snorri and one stanza in Völuspá — a forge and a hall. The Prose Edda gives him the wager that produced the gods' three greatest treasures; the Poetic Edda gives him a golden house in the dwarf-fields and a kindred to fill it. Between the two stands the corpus's most consequential craftsman: everything the Æsir trust in the last battle came off his anvil in a single afternoon.

myths.title: The Wager of the Head
myths.text:
It begins with a crime: Loki, for mischief, cuts off all the hair of Sif, Þórr's wife. Þórr seizes him and would break every bone, and Loki swears to get the svartálfar to make hair of gold for Sif that will grow like living hair. He goes first to the sons of Ívaldi, who make the golden hair and two more treasures — the ship Skíðblaðnir for Freyr and the spear Gungnir for Óðinn. Then, flushed with success, Loki goes to the dwarf Brokkr and wagers his own head that Brokkr's brother Sindri cannot make three treasures just as good.

The bet is the whole engine of the chapter: a trickster's tongue staked against a smith's hands. Brokkr accepts, and the brothers go to the forge with the terms set — Sindri lays the metal, Brokkr works the bellows, and the bellows must not stop blowing until the work comes out of the fire.

myths.title: Three Castings, Three Stings
myths.text:
Sindri lays a pigskin in the forge and tells Brokkr to blow and never cease. A fly settles on Brokkr's hand and stings, but the bellows do not stop: out comes a boar with bristles of gold, Gullinbursti. Next Sindri lays gold in the fire; the fly returns and stings Brokkr's neck, harder, but the bellows do not stop: out comes the gold ring Draupnir. Last Sindri lays iron in the fire — and now, Snorri says, the smith himself fears the work will fail if the blowing falters. The fly settles between Brokkr's eyes and stings the eyelids so the blood runs down and blinds him; Brokkr sweeps the fly away with his hand, and the bellows fall silent for one instant. When the iron comes out it is a hammer — and its handle is short by a finger's breadth.

The fly, of course, is Loki, who cannot win the wager fairly and tries to spoil it instead. The chapter's precision is unforgettable: two perfect treasures and one marred, and the marred one — the hammer Mjǫllnir — is the greatest of the six. The sabotage succeeds exactly as far as the handle and no farther.

myths.title: The Judgment and the Sewn Lips
myths.text:
The brothers bring their three treasures to Ásgarðr, and the Æsir sit in judgment with Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr as assessors. To Freyr goes the boar, which runs through air and sea faster than any horse and lights the night with its golden bristles; to Óðinn the ring, which drips eight rings of equal weight every ninth night; to Þórr the hammer — it never misses what he throws at, it never breaks, it always returns to his hand, and it shrinks small enough to carry inside his shirt. Its one fault is the short handle. The judgment is unanimous: the hammer is the best of all the treasures, the surest defense against the frost-giants, and the brothers have won the wager.

Loki offers to ransom his head, but Brokkr refuses every price. When Loki tries to flee on his sky-shoes, Þórr catches him. Then comes the trickster's last legalism: the head was staked, but not one inch of the neck. Brokkr cannot take the head without touching the neck — so he takes an awl instead and sews Loki's lips together, and the thread, Snorri says, is called Vartari. The smith does not get his stake; he gets something better, the silencing of the tongue that staked it.

myths.title: The Golden Hall at Niðavellir
myths.text:
The verse tradition knows a grander Sindri than Snorri's forge-hand. Völuspá, in its survey of the world's dwellings, counts a hall that stands north on Niðavellir, made of gold, belonging to the kindred of Sindri — beside the giant Brimir's beer-hall at Ókólnir. Here Sindri is no lone craftsman but a dwarf chieftain, the head of a family rich enough to roof its house in the metal his name throws off as sparks.

The dwarf þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál keep the name in the catalogues of dwarf heiti, and the manuscript tradition splits on the forge-scene itself: where part of the tradition names Brokkr's brother Sindri, another part calls him Eitri, and the handbooks read the two as one smith under two forge-names. The name itself is the trade: sindra is 'to sparkle, throw off sparks', sindr is the slag and spark of the forge — kin to Old English sinder and the modern English cinder, the cooled spark of the smith's fire.

sindri.syncretism: Sindri's closest kin are inside the corpus itself. His brother [[brokkr|Brokkr]] is the other half of one workshop — the two are never separated in the sources, bellows and anvil, and Snorri names the forge by the pair. [[andvari|Andvari]] is the corpus's other great dwarf of the gold, but inverted: Andvari's hoard is won by robbery and carries a curse, Sindri's gold is made in three heats and carries only a wager. Vǫlundr of Vǫlundarkviða, 'prince of elves', is the verse tradition's other smith narrative — the smith wronged who takes revenge, where Sindri is the smith wagered against who wins. Cross-culturally the comparisons are structural, not borrowed: Hephaistos, the Greek smith who forges the gods' masterworks and is himself marred; Ilmarinen of the Kalevala, who forges the Sampo under a bargain's pressure; Goibniu of the Irish Tuatha Dé Danann, whose smith-work arms the gods for their last battle. The pattern is old — the divine weapon must come from an other-than-divine hand — but Sindri's version is the only one where the masterpiece's flaw is timed to a single held breath of the bellows.
sindri.culturalLegacy: Sindri's afterlife is the afterlife of his three treasures: every retelling of Norse myth that reaches the forging of Mjǫllnir keeps his one afternoon and its three stings, from the Victorian handbooks onward — the short handle is the detail no adapter has ever dared to cut, because it is the story. The smith himself has had a quieter reception than his work, and much of it flows under his manuscript double: the variant name Eitri carries the same dwarf-smith into a robust modern afterlife in games and film, where the forge that made the hammer is restaged for new audiences — the inventions are modern, but the forge, the brother, and the interrupted casting are Skáldskaparmál's own. The sturdiest legacy is the name: Sindri never died out in Iceland and remains a living male given name, borne today by men who inherit the forge's spark in its plainest form.
sindri.extendedMeditation: Sindri is the Edda's shortest sermon on how perfection fails. The gods' three greatest treasures are made in one afternoon by a smith whose name is a forge-word for sparks, and two of them are flawless. The third — the best, the one the Æsir will trust in the last battle — is marred by a single instant: a fly, an eyelid, a held breath of the bellows, and the handle is short forever. The tradition does not call the hammer ruined; it calls it the finest thing ever forged, short handle and all. That is the forge's verdict and the story's mercy: the masterpiece is not the work that never faltered but the work that survived its interruption. Loki wins the sting and loses the wager. Sindri wins everything except the head he was promised — and takes the trickster's voice instead, one stitch at a time, with an awl. In a mythology that ends in fire, the smith who arms the gods gets the corpus's most practical blessing: his work holds, and no one remembers the fly who won.
sindri.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Sindri — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᛁᚾᛏᚱᛁ (s-i-n-t-r-i), a normalized phonetic reconstruction in which the short-twig row writes the n-d-r cluster with its undifferentiated stop rune. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: sindri.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 35 (the cutting of Sif's hair; the sons of Ívaldi's three treasures; the wager of Loki's head; Sindri at the forge and Brokkr at the bellows; Gullinbursti, Draupnir, and the short-handled Mjǫllnir; the judgment of the Æsir; the sewing of Loki's lips with Vartari); Skáldskaparmál þulur (dwarf heiti)
Poetic Edda: Völuspá 37 (the hall of gold of Sindri's kindred, standing north on Niðavellir); Grímnismál 43 (Ívaldi's sons and the making of Skíðblaðnir)
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning (the svartálfar and their world; Draupnir laid on Baldr's pyre and sent back from Hel by Hermóðr's errand)

Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. sindr ('forge-slag, sparks'), sindra ('to sparkle'), Sindri, Eitri, Brokkr, Draupnir, Mjǫllnir, Gullinbursti; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. Sindri, draupnir, mjǫllnir
de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, s.v. sindra, Sindri (the forge-word and its cognates: Old English sinder, modern English cinder)

Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology; Orchard, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend; Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide — s.v. Sindri, Eitri, Brokkr, Mjǫllnir (attestation; the Sindri/Eitri manuscript equation; dwarf-lore and the smith motif)

sindri.archaeology: Sindri is a wholly textual dwarf: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and no image can be securely identified with him. His attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses — the Codex Regius and related codices of Snorri's Edda for Skáldskaparmál 35 (with the Codex Upsaliensis tradition reading the brother's name as Eitri), and the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Völuspá's golden hall at Niðavellir. The material context is nonetheless richer for him than for most dwarfs, because his products are findable. Thor's-hammer pendants — Mjǫllnir in miniature — are the commonest amulets of the late Viking Age, known by the hundred from tenth-century graves, hoards, and settlement sites across Scandinavia and the diaspora: the forge's most famous casting, worn at the neck of the converted and unconverted alike. Gold arm-rings of Draupnir's type fill the hoards. And the corpus's visual language of the smithy survives on the Gotland picture stones — Ardre VIII shows a smithy scene with tools and a headless body, usually read as Vǫlundr — proof that the smith at his forge was a carved subject in the Viking-Age north, though no carving names Sindri himself.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless sibilant plus velar stop [sk] — plain and unpalatalized in Old Norse, unlike the English cluster in 'ship'; both sounds fully articulated, as in 'skull'.
Short close back rounded [u] — brief and dark, like German 'und' or the clipped vowel of 'book'; never the diphthong of English 'few'.
Clear alveolar lateral [l], as in English 'low' — Old Norse l is always clear, never dark.
Voiced alveolar stop [d], audibly released — Old Norse final stops are fully sounded, not devoiced or swallowed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SKULD' — one short beat: say English 'skull' and release a d at the end; the vowel is the short u of 'put', and the word sits exactly between 'skull' and 'should' spoken with a k.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Skuld — the third of the three norns at Urðarbrunnr and, in the same corpus, a shield-bearing valkyrie; the name is the common noun skuld, 'debt, what is owed', made personal.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᚴᚢᛚᛏ (s-k-u-l-t), the Viking-Age runic rendering.

kin.label: The name as word
kin.form: skuld (f.), 'debt, what is owed; that which shall be' — from the modal verb skulu 'shall'; the future conceived as an obligation not yet discharged.

kin.label: Cognates
kin.form: English shall and should, German Schuld 'debt, guilt' — the same Indo-European root, *skel-, 'to owe'.

pronunciation.note: Skuld is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The youngest norn's standing in the corpus vastly outruns her name's orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Valkyrie / Norn of Future
domains.subtitle: The Debt That Comes Due
domains.lead: Skuld is the third of the three norns who dwell at the well of Urðr beneath the root of Yggdrasill, laying laws and choosing lives for the children of men — and she is the only figure in the Norse corpus counted twice. Völuspá names her among the three maidens beneath the tree, and names her again in the tally of valkyries riding to the gods' host, bearing a shield beside Skögul, Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul. Snorri fuses the two offices in a single clause: with Gunnr and Rota always rides 'the youngest norn, who is called Skuld', to choose the slain and decide the battle. Her name is the noun for 'debt' — the future as what is still owed.

cards.name: The Well of Urðr
cards.desc: The holy well beneath Yggdrasill's heavenward root where the three maidens dwell — Urðr, Verðandi, Skuld — and where the gods hold their council; Völuspá sees it in the first vision of the world's frame.

cards.name: The Carved Slips
cards.desc: The wood-slips the norns carve as they lay laws and choose lives for the children of men — fate as inscription, each life written before it is lived.

cards.name: The Shield
cards.desc: The shield Skuld bears in Völuspá's tally of valkyries riding over the earth — the one norn who also rides to the field, death's allotment delivered in person.

cards.name: The Youngest Norn
cards.desc: Snorri's phrase: 'the youngest norn, who is called Skuld', who always rides with Gunnr and Rota to decide the battle — the youngest sister carrying the last and least avoidable portion of every life.

symbols.name: Urðarbrunnr
symbols.meaning: The well beneath the tree where the three norns dwell — fate's spring at the world's root

symbols.name: The carved wood-slips
symbols.meaning: The lots the maidens cut as they lay laws and choose lives — destiny written before it is lived

symbols.name: The shield
symbols.meaning: Skuld's valkyrie gear in Völuspá — the norn who rides, allotment armed and mounted

symbols.name: The white clay of the well
symbols.meaning: The mud with which the norns coat the ash's bark so its limbs do not rot — fate also as the world's maintenance

symbols.name: The laws and the lots
symbols.meaning: What the three maidens lay and cast for the children of men — ordinance and chance, both in their hands

mythology.lead: Skuld's dossier is short and of the highest rank: she appears where the world's frame is described, never in anecdote. The Poetic Edda names her twice — once beneath the tree, once in the air above the battlefield — and Snorri stitches the two sightings into one figure: the youngest norn who rides with the valkyries. What follows is the whole of the primary record.

myths.title: The Three Beneath the Tree
myths.text:
The seeress surveys the world's frame: the ash Yggdrasill, tall, drenched with white loam, whence come the dews that fall in the valleys, ever green, standing over Urðarbrunnr. Thence come maidens, deep in wisdom, three from the lake that stands beneath the tree: one was called Urðr, the second Verðandi — they carved on slips of wood — Skuld the third. They laid laws, they chose lives for the children of men, the fates of men.

The stanza is the foundation text of northern fate-doctrine, and it fixes Skuld's place in the triad without explaining it: the poem gives her no act, no speech, no attribute but her position — the third, the last named, the one whose name is a debt.

myths.title: The Shield in the Tally
myths.text:
Late in the same poem the seeress looks up from the roots to the sky: she saw valkyries come from far away, ready to ride to the gods' host — Skuld bore a shield, and Skögul followed her, Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul; now the tally of Herjan's maidens is told, valkyries ready to ride over the earth. The list is a roll-call, and Skuld heads it, shield in hand.

No other norn appears in a valkyrie list. The double office is the interpretive crux of the whole figure: the maiden who allots life at the root is the same maiden who collects death in the field — the two ends of one ledger.

myths.title: The Maidens Who Shape Men's Lives
myths.text:
Snorri's survey of the world-tree pauses at its heavenward root: beneath that root is the very holy well called Urðarbrunnr, and there the gods hold their court each day. By that well stand three maidens named Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld — these maidens shape men's lives, Snorri says, and we call them norns. He adds that there are other norns besides, who come to each child at birth to shape its life, of the races of gods, elves and dwarves — but the three at the well are the triad the tradition never enlarged.

Snorri also preserves the tree's upkeep: the norns take water from the well and the mud around it and pour it over the ash so that its limbs do not wither or rot, and that water is so holy that all that comes within the well turns white as the membrane within an eggshell. Fate, in this picture, is not only decree but daily maintenance of the world's fabric.

myths.title: The Youngest Norn Rides
myths.text:
In the chapter on the valkyries Snorri closes the roster with a sentence that completes Skuld's dossier: Odin's shield-maidens ride to every battle, choose who shall fall, and decide the victory — and with them, Snorri writes, always ride Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, to choose the slain and govern the engagements.

The designation is precise: of the three at the well, she is the youngest — and she rides. The tradition thus hands the future its own grim office: what is owed is collected on the battlefield, where every life's account comes due.

skuld.syncretism: The comparison that shaped Skuld's modern reading is with the Roman Parcae and the Greek Moirai — three spinners or allotters of fate matched to past, present and future. The mapping was a favourite of nineteenth-century mythography, and it is only half right: the names do not divide time so neatly. Urðr is 'what has become', Verðandi 'what is becoming', but Skuld is not 'what will be' in the same tense-logic — she is 'what is owed', a category of obligation rather than of tense; de Vries and Simek both warn that the clean past-present-future scheme is likely a learned schematization laid over older material. Within the corpus her truest kin are her own sisters [[urdr|Urðr]] and [[verdandi|Verðandi]] and the valkyrie sisterhood she alone joins — [[brynhildr|Brynhildr]] among the named riders — and, at one remove, the English fate-word [[wyrd|wyrd]], cognate with Urðr, through which the whole northern doctrine of allotted debt and doom entered English speech.
skuld.culturalLegacy: Skuld's most pervasive legacy is grammatical: her name's root is the English modal shall — and its past, should — so that every English sentence about obligation or the future conjugates, unknowingly, the youngest norn's name; German Schuld keeps the same root in its sense of debt and guilt. In mythography the three norns became the fixed northern counterpart of the Parcae in every retelling of the Eddas, and Skuld's double office — fate at the well, shield in the field — made her the standing emblem of fate that acts rather than merely decrees. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice honours the norns at birth-rites and at the year's turning, with Skuld invoked as the portion not yet owed; her name also survives as a rare Scandinavian given name, carrying its ominous register intact.
skuld.extendedMeditation:
Of the three sisters, Skuld is the one the grammar of Old Norse could not leave alone. Urðr names what has become — a fact, settled, already part of the weave. Verðandi names what is becoming — the present, unrolling. But Skuld names a debt, and a debt is the strangest tense of all: it is real now, binding now, though it falls due later. The North's deepest intuition about the future is stored in this one word — that what is coming is not empty time but an obligation already incurred, an account running toward settlement.

And then the corpus does something harsher still: it gives the debt a shield. The youngest norn does not wait at the well for the future to arrive; she rides out to collect it, choosing the slain, deciding the battle. Every life, in this theology, ends in a payment — and the collector is fate's youngest daughter, who has been counting since the slip of wood was carved.
skuld.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Skuld — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᚴᚢᛚᛏ (s-k-u-l-t), the short-twig row writing the final /d/ with the same rune as /t/. Because the name is pure ASCII, no form of the name is held in the PuniCodex collection; the domain is watched for release, and this temple claims nothing it does not hold.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 19–20 (the ash, the well, and the three maidens — Urðr, Verðandi, Skuld — who lay laws and choose lives) and 30 (Skuld bearing a shield in the tally of valkyries), trans. Carolyne Larrington

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 15–16 (Urðarbrunnr and the three norns; the white clay that preserves the tree) and 36 (Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, ride to choose the slain), trans. Anthony Faulkes; Skáldskaparmál þulur (norna heiti, valkyrja heiti)
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. skuld ('debt, duty; a Norn'); Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. skuld
de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, s.v. skuld, skulu (the etymology from *skel- 'to owe', and the caveat on the past–present–future scheme)

skuld.archaeology: Skuld is a wholly textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be securely identified with her — a silence she shares with her sisters, since the norns belong to the corpus's theological frame rather than to any named cult. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the fate-doctrine: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Völuspá 19–20 and 30, and the Codex Regius, Codex Wormianus and Codex Upsaliensis of Snorri's Edda for Gylfaginning 15–16 and 36 and the þulur lists preserved with Skáldskaparmál. The nearest material context is indirect: the valkyrie figures on Gotland picture-stones and on small Viking-Age brooches and pendants give the visual world her rider-form belongs to, though none names her. No runic carving of the theonym is known; the manuscript spelling of the Eddas remains the primary witness.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] released straight into a clear lateral [l] — Old Norse keeps the sl- cluster intact, no vowel inserted between.
The falling diphthong [ɛi], as in Old Norse steinn — a glide from open e to i, held in the stressed syllable.
Voiceless bilabial stop [p], unaspirated, closing the first syllable cleanly.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], short close [i], and the final nominative -r [r], lightly trilled — the masculine ending of the agent-noun type, fully sounded.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SLAYP-nir' — stress on the first syllable as in every Old Norse word, the ei a true two-part glide, the final r rolled and audible.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse of Óðinn; the name is attested only for this horse and as a horse-heiti in the þulur.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᛚᛁᛒᚾᛁᛦ (s-l-i-p-n-i-R), the Viking-Age runic rendering — the short-twig row writes e and i alike under ᛁ and p under bíarkan ᛒ.

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: none — Saxo Grammaticus, who euhemerizes the gods as mortal wizards, never mentions the eight-legged horse.

kin.label: Modern Scandinavian
kin.form: Sleipnir (Icelandic) / Sleipner (Swedish, Norwegian), preserved as a poetic horse-name and borrowed for ships, engines, and the North Sea Sleipner field.

Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the name's fame does nothing to change its orthography.

domains.title: Eight-Legged Steed, Journey, Offspring of Loki
domains.subtitle: The Gliding One Who Rides All Roads
domains.lead: Sleipnir, the grey eight-legged horse of Óðinn, is the best of horses among gods and men — and the strangest birth in the Edda. When the gods broke their bargain with the master builder of Ásgarðr's wall, it was Loki, in mare's shape, who lured away the giant's stallion Svaðilfari; and it was Loki who later bore the foal, grey, with eight legs. On Sleipnir's back Hermóðr rides nine nights down the Hel-road to ransom Baldr, and the horse leaps the gate of the dead with room to spare. His name means the gliding one — the creature for whom every boundary becomes a road.

cards.name: The Eight Legs
cards.desc: The mark no retelling can omit: eight legs where every honest horse has four — the body that outruns every other mount in the nine worlds, carved already on the Gotland picture stones.

cards.name: The Grey Foal
cards.desc: Born of Loki in mare's form and the giant's stallion Svaðilfari, after the night that broke the wall-builder's bargain — the only one of Loki's monstrous children who serves the gods instead of threatening them.

cards.name: The Hel-Road
cards.desc: The nine-night ride: Hermóðr borrows Sleipnir to ransom Baldr, crosses the gold-roofed Gjallarbrú, and the horse leaps Hel's gate 'with so much to spare' — the road down taken at full gallop.

cards.name: The Rune-Carved Teeth
cards.desc: Sigrdrífumál remembers runes cut 'on Sleipnir's teeth' among the places where victory-runes and mind-runes were lodged — even the horse's mouth was writing's place.

symbols.name: The eight legs
symbols.meaning: Speed beyond nature's allowance — the mount that outruns every horse in the nine worlds

symbols.name: The grey coat
symbols.meaning: The foal's colour at birth, noted by Snorri — grey, the working colour of northern horses

symbols.name: Svaðilfari
symbols.meaning: The giant builder's stallion, the sire — the bargain's price become a gift

symbols.name: The leap over Helgrindr
symbols.meaning: The gate of the dead cleared with room to spare — no boundary holds the gliding one

symbols.name: The rune-carved teeth
symbols.meaning: Sigrdrífumál's image of runes lodged in the horse's mouth — the steed as a carrier of signs as well as riders

mythology.lead: Sleipnir's dossier is three scenes and a pedigree: his begetting at the wall of Ásgarðr, his ride down the Hel-road for Baldr's sake, and the verse that crowns him best of horses. Around them the corpus keeps him the way the þulur keep him — catalogued, superlative, and never once ridden in vain.

myths.title: The Master Builder's Wage
myths.text:
A smith came to Ásgarðr offering to build the gods a wall in three seasons, high and strong against the mountain-giants — and named his wage: Freyja, and the sun and the moon. The Æsir bargained him down to one winter, alone; at Loki's urging they granted him the use of his stallion, Svaðilfari. The horse hauled boulders by night that the builder set by day, and with three days left before summer the gate-pillars stood nearly finished. The gods laid the blame on Loki, who had advised the bargain, and swore he would die an evil death unless he found a way to make the builder lose. That night, when Svaðilfari was led out to the stones, a mare ran from the wood and whinnied; the stallion broke his traces and ran after her, and the work stood still. The builder flew into a giant's rage — and the gods called on Þórr, who smashed the smith's skull with Mjölnir and sent him down to Niflhel.

Snorri closes the episode with the strangest sentence in his Edda: Loki had had such dealings with Svaðilfari that somewhat later he bore a foal. It was grey and had eight legs, and this is the best horse among gods and men. The gods' broken bargain, Loki's shame, the giant's death — and out of all of it, the greatest gift Óðinn ever received.

myths.title: The Ride Down the Hel-Road
myths.text:
When Baldr lay dead and Frigg asked who would win her love by riding to Hel to ransom him, Hermóðr the Bold, Óðinn's son, stood up. Sleipnir was led out, and Hermóðr mounted and galloped away. He rode nine nights through dark and deep valleys, seeing nothing, until he came to the river Gjöll and rode onto the Gjallarbrú, the bridge roofed with shining gold, where the maiden Móðguðr guards the crossing. She told him the dead had passed that way the day before — five companies of them — and that the road to Hel lay downward and northward. He rode on to the gates of Hel, and there Sleipnir showed what eight legs are for: Hermóðr spurred him, and the horse leapt the gate with so much to spare that the leap itself became proverb.

Inside, Hermóðr found Baldr in the high seat and Nanna beside him, and delivered the Æsir's plea. Hel set her famous condition — all things in the world, living and lifeless, must weep Baldr out — and the errand failed at the giantess Þökk's dry tears. But the ride succeeded: the only journey in the corpus that goes down the Hel-road and comes back, made on the back of Loki's foal.

myths.title: Best of Horses
myths.text:
The Poetic Edda gives Sleipnir no scene of his own, but it gives him the superlative. Grímnismál, in its catalogue of the best of all things — Yggdrasill of trees, Skíðblaðnir of ships, Óðinn of the Æsir — names Sleipnir the best of horses, one item in a list where every other entry is a god or a wonder. Sigrdrífumál lodges him in the rune-lore: among the places where runes were carved — on the shield before the shining god, on Arvakr's ear and Alsvinnr's hoof, on Bragi's tongue — the poem counts Sleipnir's teeth, the horse's mouth itself a place of writing.

And the heroic cycle keeps his bloodline. Reginsmál's prose tells that Grani, Sigurðr's peerless grey, was of Sleipnir's lineage — the best horse of the heroic age descended from the best horse of the gods, the line running down from Óðinn's stable into the Völsung story.

myths.title: The Stone-Carved Rider
myths.text:
Centuries before Snorri wrote, the image was already carved. On the Gotland picture stones of the eighth and ninth centuries — most famously the Tjängvide stone from Alskog and Ardre VIII — an eight-legged horse bears a rider toward a figure, often a woman with a drinking-horn, waiting before a hall. The standard reading sees Óðinn carried by Sleipnir, received at the boundary of the otherworld: the myth in granite, older than any manuscript that tells it.

The stones cannot be made to recite the Edda, and the identification rests on the one feature that needs no caption — eight legs, where nature and every other carved horse keep four. Whatever else the carvers meant, they meant a horse that runs between worlds; no other beast in the North was ever given the extra limbs.

sleipnir.syncretism: Sleipnir's closest kin is inside the corpus: Grani, Sigurðr's grey, whom Reginsmál's prose calls 'of Sleipnir's lineage' — the mythic superlative breeding the heroic one, as if the gods' stable stocked the sagas. Beyond the North, scholars have ranged widely and cautiously. The eight-legged world-crosser has been read as the ritual mount of shamanic journey — the animal that carries its rider through the levels of the cosmos — an interpretation Simek registers as one modern reading among others, not an attestation. The old folkloric fancy that eight legs picture four pallbearers carrying a corpse has no medieval warrant at all and the handbooks give it no house-room. What the sources support is narrower and stronger: a horse that belongs to no stable but Óðinn's, born of the one god who crosses every boundary himself, and used for the one ride — down to Hel and back — that no other mount could survive. Within the corpus his story binds Loki, Óðinn, Hermóðr, and the house of Baldr; he is the only one of Loki's children — beside the wolf, the serpent, and Hel — whose existence is a gift and not a threat.
sleipnir.culturalLegacy: Sleipnir's afterlife is the afterlife of the image: the eight-legged rider of the Gotland stones has become one of the most reproduced figures of Norse art, carried from nineteenth-century antiquarian plates into every modern handbook of the mythology. In the North itself the name never quite left the stables — Swedish and Norwegian kept Sleipner for engines and hulls, from locomotives to naval vessels, and Norway gave the name to the Sleipner gas field in the North Sea, the undersea treasure-house named for the underworld runner. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities remember Sleipnir in Óðinn rites as the mount of the road between worlds, and retellings of the Baldr cycle keep his two great moments: the leap over Hel's gate, and the grey foal standing in the wreckage of the gods' broken bargain.
sleipnir.extendedMeditation: Sleipnir is the Edda's quiet answer to the question of what Loki costs the gods. His other children are the wolf that eats the sun's lord, the serpent that girdles the world, and the daughter who keeps the dead — every one a debt that comes due at Ragnarǫk. Sleipnir alone runs the other way: the same transgression, the same mare-shape shame, and the foal is given to Óðinn and spends his strength on errands of rescue. He is the proof that in this mythology nothing is only what it cost — not the broken oath, not the trickster's punishment, not the giant's death. The wall was never finished; the horse was. And the name says what he is for: the gliding one, the creature on whose back a wall, a river, a gate of the dead are all one thing — ground. When the Æsir needed a road to the one place that has no road, they did not build one. They mounted the child of their own worst bargain, and he leapt.
sleipnir.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Sleipnir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᛚᛁᛒᚾᛁᛦ (s-l-i-p-n-i-R), the short-twig row merging e with i under ᛁ and p with b under ᛒ. No runic carving of the name is known; the manuscript spelling is the primary witness. Because the name is pure ASCII, no form of it is currently owned by the project: the plain-ASCII sleipnir.com is watched for release, and this temple claims nothing it does not hold.

sleipnir.archaeology: Sleipnir has the strongest material attestation of any horse in the corpus: the Gotland picture stones. The Tjängvide stone (Alskog parish) and Ardre VIII, carved in the eighth and ninth centuries, show an eight-legged horse bearing a rider toward a welcoming figure — an image the standard scholarship (Lindqvist; Simek s.v. Sleipnir) identifies as Óðinn carried by Sleipnir, centuries older than any written telling. No runic inscription names the horse, and no votive deposit can be tied to him — his cult, if any, was his master's. The textual witnesses are the Codex Regius and related codices of the Prose Edda for Gylfaginning 42 and 49, and the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Grímnismál and Sigrdrífumál.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], as in English 'stone'; Old Norse initial s is plain, never voiced.
Short high back rounded [u], as in English 'put', held brief — Old Norse short u, not the long ú.
The long (geminate) stop [tː] straddling the two syllables, held audibly as in modern Icelandic and Italian 'notte'.
Second short high back rounded [u], identical to the first — the name keeps its vowel uniform.
Velar nasal plus stop [ŋɡ] closing on a syllabic trill [r̩] — the nominative ending -r, sounded as a true r, not swallowed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SOOT-toongr' — two beats, the first stressed, the double t held a fraction long in the middle, and the final -r trilled as a syllable of its own, as in Icelandic Suttungur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Suttungr, son of the giant Gillingr, brother of Baugi and father of Gunnlöð; the name is attested only for this giant.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᚢᛏᛏᚢᚾᚴᚱ (normalized suttunkr), the Viking-Age runic rendering — the short-twig row writes t and d alike, and ᚴ covers both k and g.

kin.label: Manuscript Latin
